docs.text: Customize the admin ¶ A ModelAdmin states only what the model does not already say. Class attributes shape the list and the form; methods change behaviour; templates and themes change the look. # blog/adminsite.py from hinoki.admin import Admin , ModelAdmin , Tone , action from blog.models import Post site = Admin ( site = "Blog Studio" , per_page = 8 ) @site . admin ( Post ) class PostAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Post ]): columns = ( "title" , "published" , "author_id" , "created_at" ) search = ( "title" , "slug" ) readonly = ( "created_at" ,) badges = { "published" : { True : ( "Published" , Tone . OK ), False : ( "Draft" , Tone . WARN )}} tabs = ( "published" ,) # one tab per badge: Published | Draft fieldsets = { "Organization" : ( "author_id" , "published" )} @action ( confirm = "Publish the selected posts?" ) async def publish ( self , posts , principal ): await Post . filter ( id__in = [ p . id for p in posts ]) . aupdate ({ "published" : True }) Register a model ¶ @site.admin(Post) registers a ModelAdmin class for a model. site.register(...) takes a model class, which gets the default admin, or a ModelAdmin class that names its model with model= . The slug in the URL is the table name with dashes ( blog-posts ), or the class attribute slug = "posts" . Shape the list and the form ¶ Attribute Effect Default columns Columns of the list The model's fields search Columns the search box looks in The first three text columns the list shows readonly , exclude Shown but not editable; never shown () badges Value → Badge(label, tone, icon) or (label, tone[, icon]) Plain text tabs One tab per badge of the named column None fieldsets Fieldset s, or a dict of title → field names One group per_page , show_count Page size; row count in the sidebar The site's Admin(per_page=20, show_count=False) bulk_delete Offer bulk delete where can(principal, "delete") allows True Tone ( NEUTRAL , ACCENT , OK , WARN , DANGER , INFO ) is the color role of badges, stats and events. Without configuration the label and plural come from the model, the order from @db.ordered_by and the "last modified" line from its @db.timestamps() column. Search matches a row when any search column contains the typed text, compared case-insensitively as text (a number or date matches its printed form). Naming an exclude d column in search is refused at registration, because which rows match would reveal its value. Datetime fields use the app's settings.timezone (UTC without built-in settings): stored instants are shown there and edited datetime-local values are read there, then saved as UTC-aware datetimes. A time that does not exist or occurs twice during a daylight-saving change is refused for correction. Override behaviour ¶ Each method below is called by the framework; override what you need and call super() for the rest. # blog/adminsite.py from hinoki.admin import Avatar , ModelAdmin , Refusal from blog.models import Post @site . admin ( Post ) # the site created above class PostAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Post ]): def queryset ( self , principal ): # rows this caller sees, in every statement return Post . filter ( author_id = principal . user . id ) . select_related ( "author" ) def can ( self , principal , action , row = None ): # narrows a grant, never widens it if action == "delete" and row is not None and row . published : return False return super () . can ( principal , action , row ) def display ( self , row , column ): # a list cell: text, a Badge or an Avatar if column == "author_id" : return Avatar ( row . author . name ) return super () . display ( row , column ) async def check ( self , values , principal , row ): # {field: message} refuses if values . get ( "published" ) and not ( values . get ( "title" ) or ( row and row . title )): return { "title" : "A published post needs a title." } return {} async def remove ( self , row , principal ): if row . published : raise Refusal ( "Unpublish the post first." ) # shown on the page await super () . remove ( row , principal ) queryset(principal) decides which rows a caller sees; counts and pages come from it. can(principal, "view", row) then trims the fetched page, so a page may hold fewer rows than per_page . save(values, principal, row=None) and remove(row, principal) are the only places that write; run a domain operation there instead of a raw write. Refusal raised in either rolls the write back and shows its message. stats(principal) returns the dashboard Stat s for the model. Mass assignment, excluded columns and out-of-scope rows are refused by the framework. Add fields that are not columns ¶ extra_fields (or an extras() method, when the choices depend on what is registered) adds form fields that are not columns: Extra("password", "Password", "password") : a masked input, never filled in again. Extra("tags", "Tags", "choices", choices=(("a", "A"), ("b", "B"))) : checkboxes; the value is a frozenset of the checked ones. They reach check and save next to the columns, so save takes them out before writing the row; extra_initial(row) returns what the edit form shows. The Users section is built this way ( hinoki.admin.users.useradmin ). Add a bulk action ¶ Mark an async method with @action . The list shows the button once rows are selected: # blog/adminsite.py from typing import Any from hinoki import Caller from hinoki.admin import ModelAdmin , action from blog.models import Post @site . admin ( Post ) class PostAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Post ]): @action ( confirm = "Publish the selected posts?" ) async def publish ( self , posts : tuple [ Post , ... ], principal : Caller [ Any ]) -> None : ids = [ post . id for post in posts ] await Post . filter ( id__in = ids ) . aupdate ({ "published" : True }) The action name is the method name with _ written as - ; the label defaults to "Publish selected". view , add , change and delete are reserved. The name is also the permission checked by can(principal, name, row) . Every selected row is checked against the queryset and can before confirmation and again before execution; one denied row refuses the whole action. The action runs in the admin's write transaction with the selected rows locked, on at most 200 distinct rows (more answer 400 ). A failure rolls everything back; success redirects to the list with a notice. Handlers still apply their own domain conditions to writes that involve related records or external state. Replace the HTML or the stylesheet ¶ Admin(templates="admin_ui") reads admin_ui/components/NAME.html before the built-in component of the same name ( shell , sidebar , table , form , field , auth for the sign-in page, ...) and appends admin_ui/admin.css after the theme. Copy the built-in component from the package as a starting point; keep its {{ value }} (escaped) and {{{ raw }}} placeholders. /* admin_ui/admin.css */ . hn-auth-card { border-radius : 0 ; } . hn-nav-item [ aria-current = "page" ] { font-weight : 800 ; } Choose or build a theme ¶ Four built-in styles, each with light and dark modes; the system preference picks the initial mode and the toggle overrides it. Pick one with Admin(theme="bento") . Style Navigation List Edit Look Studio (default) Sidebar Cards with a table Drawer beside the list Soft violet, rounded Console Top bar Dense monospaced grid Drawer Neon cyan and teal, square Paper Quiet text index, centred column Document rows Own page Serif type, terracotta Bento Icon rail (bottom tab bar on phones) Grid of cards Own page Ink outlines, offset shadows, yellow accent Studio Console Paper Bento A Theme is a set of --hn-* design tokens for both schemes, plus edit ( "drawer" , "page" ), layout ( "sidebar" , "topbar" , "index" , "rail" ) and list_style ( "table" , "rows" , "cards" ). Start from a built-in one: # blog/adminsite.py import dataclasses from hinoki.admin import THEMES , Admin studio = THEMES [ "studio" ] forest = dataclasses . replace ( studio , name = "forest" , label = "Forest" , light = { ** studio . light , "accent" : "#1f6f50" , "accent-hover" : "#17543c" }, dark = { ** studio . dark , "accent" : "#5cc79b" , "accent-hover" : "#7ad6b0" }, layout = "topbar" , extra_css = ".hn-brand-text strong { letter-spacing: .04em; }" , ) site = Admin ( theme = forest ) extra_css is appended after the tokens; default_mode="dark" starts dark until the user switches. The text and surface colour pairs of the built-in themes are tested against WCAG AA contrast. Bento was checked in Chromium and Firefox at 1440, 390, 360 and 320 px; WebKit was not run. Errors and edge cases ¶ All of these fail when the Admin is created or the model registered, not on a request: Mistake Error A ModelAdmin naming a different model than the one registered RegistrationError search naming an exclude d column RegistrationError A bulk action named view , add , change or delete RegistrationError A template file that is not a component, an unknown placeholder, {{ }} changed to {{{ }}} , or a form , table , confirm or auth override without {{ csrf }} TemplateError A theme with a missing token, unknown layout or bad name ValueError from the Theme , before any page is served See also ¶ Add an admin Define models Admin API reference

docs.text: Add an admin ¶ hinoki.admin gives staff a list, search, create, edit, bulk actions and a dashboard for your models, behind its own sign-in page, users and per-model permissions. It ships with the framework; nothing is served until you include it, and importing it never touches a database. # blog/adminsite.py from hinoki.admin import Admin , ModelAdmin , Tone from blog.models import Post , User site = Admin ( site = "Blog Studio" ) @site . admin ( Post ) class PostAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Post ]): columns = ( "title" , "published" , "author_id" , "created_at" ) readonly = ( "created_at" ,) badges = { "published" : { True : ( "Published" , Tone . OK ), False : ( "Draft" , Tone . WARN )}} site . register ( User ) # a model with the default admin # blog/routes.py from hinoki import Includable , Mount from blog.adminsite import site routes : list [ Includable ] = [ Mount ( "/admin" , site )] The Blog example builds a fuller site the same way, with a theme, links, a dashboard and activity. Create the admin's tables ¶ The admin keeps its users in four tables of your database. Register them as an app, apply the migrations, then create the first user: hinoki app add admin --models hinoki.admin.users.models --migrations hinoki.admin.users.migrations hinoki migrations apply admin hinoki admin create-superuser alice # asks for the password twice Table Migration Holds hinoki_admin_users 0001-initial Username, Argon2id password hash, active and superuser flags, last sign-in hinoki_admin_sessions 0001-initial The SHA-256 of each session token, its user, expiry and last request hinoki_admin_grants 0001-initial One row per user, model and action hinoki_admin_login_windows 0002-login-windows Sign-in attempts per client, read only by DatabaseLoginWindow Every other user is created from the admin's Users section. hinoki admin set-password alice resets a password from a shell; both commands are described in hinoki admin . Set the signing secret ¶ The admin signs its forms and cookies with admin.secret from the app's settings. Give it at least 32 random bytes through the environment: export BLOG_ADMIN__SECRET = " $( python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(48))' ) " Setting Default Meaning admin.secret none Signing key, at least 32 bytes admin.session_hours 12 A session ends this long after sign-in admin.idle_minutes 120 A session ends after this long without a request admin.min_password_length 12 Shortest password accepted admin.theme none Built-in theme ( studio , console , paper , bento ) for an Admin that sets no theme= ; studio when neither is set Admin(secret=...) overrides the secret and Admin(theme=...) the theme for one site. An admin with neither stops the app at startup. Who may sign in ¶ Admin() without access= uses its own users: A superuser holds every permission. Other users hold grants per model and action: view , add , change , delete . A bulk action needs change . A model without a grant is missing from the sidebar, and its pages answer 404 . Grants wrap each model admin's can : an override can narrow what a grant allows, never widen it. An inactive user cannot sign in. To use your own identity instead (single sign-on, an existing user table), pass an access policy: Admin(access=Access(auth=..., permissions=[...])) . The admin then has no sign-in pages and no tables, and your callers' permissions decide what ModelAdmin.can allows. See authentication and access . The sign-in page ¶ login shows a card titled Sign in with a username and a password field. Every page of the admin redirects there ( 303 ) when the browser has no valid session. Request Answer POST login , correct credentials 303 to the admin root with a new session cookie; any previous session token is closed, never reused POST login , wrong username or password 401 "Wrong username or password." POST login , expired or forged form 403 "The form expired or is invalid. Reload and try again." POST login , too many attempts 429 (see limit sign-in attempts ) GET login while signed in 303 to the admin root POST logout 303 to login ; the session ends and its cookie is cleared Usernames are stored in lower case: 1 to 150 letters, digits and . _ @ + - , starting with a letter or digit. An unknown username costs the same hashing work as a wrong password and gets the same answer. password changes the signed-in user's password. The form asks for the current password, a new one (at least admin.min_password_length characters) and the new one again. A wrong current password, two different new ones or a password that breaks the length rule answer 422 with the reason on the form; an expired form answers 403 . Success ends every other session of the user and redirects ( 303 ) to the admin root ( ?done=password ) with a new session. Sessions and cookies ¶ The session is a random token in the hinoki_admin_session cookie: HttpOnly , SameSite=Lax , scoped to the admin's path. The database stores only its SHA-256, so a copy of the table cannot be replayed. Every form carries a signed CSRF token that must equal the SameSite=Strict hinoki_csrf cookie. On the sign-in form the token is signed for signing in; on every other form it is bound to the signed-in user. A form is also refused when the browser marks it as sent from another site ( Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site or same-site ) or its Origin header names another host; a request without these headers relies on the token alone. Cookies are Secure on HTTPS. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, set server.trusted_proxies so the forwarded scheme is believed, or pass Admin(secure_cookies=True) : cookies are then always Secure and named __Secure-hinoki_admin_session and __Secure-hinoki_csrf , so a sibling site cannot plant them. Changing the option signs everyone out once. A session ends after admin.session_hours , after admin.idle_minutes without a request, on sign-out, on a password change and when its user is deactivated. Reactivating a user never revives an old session. Manage users ¶ A superuser sees a Users section in the sidebar: create a user, choose the models and actions it may use, rename, deactivate, change a password or delete. Only a superuser opens it. No grant does, because a user who could edit users could grant itself everything. The permission checkboxes list view , add , change and delete for each registered model. An empty password on edit keeps the current one. A new one signs the user out everywhere. Passwords are never written back into the page. You cannot deactivate yourself, remove your own superuser status or delete yourself. Every write checks that an active superuser remains; hinoki admin create-superuser recovers if two superusers demote each other at the same instant. Deleting a user removes its sessions and grants. Admin(users=AdminAccounts(), manage_users=False) leaves the section out, for a site whose users are created another way. AdminAccounts.set_active(user, False) deactivates a user from code and ends its sessions. Limit sign-in attempts ¶ The sign-in and password forms pass through a rate limit policy before any password is hashed, and hold no database connection while hashing. Policy Counts in Behaviour LoginWindow(limit=10, window=60) (default) One worker's memory Each worker counts on its own and forgets on restart: a brake, not a shared limit. Holds at most 10,000 clients and drops the oldest. DatabaseLoginWindow(limit=10, window=60) hinoki_admin_login_windows One limit for every worker and host. Clients are stored as SHA-256 digests; expired windows are deleted on each attempt. # blog/adminsite.py from hinoki.admin import Admin from hinoki.admin.users import AdminAccounts from hinoki.admin.users.limits import DatabaseLoginWindow site = Admin ( users = AdminAccounts ( login_limit = DatabaseLoginWindow ())) Both count one window per client address; an IPv6 address counts by its /64. Requests without a known address share one window ten times as large, so set server.trusted_proxies behind a proxy. With DatabaseLoginWindow , keep host clocks in sync: each host stamps the windows it opens. Any other policy works too; see rate limit an action . Serve it under another path ¶ The Mount prefix decides where the admin lives; links, assets and the cookie path follow it. Mount("/ops", site) serves it at /ops . Admin(prefix="/staff") adds a path of its own after the mount ( /ops/staff ). An admin included without a Mount is served at /admin . Errors and edge cases ¶ When What fails Startup, no admin.secret and no secret= RegistrationError : "admin: no secret to sign its forms with; set admin.secret …" Admin(access=..., users=...) ValueError : pass one or the other register of AdminUser , AdminSession or AdminGrant RegistrationError : a plain model admin would show password hashes and let a grant holder promote itself register with a slug that is taken or reserved ( static , search , login , logout , password ) RegistrationError DatabaseLoginWindow before 0002-login-windows is applied The first sign-in attempt fails on the missing table; apply the migration first One address racing many sign-ins at the same instant 429 rather than an uncounted attempt See also ¶ Customize the admin hinoki admin commands Authentication and access Settings

POST login , too many attempts 429 (see limit sign-in attempts ) GET login while signed in 303 to the admin root POST logout 303 to login ; the session ends and its cookie is cleared Usernames are stored in lower case: 1 to 150 letters, digits and . _ @ + - , starting with a letter or digit. An unknown username costs the same hashing work as a wrong password and gets the same answer. password changes the signed-in user's password. The form asks for the current password, a new one (at least admin.min_password_length characters) and the new one again. A wrong current password, two different new ones or a password that breaks the length rule answer 422 with the reason on the form; an expired form answers 403 . Success ends every other session of the user and redirects ( 303 ) to the admin root ( ?done=password ) with a new session.
docs.title: The sign-in page

docs.text: The session is a random token in the hinoki_admin_session cookie: HttpOnly , SameSite=Lax , scoped to the admin's path. The database stores only its SHA-256, so a copy of the table cannot be replayed. Every form carries a signed CSRF token that must equal the SameSite=Strict hinoki_csrf cookie. On the sign-in form the token is signed for signing in; on every other form it is bound to the signed-in user. A form is also refused when the browser marks it as sent from another site ( Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site or same-site ) or its Origin header names another host; a request without these headers relies on the token alone. Cookies are Secure on HTTPS. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, set server.trusted_proxies so the forwarded scheme is believed, or pass Admin(secure_cookies=True) : cookies are then always Secure and named __Secure-hinoki_admin_session and __Secure-hinoki_csrf , so a sibling site cannot plant them. Changing the option signs everyone out once. A session ends after admin.session_hours , after admin.idle_minutes without a request, on sign-out, on a password change and when its user is deactivated. Reactivating a user never revives an old session.
docs.title: Sessions and cookies

docs.text: A superuser sees a Users section in the sidebar: create a user, choose the models and actions it may use, rename, deactivate, change a password or delete. Only a superuser opens it. No grant does, because a user who could edit users could grant itself everything. The permission checkboxes list view , add , change and delete for each registered model. An empty password on edit keeps the current one. A new one signs the user out everywhere. Passwords are never written back into the page. You cannot deactivate yourself, remove your own superuser status or delete yourself. Every write checks that an active superuser remains; hinoki admin create-superuser recovers if two superusers demote each other at the same instant. Deleting a user removes its sessions and grants. Admin(users=AdminAccounts(), manage_users=False) leaves the section out, for a site whose users are created another way. AdminAccounts.set_active(user, False) deactivates a user from code and ends its sessions.
docs.title: Manage users

docs.text: The sign-in and password forms pass through a rate limit policy before any password is hashed, and hold no database connection while hashing. Policy Counts in Behaviour LoginWindow(limit=10, window=60) (default) One worker's memory Each worker counts on its own and forgets on restart: a brake, not a shared limit. Holds at most 10,000 clients and drops the oldest. DatabaseLoginWindow(limit=10, window=60) hinoki_admin_login_windows One limit for every worker and host. Clients are stored as SHA-256 digests; expired windows are deleted on each attempt. # blog/adminsite.py from hinoki.admin import Admin from hinoki.admin.users import AdminAccounts from hinoki.admin.users.limits import DatabaseLoginWindow site = Admin ( users = AdminAccounts ( login_limit = DatabaseLoginWindow ())) Both count one window per client address; an IPv6 address counts by its /64. Requests without a known address share one window ten times as large, so set server.trusted_proxies behind a proxy. With DatabaseLoginWindow , keep host clocks in sync: each host stamps the windows it opens. Any other policy works too; see rate limit an action .
docs.title: Limit sign-in attempts

docs.text: The Mount prefix decides where the admin lives; links, assets and the cookie path follow it. Mount("/ops", site) serves it at /ops . Admin(prefix="/staff") adds a path of its own after the mount ( /ops/staff ). An admin included without a Mount is served at /admin .

docs.text: Build with a coding agent ¶ A project made by hinoki new is ready for a coding agent: rules already on, an AGENTS.md with the conventions, and an MCP server that describes the app. This page shows the loop and where the agent's authority ends. hinoki new shop # asks for the directory, database, server, agent files, skills, git and uv sync cd shop uv sync # unless you answered yes to uv sync uv run pytest uv run hinoki check The generated tests pass and hinoki check exits 0; this repository's own test suite generates a project and runs both on every change. What the project contains ¶ File Purpose AGENTS.md Commands, conventions and where the agent's authority ends; CLAUDE.md points to it rules.py Eight rules on from the start (below); the model rules HNK-DB-001 and HNK-DB-002 commented out until the first model exists, because a model rule that matches no model fails .mcp.json Starts the development MCP hinoki-rules.toml The owner's waivers Rule Promise HNK-ACC-001 , HNK-ACC-002 Every action names an access policy and a permission HNK-API-001 , HNK-API-002 Responses are concrete Schema types HNK-API-003 Lists are paginated HNK-TXN-001 Writes run in a transaction HNK-SCH-001 Fields such as password_hash never appear in a response Schema HNK-SCH-002 Request text has a length limit AGENTS.md states the same conventions as structure an application : public only on purpose, atomic=True for writes, Schema classes in responses, explicit relation loading, server values win on create, migrations as reviewed SQL. Give the agent tools ¶ The development MCP lets the agent read the real registry, rules and models, explain one action or error code, check the project and draft a model. It never writes source code, rules or waivers; only run_scenario , when you enable it, runs real handlers. See development MCP . Skills (optional): hinoki skills install writes four playbooks under .claude/skills/ : hinoki-add-endpoint , hinoki-fix-rule , hinoki-review-api and hinoki-test-api . Each names the MCP tool or command to run and what belongs to the owner. See hinoki skills . Errors that say what to do : validation errors list every problem with a path and a stable code, and a registration error names the action and parameter. The loop ¶ The agent reads the project with inspect_project . It makes one small change: a model, a Schema , an action. It runs pytest , ruff , mypy and hinoki check . A violation is a stable rule ID, a location and an explanation; the fix is a code change. Waivers are the owner's decision. hinoki-rules.toml is read by the tools, never written, and a waiver needs a reason, an owner and a bounded target. An agent that edits it to pass a check breaks AGENTS.md ; the framework cannot stop someone with write access, but the change is visible in review. Put the file under CODEOWNERS . Check a change against clients ¶ hinoki openapi --output openapi-baseline.json hinoki openapi --breaking-against openapi-baseline.json Take the baseline from the released version. The second command exits 1 and lists each change that breaks an existing client: removed operations or response fields, new required input, narrowed enums, changed types. See hinoki openapi . Generate request bodies ¶ request_cases reads an OpenAPI document and returns one RequestCase per operation with a JSON body: method , path , a valid body , and invalid , a list of (description, body) pairs that each break one constraint. # tests/bodiestest.py from hinoki.ai.samples import request_cases from shop.main import app CASES = request_cases ( app . openapi ()) # one per operation with a JSON body Parametrize a test over CASES : send case.body and expect a 2xx , then send each body in case.invalid and expect 422 . It raises CannotSample for a schema it cannot build a value for, such as a regular-expression pattern. Fill path parameters with real values before sending, and use a disposable database. Limits ¶ The development MCP describes and checks a project. To let an agent use a running app, expose selected actions over MCP . Rules check declarations, not what a function body does. Import rules read the project's own files and report dynamic imports as unverifiable. propose_model is a starting point: owner scoping, pagination and unique_together , but no business rules, state transitions or other relations. This workflow was verified by generating a project and running its tests and check , and by one fresh agent adding an owner-scoped resource from AGENTS.md alone. One run by one agent is evidence, not a benchmark. See also ¶ Development MCP Rules Structure an application

docs.text: Expose actions over MCP ¶ expose_as_mcp publishes selected HTTP actions as tools for a remote MCP client. Each tool call is dispatched through the app like an HTTP request, so the action's authentication, access policy, validation and transaction still apply. # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.ai.mcpapp import expose_as_mcp from notes.rules import project_rules from notes.security import billing_staff from notes.settings import ProjectSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , title = "Notes" , openapi_url = "/openapi.json" , docs_url = "/docs" , rules = project_rules , ) mcp = expose_as_mcp ( app , tools = [ "notes.apps.billing.api.list_invoices" ], access = billing_staff , ) app . include ( * mcp ) # POST /mcp Hinoki(...) has already included the routes listed in hinoki.toml ; expose_as_mcp selects among those, so call it after the app exists. Choose the tools ¶ tools are fnmatch patterns over qualified action names, the same names rules match: module.function , or module.Class.method for an action of an API class. "notes.apps.billing.api.*" selects every action of that module. Generated CRUD actions are named after the module that declares the crud(...) value ( notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.list , see Generated CRUD ), so a module pattern selects them too. Only GET , HEAD and QUERY actions are exposed by default. A QUERY tool takes the request body as its input. allow_writes=True also exposes POST , PUT , PATCH and DELETE actions. Use it only when write tools are intended and access permits them. The tool name, description, path and query parameters and JSON body shape come from the action's OpenAPI operation. Unknown arguments are rejected and path values are encoded as path segments. The MCP route never exposes itself. Protect the endpoint ¶ access is required. An intentionally public endpoint says so twice: access=None, public=True . Prefer bearer credentials for a remote client; cookie authentication with write tools needs particular care. The endpoint accepts JSON POST requests. Set allowed_origins to the exact browser origins when browser clients are expected; other cross-site browser requests are refused. Tool output is capped at 100,000 bytes (longer text is cut and marked truncated ); a request message over 1,000,000 bytes answers 413 . Errors and edge cases ¶ When What happens tools=[] ExposureError at the call access=None without public=True ExposureError A pattern matches no included action, or the action is not in the OpenAPI document ExposureError naming it Transactions.require_atomic() is enabled The MCP endpoint is a POST without a transaction of its own; exclude it with except_=["hinoki.ai.mcpapp.*"] . Each tool call still runs the action's own transaction. The endpoint does not provide MCP resources, prompts, sessions or OAuth discovery. See also ¶ Development MCP : a local server that describes the project to coding agents Authentication and access Rules

docs.text: Protect endpoints with authentication and access ¶ Every endpoint is public until you attach an Access policy. A policy pairs an authentication provider (how a request proves who it is) with the permissions an action needs. Write both once and name the policy on each private action. # blog/security.py from hinoki import Access , BearerAuth , Caller , Permission from .models import User class BlogPermission ( Permission ): WRITE = "posts:write" class TokenAuth ( BearerAuth [ User ]): """Looks the token up in ``blog_users``; editors get the write scope.""" async def resolve_token ( self , token : str ) -> Caller [ User ] | None : user = await User . aget_or_none ( token = token ) if user is None : return None scopes = frozenset ({ BlogPermission . WRITE }) if user . is_editor else frozenset () return Caller ( id = str ( user . id ), user = user , permissions = scopes ) auth = TokenAuth () editor = Access ( auth = auth , permissions = [ BlogPermission . WRITE ]) reader = Access ( auth = auth ) This is the Blog example's security module . Name your permissions ¶ Subclass Permission , an empty string enum, and use its members in policies and callers. Access and Caller store each permission as its string value, so BlogPermission.WRITE and "posts:write" match each other in checks, reprs and logs; plain strings are still accepted. Passing one string instead of a collection ( permissions="posts:write" ) is a TypeError . Define a provider ¶ Pick the base class for where the credential travels and implement one hook: Base class Credential Implement BearerAuth[User] Authorization: Bearer <token> resolve_token(token) APIKeyAuth[User] the x-api-key header resolve(value) HeaderAuth[User] the header named by header resolve(value) The hook returns a Caller with a stable id , your user object and its permissions, or None when the credential is unknown. It may be async def or def ; a synchronous hook runs on the bounded sync executor, so it may use blocking libraries. Attach a policy ¶ Name the policy with access= on the HTTP decorator and annotate a Caller[User] parameter to receive the authenticated caller: # blog/drafts.py from hinoki import Caller , http from .models import Post , User from .schemas import PostCreate , PostOut from .security import editor @http . post ( "/drafts" , status = 201 , access = editor , atomic = True ) async def create_draft ( data : PostCreate , caller : Caller [ User ]) -> PostOut : post = await Post . acreate ( data , author_id = caller . user . id ) return PostOut . from_model ( post , author_name = caller . user . name ) Take the owner from caller.user , never from the request body. Permissions say what a caller may do; whether a given row is theirs is still your query (the Blog's owned_post helper shows one way). To protect a whole group, set the policy once on a RouteGroup ( RouteGroup("/invoices", access=billing_staff) ); an action may override it, and access=None makes one action public on purpose. What clients receive ¶ Request Answer No credential 401 with a WWW-Authenticate challenge A credential the hook rejects (returns None ), or a value that is not Bearer <token> 401 with the challenge A valid caller without a required permission 403 A policy without permissions ( reader above) any authenticated caller passes A policy without permissions is legitimate ("any signed-in user"), and it is easy to write by accident; the rule HNK-ACC-002 asks you to list such actions explicitly. Hash passwords ¶ hinoki.crypto.PasswordHasher hashes and verifies with Argon2id in Rust, off the event loop. Create it where you own its lifetime (a factory or a module) and call close() at shutdown. # blog/passwords.py from hinoki.crypto import PasswordHasher hasher = PasswordHasher () async def change_password ( new_password : str ) -> str : return await hasher . hash ( new_password ) async def password_matches ( password : str , stored : str ) -> bool : return await hasher . verify ( password , stored ) hash_sync and verify_sync exist for scripts and seeds; needs_rehash(stored) tells you when to rehash after a parameter change, and random_token() returns a URL-safe random token for opaque credentials. When the hashing queue is full, the hasher raises HashingBusy , a 503 . The Blog's accounts module shows a complete login with constant-time behaviour for unknown users. Verify JSON Web Tokens ¶ Subclass JWTAuth[User] , list the keys and implement resolve_claims , which turns verified claims into a Caller (or None ). Read secrets from a settings.Secret field and reveal them only when you build the provider. For JWTAuth , Rust verifies the signature and registered claims using the current key snapshot. now() and the configured issuer, audience, leeway (0 to 120 seconds; a provider with another value fails when it is built) and expiry policy are read for each verification. A request already verifying with a captured key snapshot finishes with that snapshot; a later verification observes key rotation. Rust does not turn token claims into a Caller : the application's resolve_claims hook still runs for every valid token, and remains responsible for loading or rejecting the identity and deciding its permissions. Sync, async and sync functions returning awaitables follow the normal hook execution path. Claims-only tokens on the native lane ¶ ClaimsJWTAuth is a JWTAuth whose caller comes from the token alone: sub (a non-empty string) becomes Caller.id , the claim named by scope_claim (default scopes , a list of strings) becomes the permissions, and Caller.user is None . No database lookup happens, so a token cannot be revoked before it expires: keep lifetimes short. # notes/tokens.py from collections.abc import Sequence from typing import ClassVar from hinoki import Access , Caller , Permission , Schema , http from hinoki.crypto import ClaimsJWTAuth , JWTKey class NotesPermission ( Permission ): WRITE = "notes:write" class Tokens ( ClaimsJWTAuth ): keys : ClassVar [ Sequence [ JWTKey ]] = ( JWTKey ( "2026-11" , "HS256" , b "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef" ), ) # read the key from a Secret in a real application issuer = "https://api.example.com" audience = "notes" class WhoAmI ( Schema ): id : str permissions : list [ str ] tokens = Tokens () writer = Access ( auth = tokens , permissions = [ NotesPermission . WRITE ]) @http . get ( "/me" , access = writer ) async def me ( caller : Caller [ None ]) -> WhoAmI : return WhoAmI ( id = caller . id , permissions = sorted ( caller . permissions )) tokens.issue({"sub": "u1", "scopes": ["notes:write"]}, ttl=900) signs with the first key that can sign and sets iat , exp , and iss / aud when configured. The policies of the billing examples ¶ The endpoint, CRUD and transaction guides import billing_staff and billing_admin from one module. Declare the policies once and import them wherever an action or RouteGroup names them: # notes/security.py from collections.abc import Sequence from typing import ClassVar from hinoki import Access , Permission from hinoki.crypto import ClaimsJWTAuth , JWTKey class BillingPermission ( Permission ): MANAGE = "billing:manage" ADMIN = "billing:admin" class StaffTokens ( ClaimsJWTAuth ): keys : ClassVar [ Sequence [ JWTKey ]] = ( JWTKey ( "2026-11" , "HS256" , b "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef" ), ) # read the key from a Secret in a real application tokens = StaffTokens () billing_staff = Access ( auth = tokens , permissions = [ BillingPermission . MANAGE ]) billing_admin = Access ( auth = tokens , permissions = [ BillingPermission . ADMIN ]) A token from tokens.issue({"sub": "u1", "scopes": ["billing:manage"]}, ttl=900) passes billing_staff ; without a token the answer is 401 , and with a token that lacks the permission it is 403 . Generated CRUD routes protected by an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth can run on the native lane. Rust only admits requests: a single Authorization: Bearer <token> header whose token verifies (signature, expiry, issuer, audience, sub ) and carries every required permission goes straight to the native action. Every other request, including a missing, malformed, expired, forged or under-privileged one, is handed to the Python pipeline, which answers exactly as it does without the native lane ( 401 with the challenge, or 403 ). With owner and identity_key = caller_id , create, update and delete are native too: Rust sets the owner column from sub , and update/delete are constrained to rows that sub owns. Foreign or missing rows, and MySQL/MariaDB, are answered by the Python pipeline. A subclass that overrides a method, a modified instance, or any other auth class keeps the route on Python. The route's key, issuer, audience, leeway and permission snapshot is rechecked about once per second; reassigning them disarms the native plan until the worker restarts, so a rotation reaches native routes after that interval, not per verification. hinoki routes --lanes shows which lane each route uses. Rust verifies the token on these routes too: a handler route protected by an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth (not generated CRUD) is authenticated by Rust, which admits the caller or answers 401 or 403 itself with the same body and WWW-Authenticate challenge as Python, in the same order relative to path/query errors, the rate limit and body validation. Rust defers to Python for anything it cannot decide identically: several Authorization headers, a value that is not a plain Bearer <token> , or a request Rust already found malformed. A rate limit still runs afterwards in Python, with the admitted caller. Error handlers registered with app.errors do not apply to these answers, on either path, because they translate other exceptions. The provider and policy are checked about once per second as for CRUD routes. Errors and edge cases ¶ Return None for an unknown credential; let unexpected exceptions propagate, they are server errors, not 401 . JWTAuth leeway must be 0–120 seconds; another value fails when the provider is built. Providers hold no per-request state: one instance serves every request and worker thread. Hinoki does not create users, sessions or permission rules: those remain your application's data and policy. See also ¶ Rules : make "every private action has a policy" a checked promise. docs.text: Pick the base class for where the credential travels and implement one hook: Base class Credential Implement BearerAuth[User] Authorization: Bearer <token> resolve_token(token) APIKeyAuth[User] the x-api-key header resolve(value) HeaderAuth[User] the header named by header resolve(value) The hook returns a Caller with a stable id , your user object and its permissions, or None when the credential is unknown. It may be async def or def ; a synchronous hook runs on the bounded sync executor, so it may use blocking libraries.
docs.title: Define a provider

docs.text: Name the policy with access= on the HTTP decorator and annotate a Caller[User] parameter to receive the authenticated caller: # blog/drafts.py from hinoki import Caller , http from .models import Post , User from .schemas import PostCreate , PostOut from .security import editor @http . post ( "/drafts" , status = 201 , access = editor , atomic = True ) async def create_draft ( data : PostCreate , caller : Caller [ User ]) -> PostOut : post = await Post . acreate ( data , author_id = caller . user . id ) return PostOut . from_model ( post , author_name = caller . user . name ) Take the owner from caller.user , never from the request body. Permissions say what a caller may do; whether a given row is theirs is still your query (the Blog's owned_post helper shows one way). To protect a whole group, set the policy once on a RouteGroup ( RouteGroup("/invoices", access=billing_staff) ); an action may override it, and access=None makes one action public on purpose.
docs.title: Attach a policy

docs.text: Request Answer No credential 401 with a WWW-Authenticate challenge A credential the hook rejects (returns None ), or a value that is not Bearer <token> 401 with the challenge A valid caller without a required permission 403 A policy without permissions ( reader above) any authenticated caller passes A policy without permissions is legitimate ("any signed-in user"), and it is easy to write by accident; the rule HNK-ACC-002 asks you to list such actions explicitly.
docs.title: What clients receive

docs.text: hinoki.crypto.PasswordHasher hashes and verifies with Argon2id in Rust, off the event loop. Create it where you own its lifetime (a factory or a module) and call close() at shutdown. # blog/passwords.py from hinoki.crypto import PasswordHasher hasher = PasswordHasher () async def change_password ( new_password : str ) -> str : return await hasher . hash ( new_password ) async def password_matches ( password : str , stored : str ) -> bool : return await hasher . verify ( password , stored ) hash_sync and verify_sync exist for scripts and seeds; needs_rehash(stored) tells you when to rehash after a parameter change, and random_token() returns a URL-safe random token for opaque credentials. When the hashing queue is full, the hasher raises HashingBusy , a 503 . The Blog's accounts module shows a complete login with constant-time behaviour for unknown users.
docs.title: Hash passwords

docs.text: Subclass JWTAuth[User] , list the keys and implement resolve_claims , which turns verified claims into a Caller (or None ). Read secrets from a settings.Secret field and reveal them only when you build the provider. For JWTAuth , Rust verifies the signature and registered claims using the current key snapshot. now() and the configured issuer, audience, leeway (0 to 120 seconds; a provider with another value fails when it is built) and expiry policy are read for each verification. A request already verifying with a captured key snapshot finishes with that snapshot; a later verification observes key rotation. Rust does not turn token claims into a Caller : the application's resolve_claims hook still runs for every valid token, and remains responsible for loading or rejecting the identity and deciding its permissions. Sync, async and sync functions returning awaitables follow the normal hook execution path.
docs.title: Verify JSON Web Tokens

docs.text: ClaimsJWTAuth is a JWTAuth whose caller comes from the token alone: sub (a non-empty string) becomes Caller.id , the claim named by scope_claim (default scopes , a list of strings) becomes the permissions, and Caller.user is None . No database lookup happens, so a token cannot be revoked before it expires: keep lifetimes short. # notes/tokens.py from collections.abc import Sequence from typing import ClassVar from hinoki import Access , Caller , Permission , Schema , http from hinoki.crypto import ClaimsJWTAuth , JWTKey class NotesPermission ( Permission ): WRITE = "notes:write" class Tokens ( ClaimsJWTAuth ): keys : ClassVar [ Sequence [ JWTKey ]] = ( JWTKey ( "2026-11" , "HS256" , b "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef" ), ) # read the key from a Secret in a real application issuer = "https://api.example.com" audience = "notes" class WhoAmI ( Schema ): id : str permissions : list [ str ] tokens = Tokens () writer = Access ( auth = tokens , permissions = [ NotesPermission . WRITE ]) @http . get ( "/me" , access = writer ) async def me ( caller : Caller [ None ]) -> WhoAmI : return WhoAmI ( id = caller . id , permissions = sorted ( caller . permissions )) tokens.issue({"sub": "u1", "scopes": ["notes:write"]}, ttl=900) signs with the first key that can sign and sets iat , exp , and iss / aud when configured.
docs.title: Claims-only tokens on the native lane

docs.text: The endpoint, CRUD and transaction guides import billing_staff and billing_admin from one module. Declare the policies once and import them wherever an action or RouteGroup names them: # notes/security.py from collections.abc import Sequence from typing import ClassVar from hinoki import Access , Permission from hinoki.crypto import ClaimsJWTAuth , JWTKey class BillingPermission ( Permission ): MANAGE = "billing:manage" ADMIN = "billing:admin" class StaffTokens ( ClaimsJWTAuth ): keys : ClassVar [ Sequence [ JWTKey ]] = ( JWTKey ( "2026-11" , "HS256" , b "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef" ), ) # read the key from a Secret in a real application tokens = StaffTokens () billing_staff = Access ( auth = tokens , permissions = [ BillingPermission . MANAGE ]) billing_admin = Access ( auth = tokens , permissions = [ BillingPermission . ADMIN ]) A token from tokens.issue({"sub": "u1", "scopes": ["billing:manage"]}, ttl=900) passes billing_staff ; without a token the answer is 401 , and with a token that lacks the permission it is 403 . Generated CRUD routes protected by an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth can run on the native lane. Rust only admits requests: a single Authorization: Bearer <token> header whose token verifies (signature, expiry, issuer, audience, sub ) and carries every required permission goes straight to the native action. Every other request, including a missing, malformed, expired, forged or under-privileged one, is handed to the Python pipeline, which answers exactly as it does without the native lane ( 401 with the challenge, or 403 ). With owner and identity_key = caller_id , create, update and delete are native too: Rust sets the owner column from sub , and update/delete are constrained to rows that sub owns. Foreign or missing rows, and MySQL/MariaDB, are answered by the Python pipeline. A subclass that overrides a method, a modified instance, or any other auth class keeps the route on Python. The route's key, issuer, audience, leeway and permission snapshot is rechecked about once per second; reassigning them disarms the native plan until the worker restarts, so a rotation reaches native routes after that interval, not per verification. hinoki routes --lanes shows which lane each route uses. Rust verifies the token on these routes too: a handler route protected by an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth (not generated CRUD) is authenticated by Rust, which admits the caller or answers 401 or 403 itself with the same body and WWW-Authenticate challenge as Python, in the same order relative to path/query errors, the rate limit and body validation. Rust defers to Python for anything it cannot decide identically: several Authorization headers, a value that is not a plain Bearer <token> , or a request Rust already found malformed. A rate limit still runs afterwards in Python, with the admitted caller. Error handlers registered with app.errors do not apply to these answers, on either path, because they translate other exceptions. The provider and policy are checked about once per second as for CRUD routes.
docs.title: The policies of the billing examples

docs.text: Return None for an unknown credential; let unexpected exceptions propagate, they are server errors, not 401 . JWTAuth leeway must be 0–120 seconds; another value fails when the provider is built. Providers hold no per-request state: one instance serves every request and worker thread. Hinoki does not create users, sessions or permission rules: those remain your application's data and policy.

docs.text: Class-based APIs ¶ A class-based API is a subclass of API whose methods carry the same @http.* decorators as functions. A class adds a path prefix, inheritance and, with @crud(...) , generated routes with hooks. For ordinary endpoints prefer functions and a RouteGroup , which also states access, transactions and errors once. When to use it ¶ Use a class for Example Generated CRUD plus hooks or extra actions @crud(Invoice, ...) with get_queryset and a pay action Actions that several resources inherit or override A base API with a counts action, reused under two prefixes A resource you ship for other projects to include The admin A class that only puts three functions under a prefix gains nothing over a RouteGroup , and each of its actions must repeat access= , atomic= and errors= . A plain class ¶ # notes/apps/billing/reports.py from hinoki import API , Schema , http from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice class InvoiceCounts ( Schema ): open : int paid : int class Reports ( API , path = "/reports" ): @http . get ( "/counts" , access = billing_staff ) async def counts ( self ) -> InvoiceCounts : return InvoiceCounts ( open = await Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . acount (), paid = await Invoice . filter ( paid = True ) . acount (), ) path= is the class prefix; each action's path is relative to it, so this action is served at /billing/reports/counts once Reports is in routes.py . Inherit and override ¶ A subclass inherits every routed method. Members are resolved by name, most derived first: # notes/apps/billing/reports.py (continued) class ArchiveReports ( Reports , path = "/archive" ): # /archive/counts, own prefix pass class PublicReports ( Reports ): # inherits path="/reports" def counts ( self ) -> None : # redefined without a decorator: no route return None In the subclass Result Nothing The route is inherited, under the subclass's path= or the inherited one The same name with a decorator Replaces the inherited route The same name without a decorator Drops the inherited route Include only the classes you serve. A base and a subclass with the same prefix are two copies of every inherited route, and the application refuses the second. Generated CRUD with hooks ¶ @crud(...) generates list and retrieve, plus the writes you give a schema for, on a class whose only base is API . Hooks change what the generated actions do; any other decorated method is a handwritten action: # notes/apps/billing/api.py from typing import Any from uuid import UUID from hinoki import API , Caller , crud , errors , http from hinoki.orm import QuerySet from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut class InvoiceAlreadyPaid ( errors . Conflict ): code = "invoice_already_paid" message = "The invoice is already paid." @crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , access = billing_staff ) class Invoices ( API ): def get_queryset ( self , principal : Caller [ Any ] | None ) -> QuerySet [ Invoice ]: return Invoice . all () . order_by ( "reference" ) @http . post ( "/ {item_id} /pay" , access = billing_staff , atomic = True , errors = ( errors . NotFound , InvoiceAlreadyPaid ), ) async def pay ( self , item_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceOut : changed = await Invoice . aupdate_where ( { "id" : item_id , "paid" : False }, { "paid" : True } ) if not changed : await Invoice . aget ( id = item_id ) # 404 when it does not exist raise InvoiceAlreadyPaid () return InvoiceOut . from_model ( changed [ 0 ]) # notes/apps/billing/routes.py from hinoki import Includable from .api import Invoices routes : list [ Includable ] = [ Invoices ] Route Source Access GET /billing/invoices generated list (paginated) billing_staff GET /billing/invoices/{item_id} generated retrieve billing_staff POST /billing/invoices generated create ( create=InvoiceIn , atomic) billing_staff POST /billing/invoices/{item_id}/pay handwritten pay its own access= The access= of crud(...) covers generated actions only; a handwritten method states its own. pay changes the row only if it is still unpaid, in one statement, so two concurrent calls cannot both succeed. Hooks, CrudAccess , owner= and every keyword are in Generate CRUD routes . When a resource needs no code, crud(...) is a value, not a class: # notes/apps/billing/routes.py from hinoki import Includable , crud from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut routes : list [ Includable ] = [ crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , access = billing_staff , ), ] One instance per request ¶ Hinoki creates the class with no arguments for every request and calls the method on that instance. Keep self empty: Take request data as parameters: request: Request , caller: Caller[Staff] , path and body values. Reach worker resources through a module , never through attributes set on self or on the class. Do not define an __init__ that needs arguments. Hinoki refuses it when the class is included. A class that keeps the stock constructor and sets no response_headers is eligible for the native handler lane like a function. hinoki routes --lanes shows the choice per route. Best practices ¶ Use a class for @crud , inheritance or a shipped resource , functions otherwise. One base, API . A @crud class accepts no other base. Share configuration with a value ( staff_crud = functools.partial(crud, access=billing_staff) ) instead of a mixin. State access= , atomic= and errors= on every handwritten action. The class carries a path only. Scope writes in the statement ( aupdate_where with the conditions), not check-then-write. Hooks build queries. get_queryset does no I/O; load relations explicitly in to_schema or written_queryset . Let crud generate or omit, not compete. To write list or retrieve yourself, pass omit=("list",) and define a method with another name; to write create yourself, leave create= out. Test it ¶ # tests/invoicestest.py from notes.apps.billing.api import Invoices from notes.security import billing_staff def test_invoice_routes () -> None : routes = {( r . method , r . path ): r for r in Invoices . routes ()} pay = routes [ "POST" , "/invoices/ {item_id} /pay" ] assert ( pay . access , pay . atomic ) == ( billing_staff , True ) assert ( "GET" , "/invoices/ {item_id} " ) in routes Invoices.routes() lists the class routes with its own prefix, without an application. Request tests are the same as for functions: build Hinoki(include=[Mount("/billing", routes)]) and use ASGIClient ( function-based APIs , testing ). Pitfalls ¶ Symptom Cause Fix RegistrationError: … is created without arguments per request An __init__ with required arguments Remove it; take values as parameters RegistrationError on a @staticmethod or @classmethod route Routes are instance methods Drop the decorator and keep self RegistrationError: Invoices: a crud(...) class has exactly one base, API A mixin or another base Share a functools.partial(crud, ...) or Access values RegistrationError naming create (or list , …) A method named like an action crud generates Rename it, or stop generating that action ( omit= , no create= ) RegistrationError: … is declared by two classes (/a and /b) Two different classes (often two crud(...) values for one model in one module) give an action the same qualified name Rename one class, or pass crud(..., name="ArchiveCrud") A handwritten action is public crud(access=...) covers generated actions only Add access= to its decorator A route vanished in a subclass The method was redefined without a decorator Re-declare it with its decorator Old code uses replaces=Crud.CREATE An older way to swap a generated action Leave create= out and name the method freely; replaces= still works while create= is given

docs.text: Command line ¶ Every task in a Hinoki project has a hinoki command. Inside a project created by hinoki new , run them through uv run , which uses the project's locked environment: uv run hinoki dev uv run hinoki check uv run hinoki migrations apply Commands ¶ Group Command What it does Guide Start hinoki new [NAME] Create a project; asks for what the flags leave out, ending with "Create an app now?" ( --app NAME , --no-app ). Create a project hinoki app create\|add\|list Add an app, register an existing package, list the apps. below hinoki dev / serve Run with reload / run for production, on Kiso or Granian; --interface wsgi serves a WSGI callable. Serve hinoki shell Python shell with the app, its settings and models, top-level await . Shell Inspect hinoki check Run the architecture rules. Inspect hinoki doctor Environment, manifest and app diagnostics. Inspect hinoki routes Every route with its access policy and server lane. Inspect hinoki settings Effective settings and their sources, secrets redacted. Inspect hinoki openapi Print, write or diff the OpenAPI document. Inspect hinoki version The Hinoki version; --verbose adds Python, platform, native core and Granian. Inspect Data hinoki migrations plan\|status\|apply\|sql Plan and apply migrations for every registered app. below hinoki admin create-superuser\|set-password Manage admin users from the terminal. below Integrate hinoki mcp Serve project context to an AI agent over MCP. below hinoki skills list\|install Write the optional agent skills. below hinoki manage [COMMAND] Run a command your application defines. below hinoki completion SHELL Print a completion script. below Targets and short commands ¶ In a project, hinoki.toml names the application ( [project] application ), so commands take no target: hinoki dev , hinoki check , hinoki routes . To use another application, pass a target, module:attribute , imported from the current directory: hinoki dev notes.main:app . A function that returns an application ( module:create_app ) is also accepted, and hinoki settings also accepts a settings class. When a target does not import, run the command from the project root (where hinoki.toml is), check that the packages have __init__.py files and that the attribute name is right. The commands report error: cannot load notes.main:ap: ... and exit with a non-zero status. Help and completion ¶ hinoki --help lists the commands in groups (Start, Inspect, Data, Integrate); hinoki COMMAND --help shows one command's options. A mistyped command or migrations action gets a suggestion: hinoki: error: argument <command>: invalid choice: 'chek' (choose from 'check', ...) did you mean 'check'? The completion script is generated from the real parser, so it follows the commands and options of the installed version: eval " $( hinoki completion bash ) " # in ~/.bashrc eval " $( hinoki completion zsh ) " # in ~/.zshrc, after compinit hinoki completion fish | source # in ~/.config/fish/config.fish It completes command, subcommand and option names; it does not complete option values or project-specific names such as apps. Terminal output ¶ On a colour terminal, doctor , check and routes print a coloured report: a status glyph per check ( ✔ ok, ▲ warning, ✘ failed or violated, ? unverifiable, – skipped or waived) with the fix on its own line, and routes with coloured methods. The check summary is green only when the exit code is 0 . When output is piped or redirected, or with NO_COLOR or TERM=dumb , the text is plain and unchanged, and --format json is never styled. app ¶ The generated hinoki.toml registers no app unless hinoki new created one (the last question in a terminal, or --app NAME ): the project package keeps main.py , settings, rules and the health route, and models live in apps. Create each one with: uv run hinoki app create billing This creates NAME/apps/billing/{models.py,routes.py,migrations/} and registers the model, migration and routes modules in hinoki.toml ( routes = "NAME.apps.billing.routes:routes" , prefix = "/billing" ). Cross-app foreign keys require the referencing app to list the referenced app in requires in hinoki.toml ; migrations are then planned/applied in dependency order. The project registry is explicit: Hinoki does not scan arbitrary installed packages or run imports at install time. Both commands report hinoki.toml : hinoki new lists it among the generated files and app create says it registered the app there. --prefix and --requires (comma-separated) set the mount prefix and dependencies directly. In a terminal, app create asks for whatever is not given — the name, the prefix (default /NAME ) and, when other apps exist, requires — with the same prompts, Esc-to-cancel (exit 130, nothing created) and NO_COLOR handling as hinoki new . Without a terminal or with --no-input it never asks: the name is required (exit 2) and the defaults are /NAME and no requires . To register a package that already exists, name its modules. Nothing is created or imported; only hinoki.toml changes: uv run hinoki app add billing --models legacy.billing.models uv run hinoki app add invoices --models legacy.invoices.models --migrations legacy.db.invoices --routes legacy.invoices.routes:routes --prefix /invoices --requires billing --migrations defaults to the migrations package next to the models module ( legacy.billing.migrations ); a models module without a parent package needs it explicitly. --prefix defaults to /NAME once --routes is given. The whole manifest is validated before it is replaced, so a duplicate name, an unknown or cyclic --requires , or a malformed module name leaves hinoki.toml untouched and exits 2. Whether the modules import is checked later, when a command such as hinoki migrations plan loads the app. List the registered apps from the project root or any subdirectory: uv run hinoki app list uv run hinoki app list --format json The text output shows each app in dependency order with its model module, migration package, routes and prefix, and prerequisites. JSON contains the same fields under an apps key ( routes and prefix are empty strings for an app without routes). The command only reads and validates hinoki.toml : it does not import app modules, connect to a database or start the app. Without a manifest, it prints an error and exits 2. admin ¶ The admin's own users are managed from the admin itself, except the first one: uv run hinoki admin create-superuser ada # asks for the password twice, no echo printf '%s\n' " $ADA_PASSWORD " | uv run hinoki admin set-password ada --password-stdin A password is read from a terminal prompt or, with --password-stdin , from one line of standard input; it is never taken from the command line, where other users of the machine could read it, and it is never printed. Without a terminal and without the flag the command stops; with the flag on a terminal it still prompts without echo, and a line longer than a password can be is refused unread. Ctrl-C or Ctrl-D at the prompt exits with status 2 , and a refused connection is reported as such, naming the masked database and its source (status 1 ), not as missing tables. The database is chosen as for hinoki migrations : --database , HINOKI_DATABASE_URL , the project application's installed DatabaseModule or database setting, then the project's local SQLite; the command prints it on standard error as database: … (from …) , and stops with status 2 when the project's application or database cannot be resolved. The user tables must exist: register and apply them first ( hinoki app add admin ... , hinoki migrations apply admin , see who may sign in ); otherwise the command exits 1 and says so. Usernames are lower-cased; the shortest password is admin.min_password_length . Exit status is 0 on success, 2 for a refused input (a taken name, a weak or mistyped password, an unknown user). migrations ¶ In a project, migration modules come from hinoki.toml ; you never pass model or migration paths: uv run hinoki migrations plan --check uv run hinoki migrations plan billing --name add-invoice-index uv run hinoki migrations status uv run hinoki migrations apply uv run hinoki migrations sql 0001 -initial status and apply cover all registered apps in dependency order. Writing a plan in a multi-app project needs the app name ( plan billing , or --app billing ); read-only plan --check and plan --dry-run without an app cover every app in dependency order. sql searches every app; --app narrows it when two apps share a migration name. --name is optional for a focused plan: Hinoki derives a stable slug from the first planned schema change (for example, create-table-notes ); pass --name initial-notes to override it. All-app previews cannot use --name . Numbering is automatic. apply initializes the configured local SQLite database when no database is configured. In a manifest project the implicit .hinoki/local.sqlite3 file, and a relative SQLite path from the application's settings, are rooted beside hinoki.toml , even if you run the command from a subdirectory; relative SQLite URLs given with --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL remain relative to the current working directory. Added apps have separate migration ledger namespaces, so identical numbered filenames do not collide; a project whose root package was registered as an app (older scaffolds) retains its unprefixed migration keys. apply billing includes its declared prerequisite apps for migration application. plan --check fails CI (exit 1) when the models have changes that no migration file records, and exits 2 when the database it plans for cannot be resolved; it never connects to a database. In a project it imports the application to read its database unless --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL is set. Migration safety across apps, destructive changes and the ledger are explained in Migrations . Without a hinoki.toml , name the modules explicitly: hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations plan --models myapp.models --name add-index --dry-run hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations apply hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations sql 0001 -initial plan requires --models MODULE ; --name is an optional slug override and is derived from the first planned schema change when omitted. --dry-run prints operations without writing files. Destructive operations require --allow-destructive . plan/status/apply target --database , then HINOKI_DATABASE_URL , then the DatabaseModule or database setting of the project's application, then the local SQLite file at .hinoki/local.sqlite3 ( which database ); plan , status and apply print the chosen database and its source on standard error with the credentials masked, and stop with exit 2 when the project's application or database cannot be resolved. A URL given as an argument is visible in the process list and shell history, so keep a URL containing a password in the environment. When the connection fails, the command prints error: database: … with a fix: line and exits 1; the error itself does not repeat the URL. sql NAME prints a migration's SQL. Use a disposable database while reviewing migrations. On an animated terminal, plan and apply show a spinner while they work and finish with a timing line ( ✔ applied 1.2s ); the commands' own output is printed unchanged before it. Piped output, NO_COLOR , TERM=dumb , CI and HINOKI_ANIMATE=0 print only the commands' own output. mcp ¶ uv run hinoki mcp The development server uses MCP over stdio. It accepts --rules , repeatable --package , repeatable --models , and --waivers with the same target meanings as check . --rules defaults to the application's rules and --package to the package that contains it, as for hinoki check . --requests PATH names the file the recent_requests tool reads (default .hinoki/requests.jsonl ; see server.recent_requests ). --scenarios off|read|write controls whether run_scenario is registered: read allows GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and QUERY; write allows every supported method. Scenarios start the real app, run handlers and lifespan hooks, and may write data even for a GET. Keep the tool server owner-controlled and point the app at a disposable database. The development MCP is separate from application MCP, which is mounted with expose_as_mcp and an explicit action allowlist. See the development MCP guide for tool inputs and results. skills ¶ hinoki skills list hinoki skills install # from a project directory hinoki skills install --force # replace skills that already exist Agent skills are short Markdown playbooks that point an assistant at the real Hinoki tools (the development MCP and the CLI). list prints each skill name and description. install reads hinoki.toml , then writes .claude/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md for each one, with the project package name filled in; an existing file is kept and reported unless --force replaces it. Without a manifest it prints an error and exits 2 . hinoki new --skills writes the same files at creation. They are optional and never written otherwise. Skill Playbook hinoki-add-endpoint add an action with its Schema types, access policy and test hinoki-fix-rule fix a rule diagnostic without editing the rules or waivers hinoki-review-api run hinoki openapi --breaking-against before and after a change hinoki-test-api exercise operations with the generated valid and invalid bodies of hinoki.ai.samples.request_cases manage ¶ uv run hinoki manage --help uv run hinoki manage greet Peppe Commands are declared on the app with Hinoki(commands=[...]) . Each command subclasses hinoki.management.Command , gives itself a lower-case name, and adds arguments through add_arguments(parser) . In a scaffolded project, hinoki manage lists commands and hinoki manage greet Peppe runs one; the manifest's project.application supplies the app target. Outside a registered project, use hinoki manage TARGET COMMAND . --help after a command shows its arguments. # examples/project/app.py from argparse import ArgumentParser , Namespace from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.management import Command , CommandContext class Greet ( Command ): name = "greet" help = "print a greeting" def add_arguments ( self , parser : ArgumentParser ) -> None : parser . add_argument ( "name" , nargs = "?" , default = "world" ) def handle ( self , _context : CommandContext , args : Namespace ) -> None : print ( f "Hello, { args . name } !" ) app = Hinoki ( commands = [ Greet ]) The same example is in examples/project/app.py ; the examples manifest supplies its target when you run the command from the examples/ project directory. handle(context, args) may be synchronous or asynchronous. A sync handler runs on Hinoki's bounded executor. It can read context.settings and retrieve resources with context.get(Type) or context.find(Type) . Declare module classes in the command's requires tuple; Hinoki starts those modules and their dependencies for the command, then closes them before it exits. Other app modules are not started. A command with no requirements starts no app modules. Commands run inside the project process and can modify data. Use disposable databases when developing or testing a command that writes. A handler returns None for success or an exit code from 0 through 255. Unknown commands and invalid arguments exit 2; a command failure exits nonzero. App settings load when Hinoki constructs the app, but module resources open only for the selected command. Errors and edge cases ¶ A mistyped command gets a suggestion ( did you mean 'check'? ) and exits 2. A target that does not import, or is neither an application nor a factory, stops the command with an error: line before anything runs. Commands that need hinoki.toml ( app , skills install ) exit 2 without one. Interactive prompts ( new , app create ) never appear without a terminal or with --no-input ; Ctrl-C or Esc cancels with status 130 and writes nothing. See also ¶ Create a project Inspect an application Serve an application Development MCP
