docs.text: Every task in a Hinoki project has a hinoki command. Inside a project created by hinoki new , run them through uv run , which uses the project's locked environment: uv run hinoki dev uv run hinoki check uv run hinoki migrations apply
docs.title: Command line

docs.text: Group Command What it does Guide Start hinoki new [NAME] Create a project; asks for what the flags leave out, ending with "Create an app now?" ( --app NAME , --no-app ). Create a project hinoki app create\|add\|list Add an app, register an existing package, list the apps. below hinoki dev / serve Run with reload / run for production, on Kiso or Granian; --interface wsgi serves a WSGI callable. Serve hinoki shell Python shell with the app, its settings and models, top-level await . Shell Inspect hinoki check Run the architecture rules. Inspect hinoki doctor Environment, manifest and app diagnostics. Inspect hinoki routes Every route with its access policy and server lane. Inspect hinoki settings Effective settings and their sources, secrets redacted. Inspect hinoki openapi Print, write or diff the OpenAPI document. Inspect hinoki version The Hinoki version; --verbose adds Python, platform, native core and Granian. Inspect Data hinoki migrations plan\|status\|apply\|sql Plan and apply migrations for every registered app. below hinoki admin create-superuser\|set-password Manage admin users from the terminal. below Integrate hinoki mcp Serve project context to an AI agent over MCP. below hinoki skills list\|install Write the optional agent skills. below hinoki manage [COMMAND] Run a command your application defines. below hinoki completion SHELL Print a completion script. below
docs.title: Commands

docs.text: In a project, hinoki.toml names the application ( [project] application ), so commands take no target: hinoki dev , hinoki check , hinoki routes . To use another application, pass a target, module:attribute , imported from the current directory: hinoki dev notes.main:app . A function that returns an application ( module:create_app ) is also accepted, and hinoki settings also accepts a settings class. When a target does not import, run the command from the project root (where hinoki.toml is), check that the packages have __init__.py files and that the attribute name is right. The commands report error: cannot load notes.main:ap: ... and exit with a non-zero status.
docs.title: Targets and short commands

docs.text: hinoki --help lists the commands in groups (Start, Inspect, Data, Integrate); hinoki COMMAND --help shows one command's options. A mistyped command or migrations action gets a suggestion: hinoki: error: argument <command>: invalid choice: 'chek' (choose from 'check', ...) did you mean 'check'? The completion script is generated from the real parser, so it follows the commands and options of the installed version: eval " $( hinoki completion bash ) " # in ~/.bashrc eval " $( hinoki completion zsh ) " # in ~/.zshrc, after compinit hinoki completion fish | source # in ~/.config/fish/config.fish It completes command, subcommand and option names; it does not complete option values or project-specific names such as apps.
docs.title: Help and completion

docs.text: On a colour terminal, doctor , check and routes print a coloured report: a status glyph per check ( ✔ ok, ▲ warning, ✘ failed or violated, ? unverifiable, – skipped or waived) with the fix on its own line, and routes with coloured methods. The check summary is green only when the exit code is 0 . When output is piped or redirected, or with NO_COLOR or TERM=dumb , the text is plain and unchanged, and --format json is never styled.
docs.title: Terminal output

docs.text: The generated hinoki.toml registers no app unless hinoki new created one (the last question in a terminal, or --app NAME ): the project package keeps main.py , settings, rules and the health route, and models live in apps. Create each one with: uv run hinoki app create billing This creates NAME/apps/billing/{models.py,routes.py,migrations/} and registers the model, migration and routes modules in hinoki.toml ( routes = "NAME.apps.billing.routes:routes" , prefix = "/billing" ). Cross-app foreign keys require the referencing app to list the referenced app in requires in hinoki.toml ; migrations are then planned/applied in dependency order. The project registry is explicit: Hinoki does not scan arbitrary installed packages or run imports at install time. Both commands report hinoki.toml : hinoki new lists it among the generated files and app create says it registered the app there. --prefix and --requires (comma-separated) set the mount prefix and dependencies directly. In a terminal, app create asks for whatever is not given — the name, the prefix (default /NAME ) and, when other apps exist, requires — with the same prompts, Esc-to-cancel (exit 130, nothing created) and NO_COLOR handling as hinoki new . Without a terminal or with --no-input it never asks: the name is required (exit 2) and the defaults are /NAME and no requires . To register a package that already exists, name its modules. Nothing is created or imported; only hinoki.toml changes: uv run hinoki app add billing --models legacy.billing.models uv run hinoki app add invoices --models legacy.invoices.models --migrations legacy.db.invoices --routes legacy.invoices.routes:routes --prefix /invoices --requires billing --migrations defaults to the migrations package next to the models module ( legacy.billing.migrations ); a models module without a parent package needs it explicitly. --prefix defaults to /NAME once --routes is given. The whole manifest is validated before it is replaced, so a duplicate name, an unknown or cyclic --requires , or a malformed module name leaves hinoki.toml untouched and exits 2. Whether the modules import is checked later, when a command such as hinoki migrations plan loads the app. List the registered apps from the project root or any subdirectory: uv run hinoki app list uv run hinoki app list --format json The text output shows each app in dependency order with its model module, migration package, routes and prefix, and prerequisites. JSON contains the same fields under an apps key ( routes and prefix are empty strings for an app without routes). The command only reads and validates hinoki.toml : it does not import app modules, connect to a database or start the app. Without a manifest, it prints an error and exits 2.
docs.title: app

docs.text: The admin's own users are managed from the admin itself, except the first one: uv run hinoki admin create-superuser ada # asks for the password twice, no echo printf '%s\n' " $ADA_PASSWORD " | uv run hinoki admin set-password ada --password-stdin A password is read from a terminal prompt or, with --password-stdin , from one line of standard input; it is never taken from the command line, where other users of the machine could read it, and it is never printed. Without a terminal and without the flag the command stops; with the flag on a terminal it still prompts without echo, and a line longer than a password can be is refused unread. Ctrl-C or Ctrl-D at the prompt exits with status 2 , and a refused connection is reported as such, naming the masked database and its source (status 1 ), not as missing tables. The database is chosen as for hinoki migrations : --database , HINOKI_DATABASE_URL , the project application's installed DatabaseModule or database setting, then the project's local SQLite; the command prints it on standard error as database: … (from …) , and stops with status 2 when the project's application or database cannot be resolved. The user tables must exist: register and apply them first ( hinoki app add admin ... , hinoki migrations apply admin , see who may sign in ); otherwise the command exits 1 and says so. Usernames are lower-cased; the shortest password is admin.min_password_length . Exit status is 0 on success, 2 for a refused input (a taken name, a weak or mistyped password, an unknown user).
docs.title: admin

docs.text: In a project, migration modules come from hinoki.toml ; you never pass model or migration paths: uv run hinoki migrations plan --check uv run hinoki migrations plan billing --name add-invoice-index uv run hinoki migrations status uv run hinoki migrations apply uv run hinoki migrations sql 0001 -initial status and apply cover all registered apps in dependency order. Writing a plan in a multi-app project needs the app name ( plan billing , or --app billing ); read-only plan --check and plan --dry-run without an app cover every app in dependency order. sql searches every app; --app narrows it when two apps share a migration name. --name is optional for a focused plan: Hinoki derives a stable slug from the first planned schema change (for example, create-table-notes ); pass --name initial-notes to override it. All-app previews cannot use --name . Numbering is automatic. apply initializes the configured local SQLite database when no database is configured. In a manifest project the implicit .hinoki/local.sqlite3 file, and a relative SQLite path from the application's settings, are rooted beside hinoki.toml , even if you run the command from a subdirectory; relative SQLite URLs given with --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL remain relative to the current working directory. Added apps have separate migration ledger namespaces, so identical numbered filenames do not collide; a project whose root package was registered as an app (older scaffolds) retains its unprefixed migration keys. apply billing includes its declared prerequisite apps for migration application. plan --check fails CI (exit 1) when the models have changes that no migration file records, and exits 2 when the database it plans for cannot be resolved; it never connects to a database. In a project it imports the application to read its database unless --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL is set. Migration safety across apps, destructive changes and the ledger are explained in Migrations . Without a hinoki.toml , name the modules explicitly: hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations plan --models myapp.models --name add-index --dry-run hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations apply hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations sql 0001 -initial plan requires --models MODULE ; --name is an optional slug override and is derived from the first planned schema change when omitted. --dry-run prints operations without writing files. Destructive operations require --allow-destructive . plan/status/apply target --database , then HINOKI_DATABASE_URL , then the DatabaseModule or database setting of the project's application, then the local SQLite file at .hinoki/local.sqlite3 ( which database ); plan , status and apply print the chosen database and its source on standard error with the credentials masked, and stop with exit 2 when the project's application or database cannot be resolved. A URL given as an argument is visible in the process list and shell history, so keep a URL containing a password in the environment. When the connection fails, the command prints error: database: … with a fix: line and exits 1; the error itself does not repeat the URL. sql NAME prints a migration's SQL. Use a disposable database while reviewing migrations. On an animated terminal, plan and apply show a spinner while they work and finish with a timing line ( ✔ applied 1.2s ); the commands' own output is printed unchanged before it. Piped output, NO_COLOR , TERM=dumb , CI and HINOKI_ANIMATE=0 print only the commands' own output.
docs.title: migrations

docs.text: uv run hinoki mcp The development server uses MCP over stdio. It accepts --rules , repeatable --package , repeatable --models , and --waivers with the same target meanings as check . --rules defaults to the application's rules and --package to the package that contains it, as for hinoki check . --requests PATH names the file the recent_requests tool reads (default .hinoki/requests.jsonl ; see server.recent_requests ). --scenarios off|read|write controls whether run_scenario is registered: read allows GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and QUERY; write allows every supported method. Scenarios start the real app, run handlers and lifespan hooks, and may write data even for a GET. Keep the tool server owner-controlled and point the app at a disposable database. The development MCP is separate from application MCP, which is mounted with expose_as_mcp and an explicit action allowlist. See the development MCP guide for tool inputs and results.
docs.title: mcp

docs.text: hinoki skills list hinoki skills install # from a project directory hinoki skills install --force # replace skills that already exist Agent skills are short Markdown playbooks that point an assistant at the real Hinoki tools (the development MCP and the CLI). list prints each skill name and description. install reads hinoki.toml , then writes .claude/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md for each one, with the project package name filled in; an existing file is kept and reported unless --force replaces it. Without a manifest it prints an error and exits 2 . hinoki new --skills writes the same files at creation. They are optional and never written otherwise. Skill Playbook hinoki-add-endpoint add an action with its Schema types, access policy and test hinoki-fix-rule fix a rule diagnostic without editing the rules or waivers hinoki-review-api run hinoki openapi --breaking-against before and after a change hinoki-test-api exercise operations with the generated valid and invalid bodies of hinoki.ai.samples.request_cases
docs.title: skills

docs.text: uv run hinoki manage --help uv run hinoki manage greet Peppe Commands are declared on the app with Hinoki(commands=[...]) . Each command subclasses hinoki.management.Command , gives itself a lower-case name, and adds arguments through add_arguments(parser) . In a scaffolded project, hinoki manage lists commands and hinoki manage greet Peppe runs one; the manifest's project.application supplies the app target. Outside a registered project, use hinoki manage TARGET COMMAND . --help after a command shows its arguments. # examples/project/app.py from argparse import ArgumentParser , Namespace from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.management import Command , CommandContext class Greet ( Command ): name = "greet" help = "print a greeting" def add_arguments ( self , parser : ArgumentParser ) -> None : parser . add_argument ( "name" , nargs = "?" , default = "world" ) def handle ( self , _context : CommandContext , args : Namespace ) -> None : print ( f "Hello, { args . name } !" ) app = Hinoki ( commands = [ Greet ]) The same example is in examples/project/app.py ; the examples manifest supplies its target when you run the command from the examples/ project directory. handle(context, args) may be synchronous or asynchronous. A sync handler runs on Hinoki's bounded executor. It can read context.settings and retrieve resources with context.get(Type) or context.find(Type) . Declare module classes in the command's requires tuple; Hinoki starts those modules and their dependencies for the command, then closes them before it exits. Other app modules are not started. A command with no requirements starts no app modules. Commands run inside the project process and can modify data. Use disposable databases when developing or testing a command that writes. A handler returns None for success or an exit code from 0 through 255. Unknown commands and invalid arguments exit 2; a command failure exits nonzero. App settings load when Hinoki constructs the app, but module resources open only for the selected command.
docs.title: manage

docs.text: A mistyped command gets a suggestion ( did you mean 'check'? ) and exits 2. A target that does not import, or is neither an application nor a factory, stops the command with an error: line before anything runs. Commands that need hinoki.toml ( app , skills install ) exit 2 without one. Interactive prompts ( new , app create ) never appear without a terminal or with --no-input ; Ctrl-C or Esc cancels with status 130 and writes nothing.

docs.text: Parsers and renderers ¶ A parser turns a request body into Python data; a renderer turns a handler's result into response bytes. Built-ins use Rust for selected parsing and JSON encoding work; Python still selects codecs, calls customization hooks and assembles framework objects. Built in Rust work Python work and options JSONParser Strict JSON decoding (no NaN, no lone surrogates, depth limit) prepare(data) hook and media_type Form[Schema] marker A Schema read from form text, converted per field Rust conversion, then strict Schema validation XMLParser application/xml into a tree (children → dict , repeated name → list , text → str , empty → None ), parsed with the GIL released; no DTDs, custom entities, characters XML 1.0 forbids or encodings other than UTF-8; depth and element caps Rust; max_depth (default 32, at most MAX_XML_DEPTH = 1000, larger raises ValueError ), max_elements (default 10,000); attributes are not read XML[Schema] marker A Schema read from an XML body, converted per field Rust conversion, then strict Schema validation Query[Schema] marker A Schema read from the query string, converted per field Rust conversion, then strict Schema validation FormParser application/x-www-form-urlencoded parsing with a field cap Builds the Python mappings; max_fields MultiPartParser multipart/form-data parsing and byte/part limits Builds UploadedFile and form objects; max_parts , max_part_bytes (each part, including text fields) TextParser — Decodes UTF-8 in Python; media_type BytesParser — Hands request.data the raw bytes of an application/octet-stream body JSONRenderer Encodes dict , list , Schema , UUID, datetime and dump() objects prepare(value, request) and default callbacks run in Python; indent , sort_keys , media_type HTMLRenderer , TextRenderer — Type-check and UTF-8 encode strings in Python; media_type XMLRenderer — Writes the JSON-compatible result as UTF-8 XML in Python; root , item Content negotiation ( Accept , quality values, wildcards) also runs in Rust; with nothing acceptable the answer is 406 before the handler runs. Upload files ¶ An action that binds an UploadedFile and has no parsers of its own gets MultiPartParser() with its default limits (100 parts, 1 MiB per part), unless the application's parsers= already include a MultiPartParser , which is then used. Other actions accept multipart only when it is listed. The parser handles bounded multipart bytes in Rust, then Python creates UploadedFile objects. For typed handler binding, annotate a parameter as UploadedFile , UploadedFile | None = None , or list[UploadedFile] ; the parameter name selects the multipart field. A single value rejects duplicates, while a list preserves repeated values. The same objects are visible through request.FILES ; text fields are available in request.POST . See endpoint upload declarations for a complete example and status-code behavior. The complete request body and every part are buffered in memory. The default body cap is 1 MiB; increasing it also increases potential memory use across concurrent requests. This parser does not stream or spool files. Keep both the runtime body cap and max_part_bytes bounded, and treat filenames and media types as untrusted client input. JSONParser , JSONRenderer , HTMLRenderer , XMLParser , XMLRenderer , FormParser , MultiPartParser and BytesParser are importable from hinoki ; TextParser and TextRenderer come from hinoki.parsers and hinoki.renderers . Choose them ¶ Per action, or for the whole application (an action's own choice wins): # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki , JSONRenderer from hinoki.project import manifest_routes from hinoki.renderers import TextRenderer from notes.rules import project_rules from notes.settings import ProjectSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , include = manifest_routes (), rules = project_rules , renderers = [ JSONRenderer ( sort_keys = True ), TextRenderer ()], ) # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) from hinoki import JSONParser , JSONRenderer , Request from hinoki.parsers import TextParser @invoices . get ( "/report" , renderers = [ JSONRenderer ( indent = 2 )]) async def report () -> InvoiceReport : ... @invoices . post ( "/hook" , parsers = [ JSONParser (), TextParser ()], atomic = True ) async def hook ( request : Request ) -> HookReceipt : ... # request.data is a dict or a str Answer XML ¶ XMLRenderer renders the handler's result in its JSON-compatible form, as application/xml; charset=utf-8 with an XML declaration. That is the data a default JSONRenderer() writes: a Schema or dump() object becomes its mapping, a UUID or datetime its text, and a tuple a list, at any depth. A JSONRenderer 's own options ( default , prepare , sort_keys ) do not apply to it: from hinoki import JSONRenderer , XMLRenderer @http . get ( "/report" , renderers = [ JSONRenderer (), XMLRenderer ( root = "report" )]) async def report () -> dict [ str , object ]: return { "id" : 1 , "tags" : [ "a" , "b" ], "note" : None } Accept: application/xml answers <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?><report><id>1</id><tags><item>a</item><item>b</item></tags><note/></report> ; without it the first renderer (JSON) answers. A mapping becomes child elements named by its keys, a list becomes repeated item elements ( item= renames them), None an empty element and booleans true / false . Keys are spelled as the JSON encoder spells them: a string as is, an integer in decimal, None as null and booleans as true / false ; any other key (a float, a UUID, a tuple) raises an error ( 500 ), as it does for JSON. A key that is not a valid XML name (a space, a leading digit, a name starting with xml , so also an integer key) is written as <item key="..."> , escaped, instead of failing the request. Tab and line breaks are written as character references so a parser keeps them, and characters XML 1.0 cannot carry are replaced by U+FFFD. Non-finite floats, which JSON refuses, are written NaN , INF and -INF . Nesting deeper than 200 levels (the JSON encoder's limit), an integer of more than 4300 digits or a value that is not JSON-compatible raises an error ( 500 ). The renderer runs in Python, but it never reads the request, so an action that lists it stays on the native handler lane. Configure the Rust JSON encoder ¶ JSONRenderer ( indent = 2 , sort_keys = True ) # pretty, stable output JSONRenderer ( default = str ) # Decimal, Path, ... become text default is a Python callback for a value the encoder does not know and must return something that is JSON (returning the same object is an error). It does not override what the encoder already handles (UUID, datetime, Schema , anything with dump() ). With sort_keys=True object keys are ordered by their encoded text (quotes and escapes included), which is deterministic but not always json.dumps order for unusual keys, and integer keys sort as text. The public renderer accepts indent from 0 to 16, or None for compact output. Inherit and override ¶ # notes/apps/billing/codecs.py from hinoki import JSONParser , JSONRenderer class Envelope ( JSONRenderer ): media_type = "application/vnd.myapp+json" def prepare ( self , value , request ): # reshape, then Rust encodes return { "data" : value , "request_id" : request . request_id } class SnakeCase ( JSONParser ): def prepare ( self , data ): # Rust decodes, then reshape return rename_keys ( data ) if isinstance ( data , dict ) else data For a different format write a Renderer ( media_type , render(value, request) -> bytes ) or a Parser ( media_type , parse(raw, content_type) -> Parsed ); set consumes_objects = True on a renderer that can take Schema instances directly. Media types must be distinct within one list; a failing parse raises InvalidBody(code, message) (a 400 with that stable code).

docs.text: Concepts ¶ How the parts of Hinoki fit together. Each guide explains one part in detail. A model is stored data; a Schema is API data ¶ A Model describes a table and its queries (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB). A Schema validates what an endpoint accepts or returns. A response Schema exposes only the fields clients should see: @derive(Invoice) copies fields from a model, but you still decide the boundary, and a handler returns InvoiceOut.from_model(row) , never the row. A declaration is reused ¶ An action's signature and decorator options state its route, inputs, access policy, transaction ( atomic= ), declared errors and response. Routing, binding, the OpenAPI document, the rules, the admin and MCP all read that one declaration. Actions are plain functions , optionally grouped in a RouteGroup with shared options, or methods of an API class . Each app lists them in its routes.py , and hinoki.toml mounts every app under its prefix ( register routes ). One application object ¶ A server process serves one Hinoki object: the one project.application in hinoki.toml names, or the target given to hinoki serve . Declare it at module level: # notes/main.py import stripe from hinoki import Hinoki , errors from notes.rules import project_rules from notes.settings import ProjectSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , title = "Notes" , rules = project_rules ) @app . error_handler ( stripe . CardError ) def card_error ( error : stripe . CardError ) -> errors . APIError : return errors . APIError ( error . user_message , status = 402 , code = "card_declined" ) Hinoki(...) includes the routes listed in hinoki.toml ( include=manifest_routes() ) and opens nothing, so importing the module is safe: commands, servers and tests use the same app . The [[apps]] of hinoki.toml are packages of models, migrations and routes, not further Hinoki objects. One request ¶ The server hands each request to the compiled router and binding layer: Kiso, the default server, does so from Rust and queues matched requests for the Python pipeline; with Granian the request crosses the ASGI adapter first. Hinoki authenticates the caller, checks access, validates inputs, runs the handler, checks the return value against its annotation and renders the response. A transactional action commits after the response is prepared; a failure rolls back before it becomes an HTTP error. Handwritten handlers and hooks run in Python on both servers: the runtime is not an all-Rust server. Details: request lifecycle . Worker resources ¶ Each server worker owns its module lifespan and database pool: startup creates them, shutdown closes them. Nothing is opened at import or shared across workers. Scripts outside the server manage their own short-lived connections. See modules . Optional rules ¶ Rules check declared routes, schemas, models and imports. Hinoki ships eleven; each reports a violation, a pass, or that it could not verify its promise. They do not prove what a function body does. Turn on the ones that suit the application and run them at startup and in development. See rules . See also ¶ Request lifecycle Structure an application Sync and async code Glossary

docs.text: Generate CRUD routes ¶ crud(...) generates model-backed routes: list and retrieve always, create, update and delete when you ask for them. Use it as a value in routes.py for plain CRUD, or apply it to an API class to add hooks and handwritten actions ( class-based APIs ). # notes/apps/billing/routes.py from hinoki import Includable , crud from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut , InvoicePatch routes : list [ Includable ] = [ crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , update = InvoicePatch , delete = True , access = billing_staff , ), ] # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py (continued) @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "reference" , "paid" ), partial = True ) class InvoicePatch ( Schema ): ... Generated actions ¶ Keyword Action Method and path Success always list GET /invoices Page[InvoiceOut] always retrieve GET /invoices/{item_id} InvoiceOut create=InvoiceIn create POST /invoices 201 , InvoiceOut update=InvoicePatch update PATCH /invoices/{item_id} 200 , InvoiceOut delete=True delete DELETE /invoices/{item_id} 204 , no body Writes run in a transaction. pagination= selects the page-number policy of the list route (default PageNumberPagination() ). omit=("list",) or omit=("retrieve",) drops a read so that you can write it yourself. The generated actions are ordinary routes, visible to OpenAPI, hinoki routes and the route registry; nothing is registered at import time. Access per action ¶ access= takes one Access , which protects every generated action including reads, or CrudAccess to set actions apart. An action without its own entry uses default ; None means public: # notes/apps/billing/routes.py (variant) from hinoki import CrudAccess from notes.security import billing_admin , billing_staff access = CrudAccess ( default = billing_staff , list = None , retrieve = None , delete = billing_admin ) Here list and retrieve are public, create and update need billing_staff , delete needs billing_admin . Unknown action names raise TypeError . Generated writes always need a policy: a write left without one raises RegistrationError (when a @crud class is declared, or when a crud(...) value is included) unless you pass public_writes=True on purpose. The access= of crud(...) covers generated actions only; a handwritten action in the class form states its own. Rules see a generated action under the module that declares the crud(...) value: the value in notes/apps/billing/routes.py produces notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.list , .retrieve , .create , .update and .delete , and the class form uses its class ( notes.apps.billing.api.Invoices.list ). So the scaffold's match="notes.*" rules check them, and a public list goes in except_ like any other action: Actions . require_access ( match = "notes.*" , except_ = [ "notes.api.health" , "notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.list" ], ) The same names select MCP tools : tools=["notes.apps.billing.*"] also publishes the generated reads, and the writes with allow_writes=True . How the name is chosen: A shared helper that wraps crud(...) and is called at the top level of a feature module names the actions after that feature module, not after the helper's module. name="ArchiveCrud" sets the class name; name="notes.apps.archive.ArchiveCrud" sets the module too. Pass it when the value is built deeper (a factory that calls another factory, or a function run from main.py ), or when one module declares two crud(...) values for the same model. name= is for the function form only. Two different classes whose actions would share a name raise RegistrationError when included, naming both paths, so one except_ entry, waiver or MCP pattern never covers both by accident. One value mounted twice ( Mount("/a", notes) and Mount("/b", notes) ) keeps one name, as any API class or function does: an exception for it covers both mounts. Hooks in the class form ¶ Apply @crud(...) to a class whose only base is API . These methods change what the generated actions do; every other decorated method is a handwritten action: Hook Called for Purpose get_queryset(principal) every action The base query: tenant or visibility filters. Builds a query, does no I/O to_schema(item) every answer A response shape that needs loaded relations written_queryset(principal) after a write Loads response relations of the written row store(values, principal) create Creates the row change(item, scoped_queryset, values, principal) update Updates the row remove(item, scoped_queryset, principal) delete Deletes the row # notes/apps/billing/api.py from typing import Any from hinoki import API , Caller , crud from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut def normalised ( reference : str ) -> str : return reference . strip () . upper () @crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , access = billing_staff ) class Invoices ( API ): async def store ( self , values : dict [ str , Any ], principal : Caller [ Any ]) -> Invoice : values [ "reference" ] = normalised ( str ( values [ "reference" ])) return await Invoice . acreate ( ** values ) Each hook may be def or async def . Sync hooks run on Hinoki's bounded executor and use the sync ORM methods ( Invoice.create(**values) ); async hooks run on the event loop and use the async ones. A sync hook must not return an un-awaited coroutine. When reads are public, principal is None ; when the action has an access policy, it is the authenticated Caller . Apply tenant or visibility filters in get_queryset ; owner= is an independent write safeguard, not read authorization. Relations are never loaded implicitly: load them in to_schema , and in written_queryset for the answer to a write, independently of filters that might hide the changed row from later list requests. Writes are constrained by the query of get_queryset , the primary key and the owner column, inside the mutation statement. change and remove receive that scoped query; call super() to keep the default mutation. Hooks run inside the transaction and before the commit, so do not send mail or publish external events from them. They are trusted application code: do not bypass the scoped query with an unscoped write or raw SQL. Hinoki checks the persisted item after create and update for model identity and server-assigned fields, but cannot sandbox arbitrary side effects. Generate or hand-write ¶ Each action is generated or handwritten, never both: To hand-write Do this create , update , delete Leave create= , update= or delete=True out, and declare your own method list , retrieve Pass omit=("list",) or omit=("retrieve",) and declare a method with another name A method named like an action that crud(...) still generates ( list , retrieve , create , update , delete ) raises RegistrationError when the class is declared. A handwritten route at the same method and path as a generated one fails when the class is included. Reuse ¶ CRUD configuration is plain Python values. Share one Access or CrudAccess , or bind your defaults once: # notes/apps/billing/resources.py from functools import partial from hinoki import crud from notes.security import billing_staff staff_crud = partial ( crud , access = billing_staff ) staff_crud(Invoice, path="/invoices", read=InvoiceOut) works as a value and as a class decorator. A @crud class accepts no base other than API , so mixins do not apply. Security and validation ¶ Set owner="author_id" to assign that column from the authenticated caller on create and constrain update and delete. identity_key extracts the owner value from Caller.user ; its default reads .id . assign maps additional server-owned columns to functions of the caller's user object. Client schemas cannot accept server-assigned fields. Generated writes require an access policy even when owner is configured. With ClaimsJWTAuth there is no user object, so use identity_key=caller_id (from hinoki.resources ): the owner value is then the caller's Caller.id (the token sub ). A foreign update or delete answers 403 and a missing row 404 . This is the only owner declaration that can run natively; see authentication . At declaration Hinoki rejects abstract models, unknown schema fields, unsafe nullable fields, missing required create values, update schemas that can overwrite omitted fields, primary-key updates, unknown assigned columns and incompatible derived schemas. only= and exclude= schemas remain subject to the same checks. A stored row that the read= schema refuses (for example a max_length that the data exceeds) is a server fault: the action answers 500 , the response does not repeat the stored values, and the server log names the model, the read schema, the field and the code. Client input that fails a create or update schema answers 422 . A create that breaks a unique constraint answers 409 unique_conflict unless an error handler you register says otherwise. Model hooks and Kiso ¶ Generated create and PATCH update write through the model, so its lifecycle hooks run: create calls acreate , and update saves the item with the scoped query's conditions in its UPDATE, so a row that left the caller's scope since it was read is refused ( 403 / 404 ). A model that defines any of before_save , before_create , after_create or after_save is not eligible for the native create and update routes; they use the Python lane, while its list, retrieve and delete routes stay native. Deleting does not run hooks. On Kiso, eligible generated routes execute in Rust when their schemas and model are supported and the resource has no access policy (other than an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth ), owner or assignment rule (other than identity_key=caller_id ) or custom hook. Ineligible and stale plans use the Python lane. See Kiso: generated CRUD ; no switch is required. Inspect the generated routes ¶ hinoki routes --path /billing/invoices GET /billing/invoices StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.list POST /billing/invoices StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.create DELETE /billing/invoices/{item_id} StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.delete GET /billing/invoices/{item_id} StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.retrieve PATCH /billing/invoices/{item_id} StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.update Generated routes appear in the OpenAPI document with their schemas, access policies, status codes and pagination. See the CRUD API reference . Prefer a handwritten action when a workflow has its own state transitions, errors or side effects beyond one model mutation.

docs.text: Configure a database ¶ Hinoki's ORM runs on SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB. The database URL selects the backend; models and queries stay the same wherever the backends' SQL features overlap. With nothing configured, the database is local SQLite at .hinoki/local.sqlite3 . Set up a database in four steps ¶ Declare it. hinoki new notes --database postgresql does this for you; otherwise add the field to your settings class. Name a TOML file only if you will use one (step 2): the file named by toml= must exist. # notes/settings.py class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings Populate it. With nothing set, DatabaseSettings points at a local SQLite file, .hinoki/local.sqlite3 . To use another database, pick one source: Source Use it for Example Nothing local development on SQLite – .env one URL on your machine ( hinoki new --database postgresql writes a .env.example to copy; keep .env out of git) NOTES_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://notes:secret@localhost:5432/notes Environment containers and CI export NOTES_DATABASE__URL_FILE=/run/secrets/database-url settings.toml non-secret fields ( engine , host , name , user ), with the password from the environment; add toml="settings.toml" to the class connection fields The prefix ( NOTES_ ) comes from the settings class, and __ separates the group from the field. Until you set one of them, a project created with --database postgresql still uses the local SQLite file, and so do its migrations. Check it. hinoki settings , run from the project root, shows each value with its source; the URL and the password are redacted: $ hinoki settings | grep DATABASE__URL NOTES_DATABASE__URL .env *** hinoki migrations status names the database it will use, and fails with a clear error if the server does not answer: $ hinoki migrations status database: postgresql://***@127.0.0.1:5432/notes (from settings: ProjectSettings.database) status connects and records its migration ledger, so on SQLite it creates the database file. Create the tables. Hinoki never creates tables or runs migrations at startup (it only creates the local SQLite file): run hinoki migrations apply once you have models ( migrations ). The rest of this page lists every field, the URL forms and each backend. Configure the application ¶ Declare a database field on the project settings. hinoki new adds it when you choose a database. # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" , toml = "settings.toml" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings Each worker opens one bounded pool during startup and closes it during shutdown. Importing models or routes never opens a connection, and no modules= entry is needed. The file named by toml= must exist, even if it is empty: otherwise the settings fail to load with settings.toml: TOML file cannot be read or parsed . Configure a server database with connection fields or with one URL . Setting both is an error when settings load. Connection fields ¶ Put non-secret fields in the TOML file named by toml= . Keep the settings in their own file: hinoki.toml is the project manifest, and its tables are not settings. PostgreSQL MySQL MariaDB SQLite # settings.toml [database] engine = "postgresql" name = "notes" user = "notes" host = "db.example.test" port = 5432 options = [ "sslmode=verify-full" , "sslrootcert=/run/secrets/db-ca.pem" ] max_size = 10 # per worker # settings.toml [database] engine = "mysql" name = "notes" user = "notes" host = "db.example.test" # settings.toml [database] engine = "mariadb" name = "notes" user = "notes" host = "db.example.test" # settings.toml [database] engine = "sqlite" name = ".hinoki/local.sqlite3" The password is a secret setting. It never comes from TOML: export NOTES_DATABASE__PASSWORD_FILE = /run/secrets/db-password Field Meaning Default engine sqlite , postgresql , mysql or mariadb ( settings.DatabaseEngine ) – name database name, or the file path for SQLite – user , password credentials; password is secret ( *_PASSWORD or *_PASSWORD_FILE ) – host , port server address; for PostgreSQL host may be a Unix-socket directory such as /var/run/postgresql localhost , backend port options key=value URL query pairs, such as sslmode () max_size connections per worker 10 Hinoki builds DatabaseSettings.url from these fields and percent-encodes the user, password and name. SQLite takes only name . options cannot carry credentials or override user , host , port or the name. In an environment variable, options uses the settings sequence syntax (commas between pairs); a value that itself contains a comma belongs in the TOML array. One URL ¶ export NOTES_DATABASE__URL_FILE = /run/secrets/database-url Backend URL SQLite sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 PostgreSQL postgresql://notes:password@db.example.test/notes?sslmode=verify-full MySQL mysql://notes:password@db.example.test/notes MariaDB mariadb://notes:password@db.example.test/notes Percent-encode reserved characters in the user name and password of a hand-written URL. Prefer NOTES_DATABASE__URL_FILE or a secret manager over a URL in shell history or a process argument. Hinoki redacts the URL in settings output and connection errors. Credentials settings.Secret values, url and password included, are never read from TOML. SQLite has no database credentials: protect the file and its backups with operating-system permissions. Backends ¶ Backend Security defaults Limits SQLite no network, no TLS one writer at a time; bounded connections and a five-second busy timeout; a relative path resolves from the server's working directory (start it from the project root; migrations anchor it beside hinoki.toml ) PostgreSQL sslmode=prefer ; use verify-full for remote servers; sslrootcert adds a PEM CA to the system roots. require , verify-ca and verify-full all verify the certificate native UUID, timestamp, JSON and byte types MySQL TLS required, certificate and host verified against the system trust store; require_ssl=false only for an isolated disposable local server InnoDB, native JSON; no RETURNING MariaDB TLS required by default separate backend, tested on MariaDB 11.4 with its own conformance job. JSON is a text alias: typed dict / list fields decode by declaration; low-level Database.fetch() returns JSON values as bytes SQL Server and Oracle are not supported. Any other scheme, such as oracle:// or mssql:// , fails when the pool is created with DatabaseError: unsupported database URL scheme ; the message does not repeat the URL. A supported scheme written without its slashes, such as sqlite:./app.db , fails with invalid database URL: the scheme needs :// . PostgreSQL TLS ¶ PostgreSQL URLs accept sslmode=disable , prefer , require , verify-ca or verify-full , and sslrootcert=/path/to/ca.pem . prefer tries TLS first and falls back to plaintext only if the server declines TLS; a certificate or handshake error fails closed. All TLS connections verify the server certificate chain and hostname: require , verify-ca and verify-full all require TLS, and Hinoki's verify-ca also verifies the hostname. Trust uses Mozilla WebPKI roots plus any PEM certificates in sslrootcert (at most 1 MiB), so sslmode=require needs a trusted certificate too. sslmode=allow is unsupported. Mount the CA file where each worker can read it. Hinoki does not create the PostgreSQL role or database: create them once with your usual tools before the first hinoki migrations apply . SQLite storage ¶ SQLite uses bundled SQLite 3.35 or newer. UUID and timestamp columns use text storage; JSON uses JSON text. contains matching is ASCII case-insensitive. In-memory databases are not supported, because each pooled connection would have an independent database. Use the database from a script ¶ A script, a one-off task or a test fixture opens its own pool with Database.connect and makes it current with use_database , so model queries find it. Run it from the project root so a relative SQLite path and .env match the server's: # scripts/unpaid.py import asyncio from hinoki.db import Database from hinoki.orm import use_database from notes.apps.billing.models import Invoice from notes.settings import ProjectSettings async def main () -> None : settings = ProjectSettings . load () database = await Database . connect ( settings . database . url . reveal (), max_size = settings . database . max_size ) try : with use_database ( database ): print ( await Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . acount ()) finally : database . close () asyncio . run ( main ()) Database.close() is a plain call, not awaited. The script does not create tables: run hinoki migrations apply against the same database first. Replace the database module ¶ A DatabaseModule in modules= , or installed with app.install(...) , replaces the one Hinoki builds from the settings, for example to use a URL chosen at runtime: # notes/main.py (excerpt) from hinoki.db import DatabaseModule app . install ( DatabaseModule ( url , max_size = 4 )) The migration commands use this module's URL too, and print (from application: DatabaseModule) . A database module of your own whose URL Hinoki cannot read stops them; pass --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL . Migrations use the application's database ¶ hinoki migrations reads the database of the project's application (its DatabaseModule , or its database setting), so the variables above configure both the server and the migration commands. --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL override it for one run; with none of them set, the local SQLite default is anchored beside hinoki.toml : export NOTES_DATABASE__URL = postgresql://notes:secret@db.internal/notes hinoki migrations status # database: postgresql://***@db.internal/notes (from settings: ...) hinoki migrations apply Hinoki never runs migrations at startup. An application that declares no database setting and installs no DatabaseModule has no database at run time, although its migrations still fall back to the local SQLite file: declare the field before you add models. See which database for the full order, and migrations for planning, review and per-backend behaviour. docs.title: Configure a database

docs.text: Hinoki's ORM runs on SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB. The database URL selects the backend; models and queries stay the same wherever the backends' SQL features overlap. With nothing configured, the database is local SQLite at .hinoki/local.sqlite3 .
docs.title: Configure a database

docs.text: Declare it. hinoki new notes --database postgresql does this for you; otherwise add the field to your settings class. Name a TOML file only if you will use one (step 2): the file named by toml= must exist. # notes/settings.py class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings Populate it. With nothing set, DatabaseSettings points at a local SQLite file, .hinoki/local.sqlite3 . To use another database, pick one source: Source Use it for Example Nothing local development on SQLite – .env one URL on your machine ( hinoki new --database postgresql writes a .env.example to copy; keep .env out of git) NOTES_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://notes:secret@localhost:5432/notes Environment containers and CI export NOTES_DATABASE__URL_FILE=/run/secrets/database-url settings.toml non-secret fields ( engine , host , name , user ), with the password from the environment; add toml="settings.toml" to the class connection fields The prefix ( NOTES_ ) comes from the settings class, and __ separates the group from the field. Until you set one of them, a project created with --database postgresql still uses the local SQLite file, and so do its migrations. Check it. hinoki settings , run from the project root, shows each value with its source; the URL and the password are redacted: $ hinoki settings | grep DATABASE__URL NOTES_DATABASE__URL .env *** hinoki migrations status names the database it will use, and fails with a clear error if the server does not answer: $ hinoki migrations status database: postgresql://***@127.0.0.1:5432/notes (from settings: ProjectSettings.database) status connects and records its migration ledger, so on SQLite it creates the database file. Create the tables. Hinoki never creates tables or runs migrations at startup (it only creates the local SQLite file): run hinoki migrations apply once you have models ( migrations ). The rest of this page lists every field, the URL forms and each backend.
docs.title: Set up a database in four steps

docs.text: Declare a database field on the project settings. hinoki new adds it when you choose a database. # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" , toml = "settings.toml" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings Each worker opens one bounded pool during startup and closes it during shutdown. Importing models or routes never opens a connection, and no modules= entry is needed. The file named by toml= must exist, even if it is empty: otherwise the settings fail to load with settings.toml: TOML file cannot be read or parsed . Configure a server database with connection fields or with one URL . Setting both is an error when settings load.
docs.title: Configure the application

docs.text: Put non-secret fields in the TOML file named by toml= . Keep the settings in their own file: hinoki.toml is the project manifest, and its tables are not settings. PostgreSQL MySQL MariaDB SQLite # settings.toml [database] engine = "postgresql" name = "notes" user = "notes" host = "db.example.test" port = 5432 options = [ "sslmode=verify-full" , "sslrootcert=/run/secrets/db-ca.pem" ] max_size = 10 # per worker # settings.toml [database] engine = "mysql" name = "notes" user = "notes" host = "db.example.test" # settings.toml [database] engine = "mariadb" name = "notes" user = "notes" host = "db.example.test" # settings.toml [database] engine = "sqlite" name = ".hinoki/local.sqlite3" The password is a secret setting. It never comes from TOML: export NOTES_DATABASE__PASSWORD_FILE = /run/secrets/db-password Field Meaning Default engine sqlite , postgresql , mysql or mariadb ( settings.DatabaseEngine ) – name database name, or the file path for SQLite – user , password credentials; password is secret ( *_PASSWORD or *_PASSWORD_FILE ) – host , port server address; for PostgreSQL host may be a Unix-socket directory such as /var/run/postgresql localhost , backend port options key=value URL query pairs, such as sslmode () max_size connections per worker 10 Hinoki builds DatabaseSettings.url from these fields and percent-encodes the user, password and name. SQLite takes only name . options cannot carry credentials or override user , host , port or the name. docs.text: Give an agent the development MCP ¶ hinoki mcp starts an MCP server on stdio that describes your app, its rules and its models to a coding agent. It never writes source code, rules or waivers. The one exception to reading only is run_scenario , which you enable with --scenarios : it runs real handlers and can change data ( below ). hinoki mcp The application defaults to project.application in hinoki.toml , the rules to the app's own Hinoki(rules=...) and the package to the application's package; pass --models to describe models. Projects made by hinoki new contain a .mcp.json that starts this server for the agent. Protocol messages go to stdout as newline-delimited JSON-RPC; diagnostics go to stderr. Options ¶ Option Default Meaning TARGET the project application Another app, as module:app --models MODULE none Model modules to describe; repeatable --rules MODULE:NAME the app's rules Another RuleSet --package NAME the target's package Packages the rules inspect; repeatable --waivers PATH as for hinoki check ( which file ) The owner's waiver file, read only; must exist. run_scenario starts the app with it too --requests PATH .hinoki/requests.jsonl Where recent_requests reads --scenarios off\|read\|write off Registers run_scenario (see below) Tools ¶ Each result is JSON in structuredContent and in a text block, with a tool_version . A failed call sets isError and carries an error message. Tool Input Result inspect_project {} App title and version; each action's id , method , path , status , access , atomic , pagination , parsers , renderers and location ; model metadata (with --models ); the enabled rule count list_rules {} Enabled rules and the waivers with their file, target, reason, owner and expiry explain_action {"action": "module.function"} Signature, docstring, access and atomic , the OpenAPI operation and the action's diagnostics. A class method or a unique bare handler name also works explain_error {"code": "validation_error"} Meaning and fix of a framework error code, HTTP error code or rule ID check_project {} or {"phase": "static"} Rule diagnostics with waivers applied, plus ok and failing ; phase is startup or static . Effectful checks are not run propose_model {"name": "Article", "fields": [...]} ; optional table , owner , path , unique_together Source text for a model, its input, patch and output Schema classes and CRUD actions. Returned, never written. Field types: str , int , float , bool , uuid , datetime , with nullable , unique , max_length recent_requests {} or {"limit": 20, "status_min": 400, "path_contains": "/invoices"} The newest requests the development server answered ( method , path , query , status , duration_ms , lane ), oldest first; limit is 1 to 200 recent_requests reads the file Kiso writes when server.recent_requests is set; it keeps about the last 1 to 2 MiB, and without it the result is empty with a note. The query field is the raw query string and is not redacted: keep tokens out of query strings and treat the file as sensitive. Run requests against the app ¶ --scenarios read or --scenarios write adds run_scenario . Its input needs path (a plain URL path starting with / ); method (default GET ), query (without ? ), string headers and json are optional. The result holds the HTTP status , response headers , the body text (at most 20,000 bytes, with truncated ) and the parsed JSON when there is some. Mode Methods read GET , HEAD , OPTIONS , QUERY write Also POST , PUT , PATCH , DELETE Scenarios run your real handlers The app's lifespan and handlers run in-process, so even read can change data (a GET handler may write). Each request has a 15-second limit. Enable scenarios only yourself, never on an agent's request, and only against a disposable database. Errors and edge cases ¶ A failed app startup is reported to the client without its message, which may contain a connection string; the details go to stderr. Rule checks with side effects are never run by this server; use hinoki check --allow-effects . The server was exercised with the official mcp Python client (initialize, tools/list , tools/call ); other clients are untested. See also ¶ Build with a coding agent Expose actions over MCP hinoki mcp options

docs.text: Use other libraries ¶ Hinoki has its own Schema and Model classes. It does not accept Pydantic, SQLAlchemy or Django models as request bodies, responses or tables. This page says why, what that costs, and which extension points exist today. Why the framework owns them ¶ One declaration feeds every output. Request binding, the response check, OpenAPI, application MCP, the admin and rules read the same Schema and Model classes, so they can promise the same contract. The hot paths are native. Routing, selected request parsing and ORM execution run in Rust against Hinoki's own declarations, without calling back into a validation library or a foreign ORM per request. Rules need known structure. "A response Schema never exposes password_hash " is checkable because the Schema is an inspectable Hinoki class. What this costs ¶ A library that expects its own model type does not plug in: a Pydantic-based SDK, a SQLAlchemy extension or a Django app cannot be given a Hinoki Model or Schema . There is no adapter from SQLAlchemy, Django or Pydantic models, and no plugin system. Databases are SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB through Hinoki's own drivers; another ORM's connections are not shared with its pool. Bring a library anyway ¶ Anything that works on plain Python data works with Hinoki. Schema.to_dict() and Schema.dump() return plain data, and a Schema is built from plain values: # notes/apps/quotes/api.py from hinoki import Schema , http from notes.apps.quotes.client import fetch_quote # any library returning plain data class Quote ( Schema ): symbol : str price : float @http . get ( "/ {symbol} " , access = None ) async def quote ( symbol : str ) -> Quote : raw = await fetch_quote ( symbol ) return Quote ( symbol = raw [ "symbol" ], price = raw [ "price" ]) Keep the translation at the edge of the handler, and keep a second store's connections in a module so their lifetime follows the worker. Hinoki does not time-box what that code does. Extension points ¶ You want to Use Guide Add an authentication scheme Subclass BearerAuth , APIKeyAuth or HeaderAuth Authentication Reuse a permission rule A typed Access policy Authentication Accept or answer another body format A parser or renderer Parsers and renderers Translate a library's exception app.error_handler(Kind) Errors Own a resource per worker A module with ctx.provide and ctx.get , or a DatabaseModule subclass Modules Enforce a team convention Subclass hinoki.rules.Rule Rules Add typed configuration settings.AppSettings Settings Ship routes in a package Anything a routes list accepts: a function, a RouteGroup , an API class, a Mount , or an object with an api() method Register routes Expose actions to an agent expose_as_mcp with an allowlist Expose actions over MCP Add metrics, tracing or other cross-cutting behaviour Wrap the ASGI application Serving Run where only WSGI is available WSGIAdapter Serving Cross-cutting behaviour around an action belongs in a middleware , which behaves the same on Kiso and Granian. An ASGI wrapper still works on Granian and sees the request before and after Hinoki. To run another web application next to Hinoki, put it behind the same reverse proxy or dispatch by path in your own ASGI code. See also ¶ Concepts Project status Glossary

docs.text: Requests and responses ¶ This page covers what one action receives and what it returns. How to organise actions is in Function-based APIs and Class-based APIs ; how they reach the application is in Register routes . The fragments below add actions to the invoices group of the Billing app, which supplies their access policy and transactions. Declare an action ¶ # notes/api.py from hinoki import Schema , http class Health ( Schema ): status : str @http . get ( "/health" ) def health () -> Health : return Health ( status = "ok" ) Use @http.get , @http.post , @http.put , @http.patch , @http.delete or @http.query ( from hinoki import http ), or the same methods on a RouteGroup . Hinoki also answers HEAD through each GET route: it runs the GET response path and returns the same status and representation headers without a body, so the GET handler runs for HEAD requests too. A 405 response's Allow header includes HEAD whenever GET is available. Option Meaning status Success status (default 200 ) access Access policy; None is public atomic True runs the action in a transaction ( transactions ); there is no transaction option pagination Page-number policy ( pagination ) parsers , renderers Body formats in and out ( codecs ) errors APIError classes the action may raise ( errors ) rate_limit A rate-limit policy ( below ) validate_response False skips the response check replaces Class form only ( class pitfalls ) Each option is checked when the route is declared or registered. The fragments below continue notes/apps/billing/api.py from function APIs . Besides its imports they use these: from typing import Annotated from hinoki import XML , Field , Form , MultiPartParser , Query , Request , UploadedFile Read with a body: @http.query ¶ QUERY is the HTTP method for a read whose input does not fit a query string: it is safe and idempotent like GET , and carries a body like POST . # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) class InvoiceSearch ( Schema ): text : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 40 )] limit : Annotated [ int , Field ( ge = 1 , le = 100 )] = 20 @invoices . query ( "/search" ) async def search_invoices ( data : InvoiceSearch ) -> list [ InvoiceOut ]: rows = await Invoice . filter ( reference__contains = data . text ) . limit ( data . limit ) return InvoiceOut . from_models ( rows ) curl -X QUERY http://127.0.0.1:8000/billing/invoices/search -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"text": "2026"}' The body is bound, parsed and validated exactly as for POST : the same parsers, size limit and 400 / 413 / 415 / 422 answers. A QUERY action must not change state. RouteGroup(atomic=True) applies to POST , PUT , PATCH and DELETE only; pass atomic=True on the action if the read needs a transaction. @http.query inside an API class works like the other methods. A 405 answer lists QUERY in Allow where it is available; HEAD is answered through GET routes only. Hinoki sends no Accept-Query or cache headers by itself. The method is recent. Granian passes it through over ASGI and WSGI (both are tested), but a proxy, gateway, firewall or HTTP client may reject it, and browsers send a CORS preflight for it. Keep a GET or POST route beside it when clients cannot send QUERY . In the OpenAPI document a QUERY operation appears under the path's x-query field; see OpenAPI . Bind request values ¶ Typed path parameters come from the path, query parameters from the query string, and a body parameter from the request body. Declare request: Request as the first parameter when you need headers, cookies or raw request data; it is injected only when that parameter is annotated. # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) class InvoiceLabel ( Schema ): id : UUID locale : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 35 )] @invoices . get ( "/ {invoice_id} /label" ) async def invoice_label ( request : Request , invoice_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceLabel : locale = request . headers . get ( "accept-language" , "en" )[: 35 ] return InvoiceLabel ( id = invoice_id , locale = locale ) Request path, query and body values are validated before the handler runs; a Schema body uses Schema.validate() and reports nested field errors with its parameter prefix. Discriminated request variants belong in a wrapper Schema field ( Annotated[Cat | Dog, Field(discriminator="kind")] ); bare union body parameters are not supported. Hinoki does not coerce input values into different types, except in Query[...] , Form[...] and XML[...] . Return a Schema built from the row: InvoiceOut.from_model(row) or InvoiceOut.from_models(rows) ( model schemas ). A returned dict where a Schema is declared is a 500 internal_error ( the response check ). Use a wrapper Schema for a discriminated response union too; bare union return annotations are rejected by OpenAPI generation. Query strings as a Schema ¶ Query[...] reads a whole query string into a Schema , for any method: # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) class InvoiceFilter ( Schema ): paid : bool = False limit : Annotated [ int , Field ( ge = 1 , le = 100 )] = 20 @invoices . get ( "/recent" ) async def recent_invoices ( filters : Query [ InvoiceFilter ]) -> InvoiceRecent : rows = await Invoice . filter ( paid = filters . paid ) . limit ( filters . limit ) return InvoiceRecent ( items = InvoiceOut . from_models ( rows )) # ?paid=true&limit=5 Text is converted to the int , float and bool the Schema declares before the strict validation (a repeated key fills a list field, a single one still does). A value that does not convert, a repeated key for a scalar, a missing required field and an unknown key (by default) are 422 errors, reported with the parameter name as prefix. The Schema owns the whole query string, so the action takes no other query or page parameters, at most one Query[...] , and it cannot be a path parameter. OpenAPI lists one query parameter per field. Form bodies ¶ A plain Schema parameter is a strict JSON body. Wrap it in Form[...] to read the same Schema from a form, whose values are all text: # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . post ( "/import" , status = 201 ) async def import_invoice ( data : Form [ InvoiceIn ]) -> InvoiceOut : return InvoiceOut . from_model ( await Invoice . acreate ( data )) # reference=INV-1 Before validation, text is converted to the int , float and bool the Schema declares (and a lone value of a list field becomes a one-item list); Schema and JSON stay strict. A value that does not convert, or several values for a scalar, fails with the normal 422 type error. Empty text is not turned into None , and nested Schema fields are not read from form keys. An action with a Form[...] parameter and no parsers= uses FormParser (add MultiPartParser() explicitly for multipart text fields). Form[...] is valid only for the Schema body of a POST, PUT, PATCH or QUERY action, takes only form parsers (a JSON body needs a plain Schema parameter, so one cannot be coerced by mistake), and appears in OpenAPI as application/x-www-form-urlencoded . XML bodies ¶ XML[...] reads a Schema from an application/xml body: the elements under the root become the fields, text is converted to the declared int , float and bool , and the strict validation follows. # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) class Line ( Schema ): sku : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 40 )] qty : int class Order ( Schema ): customer : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 120 )] lines : list [ Line ] @invoices . post ( "/orders" , status = 201 ) async def receive_order ( data : XML [ Order ]) -> OrderReceipt : return OrderReceipt ( lines = len ( data . lines )) # <order><customer>Ada</customer><lines><sku>a</sku><qty>2</qty></lines></order> A repeated element is a list (a single one still fills a list field), nested elements fill nested Schema fields, and an empty element is None . Attributes are not read and namespace prefixes are dropped ( <a:x> and <b:x> are both x ). Malformed XML, a DTD, a custom entity, mixed text and child elements, a character XML 1.0 forbids (a control character other than tab, carriage return and line feed, written directly or as  ), an encoding declaration other than UTF-8, or exceeding XMLParser(max_depth=..., max_elements=...) is 400 invalid_xml . max_depth defaults to 32 and may be raised to at most 1000 ( hinoki.parsers.MAX_XML_DEPTH ); a larger value raises ValueError when the parser is created. As with Form[...] , the action takes only XMLParser (selected when parsers= is omitted), and the OpenAPI document lists application/xml . Upload files ¶ Bind a file by the multipart field name. An action that declares a file parameter and no parsers= gets MultiPartParser() automatically, with its default limits, unless the application's parsers= include one; pass parsers=[MultiPartParser(...)] to change them. UploadedFile contains the client filename, claimed content type and in-memory bytes ; it does not save files or validate their content. # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . post ( "/ {invoice_id} /attachments" , status = 201 , parsers = [ MultiPartParser ( max_parts = 4 , max_part_bytes = 512_000 )], ) async def attach ( request : Request , invoice_id : UUID , document : UploadedFile ) -> Attached : title = request . POST . get ( "title" , "" )[: 120 ] # Validate content and choose a generated storage name before saving. return Attached ( title = title , filename = document . filename , size = document . size ) @invoices . post ( "/ {invoice_id} /scans" , status = 201 ) # MultiPartParser() selected async def attach_scans ( invoice_id : UUID , scans : list [ UploadedFile ]) -> Attached : ... UploadedFile requires exactly one part with that name. list[UploadedFile] requires at least one and keeps repeated parts in order. To make a single file optional, write file: UploadedFile | None = None . These declarations cannot be combined with a Schema body parameter. Use request.POST for adjacent text fields or request.FILES when names or repetitions are dynamic. Parser precedence for a file action: its own parsers= (which must then include MultiPartParser , or registration fails), then an application-wide Hinoki(parsers=[...]) that includes a MultiPartParser , then the automatic MultiPartParser() . An application parser list without multipart does not apply to file actions, and actions without file parameters keep their parsers. All declared files require multipart/form-data . A missing file is a 422 validation error; a wrong media type is 415 ; malformed multipart is 400 ; a part or complete body over its configured limit is 413 payload_too_large . A zero-byte body with no Content-Type is treated as absent input for optional files; an explicitly multipart empty body is malformed, while a valid closing-boundary-only body has no parts. The default complete-body limit is 1 MiB, and the parser buffers bytes in memory: this API is for bounded small uploads, not streaming. Warning Concurrent uploads multiply memory use. Keep limits conservative, never use the supplied filename as a filesystem path, and verify content instead of trusting the declared media type. See parsers and renderers and testing uploads . Responses ¶ Return a value matching the declared response type, or return Response ( from hinoki import Response ) when the handler must set a status, headers or body that a typed result cannot express, annotated as InvoiceOut | Response . Declare expected APIError subclasses in errors=(...) ; their status, stable code and message feed the OpenAPI document and the strict test client ( errors ). Paginated actions are described in pagination . Rate limit an action ¶ Hinoki ships no limiter. A route names a policy with rate_limit= , and the application owns the rule, the key and the storage, because a counter kept in one worker's memory is wrong across workers and after a restart: # notes/apps/accounts/api.py from hinoki import RateLimitContext , errors , http from .schemas import LoginIn , SessionOut from .stores import RedisStore # your module's resource class LoginLimit : async def check ( self , context : RateLimitContext ) -> None : store = context . resource ( RedisStore ) # provided by a module, per worker if not await store . allow ( f "login: { context . client } " , limit = 5 , window = 60 ): raise errors . TooManyRequests ( retry_after = 60 ) @http . post ( "/auth/login" , rate_limit = LoginLimit (), atomic = True ) async def login ( data : LoginIn ) -> SessionOut : ... check is def or async def and returns to allow the request. It runs after the route is matched and the caller authenticated, and before the body is read, parsed or handled, so a refused request costs neither a body read nor a password hash. A sync check runs on the bounded executor, so it must use a sync client with finite timeouts (cancelling the waiter does not stop its thread); an async one runs on the event loop. RateLimitContext holds only method , route (the path template), client (the trusted client address, None when unknown; a forwarded address counts only from a configured trusted proxy), caller (the authenticated Caller , None on a public route) and resource(kind) , which returns the worker-owned resource that a module provided, such as a Redis client or the Database . It carries no headers, credentials, body or query values. The refusal is errors.TooManyRequests(retry_after) : status 429, code rate_limited , and Retry-After set to retry_after , a whole number of seconds from 1 to 86,400 (anything else is refused when the error is created). The route documents it in OpenAPI by itself, with Retry-After as a required integer header. Only that error answers 429. Any other exception from the policy or its store, including a TooManyRequests that was built without its constructor, is answered 503 rate_limit_unavailable : the request is refused rather than allowed unchecked, the answer and the log name the route and never the exception, and the application's error handlers and debug output never see it. Cancellation is not caught. Limiting failed credentials of a BearerAuth provider belongs in that provider, because authentication runs first. The response is checked against the annotation ¶ Every action's return value is checked against its return annotation, and the annotation itself is checked when the app starts. There is nothing to switch on. # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . get ( "/ {invoice_id} /raw" ) async def raw_invoice ( invoice_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceOut : return { "id" : invoice_id } # a dict is not an InvoiceOut: 500 internal_error At startup. An annotation that cannot be checked stops the app with a RegistrationError that names the action: no annotation, Any , object , set[...] , a plain class, or Response inside a collection. Annotate a concrete type, or declare the action with validate_response=False to skip the check for that action. At runtime. A result that does not match is a 500 internal_error , because the fault is the server's, not the client's. With the debug setting on (development only; hinoki dev does not turn it on) the answer names the action, the type it returned and the annotation it broke, for example raw_invoice returned a dict that does not match its return annotation InvoiceOut . Without debug the body is generic. The log and the answer never contain the value itself. With atomic=True the check runs inside the transaction, so a mismatch rolls the write back. What is accepted. A Schema class, list[...] , dict[str, ...] and Page[...] of these, str , int , float , bool (a bool is not an int ), bytes , datetime , date , UUID , Decimal , None , plain dict and list , Any or object as an item type, and unions of these. Annotated[...] is unwrapped. The check never coerces. Response . -> Response and InvoiceOut | Response are accepted: a returned Response carries its own status, headers and body and is not checked. The OpenAPI document describes InvoiceOut | Response by its typed arm, InvoiceOut . Actions with a bodyless status ( 204 , 304 ) are not checked. What it does not check. A Schema instance is valid by construction, so the check is about the shape of the result, not the field values. A custom renderer or a dump() override can still change the bytes afterwards. See also ¶ Errors Parsers and renderers Authentication
