docs.text: Errors ¶ Hinoki separates malformed requests, authentication failures and application errors. Handlers may declare the application errors they can raise so clients and generated tools can inspect the contract. Built-in HTTP errors ¶ Every public error type lives in one namespace: from hinoki import errors . It holds errors.BadRequest , errors.Unauthorized , errors.Forbidden , errors.NotFound and errors.Conflict , each derived from errors.APIError , plus the framework's own failures ( errors.RegistrationError , errors.ValidationError , errors.ObjectNotFound , errors.ErrorRegistry and the others listed in the reference ). They carry an HTTP status and a stable code . Raise them when the response is an expected part of the API: from hinoki import errors , http class TaskAlreadyDone ( errors . Conflict ): code = "task_already_done" message = "The task is already done." @http . post ( "/tasks/ {task_id} /complete" , errors = ( errors . NotFound , TaskAlreadyDone )) async def complete ( task_id : UUID ) -> TaskOutput : ... An action may declare several errors. The runtime maps a declared APIError to its status and response body. Unexpected exceptions remain server errors; do not expose exception text to clients. Your own errors need no registration ¶ Every APIError subclass answers by itself with its status , code and message . Pick the base class whose status you want and raise it: Base class Status Use it for errors.BadRequest 400 a malformed or refused request errors.Unauthorized 401 the caller is not authenticated errors.Forbidden 403 the caller may not do this errors.NotFound 404 the resource does not exist errors.Conflict 409 the request contradicts the current state (a duplicate, already done) errors.TooManyRequests 429 a route's rate limit policy refused the request; retry_after seconds are sent as Retry-After errors.APIError the status you set anything else class PaymentDeclined ( errors . BadRequest ): # answers 400 on its own code = "payment_declined" message = "The payment was declined." class QuotaExceeded ( errors . APIError ): # any other status status = 402 code = "quota_exceeded" message = "The quota is used up." Declare them on the action with errors=(PaymentDeclined,) for the contract (OpenAPI, MCP, strict_errors ). Nothing else is needed. Exceptions you cannot change ¶ A library or the database raises its own exception, which is not an HTTP error, and the client would receive 500 internal_error . Answer it with a function on the app. The function receives the exception and returns the APIError to send; an instance can set its own status : # notes/main.py (continued) from hinoki import errors from notes.apps.billing.gateway import CardDeclined @app . error_handler ( CardDeclined ) def card_declined ( error : CardDeclined ) -> errors . APIError : return errors . APIError ( error . reason , status = 402 , code = "card_declined" ) CardDeclined stands for any exception your code or a library raises, here one the Billing app's payment gateway client defines. The most specific class wins: a handler for HardQuota is used before one for its base Quota . Application handlers are consulted before the built-in ones. A handler may be def or async def . One that fails, or does not return an APIError , counts as "not handled" and the client receives 500 internal_error without the exception text. An exception type can be registered once (a second registration raises ValueError ), and only before the app serves (afterwards RegistrationError ). The decorator returns the function unchanged. A class or a value that is not a function is refused with TypeError . app.errors.handle(Kind) is the same call without the app checks. The decorator needs the module-level app ( Register routes ); app.error_handler(Kind)(handler) registers a function defined elsewhere. Built in, with nothing to write: ObjectNotFound is answered with 404 not_found , and a database UniqueViolation with 409 unique_conflict ( errors.UniqueConflict ) without exposing the constraint name. Register your own handler to replace either. Validation and binding errors ¶ Input that does not match a path, query, header or body annotation fails before the handler runs. Schema validation is strict and reports field paths with 422 . Unsupported content types receive 415 ; malformed supported content receives a parser error. A body larger than execution.max_body_bytes , or a multipart part larger than its parser's max_part_bytes , receives 413 payload_too_large . Query strings over execution.max_query_bytes receive 414 uri_too_long ; combined headers over execution.max_header_bytes receive 431 headers_too_large . A Host outside the allowed_hosts setting receives 400 disallowed_host , and a CORS preflight from an origin outside cors.origins receives 403 cors_origin_denied ( hosts, CORS and HTTPS ). These are framework-level failures and do not need to be listed in the action's errors= . When security.redirect_https is enabled, a plain HTTP request receives 308 with an HTTPS Location before routing or body parsing. The redirect requires an explicit allowed_hosts list and preserves the request method and target. A target that is not a path, such as OPTIONS * , is not redirected. See browser security settings . ModelValidationError is raised before an ORM insert or update when a Model field constraint or custom validator refuses a value. In an HTTP request it uses the same 422 validation_error response shape as Schema validation, including field paths, codes and messages. The admin displays the field messages in its form. Keep Schema validation at the request boundary; Model checks also cover non-HTTP writes. See Model field constraints and validators . Every HTTP request receives a request ID in the configured server.request_id_header header ( x-request-id by default). Hinoki generates the ID unless server.trust_request_id=True and the request comes from a configured trusted proxy with a valid inbound ID. Built-in error bodies also include request_id . Use the ID to connect a client report with the server log entry. Unhandled exceptions are logged with the ID and returned as 500 internal_error without exposing exception text. The debug setting adds the exception type, message and traceback to that answer for development. Check the contract ¶ Use ASGIClient(..., strict_errors=True) in tests to fail if a handler returns an error that it did not declare (an error answered by an app.error_handler counts too). hinoki check can also enforce rules about access, transaction, response and schema declarations; see rules . Earlier revisions exported these names from hinoki itself and kept the HTTP errors in hinoki.httperrors ; both are gone. Use errors.<Name> ; from hinoki import NotFound raises ImportError .

docs.text: Function-based APIs ¶ A function-based API is a set of plain async def functions, each decorated with an HTTP method, grouped by a RouteGroup that states their shared prefix, access policy, transactions and errors once. It is the default pattern in Hinoki: use it unless a class gives you something concrete. When to use it ¶ Use functions and a RouteGroup when Use a class instead when The endpoints are ordinary reads, writes or workflows You want generated CRUD routes with hooks ( @crud ) Several actions share access= , atomic= or errors= Several resources inherit or override the same actions You want handlers a test can call as plain functions You ship a resource for other projects to include A complete example ¶ The Billing app of the Notes project serves invoices. hinoki app create billing created the app directory, its routes.py and its block in hinoki.toml ; the files below are what you write. api.py routes.py hinoki.toml models.py schemas.py # notes/apps/billing/api.py from uuid import UUID from hinoki import RouteGroup , errors from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageNumberPagination , PageParams from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut invoices = RouteGroup ( "/invoices" , access = billing_staff , atomic = True ) @invoices . get ( "/" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_invoices ( page : PageParams ) -> Page [ InvoiceOut ]: """Invoices, newest first.""" return ( await Invoice . all () . apaginate ( page )) . map ( InvoiceOut . from_model ) @invoices . get ( "/ {invoice_id} " , errors = ( errors . NotFound ,)) async def get_invoice ( invoice_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceOut : return InvoiceOut . from_model ( await Invoice . aget ( id = invoice_id )) @invoices . post ( "/" , status = 201 ) async def create_invoice ( data : InvoiceIn ) -> InvoiceOut : return InvoiceOut . from_model ( await Invoice . acreate ( data )) # notes/apps/billing/routes.py from hinoki import Includable from .api import invoices routes : list [ Includable ] = [ invoices ] # hinoki.toml (the block hinoki app create billing appended) [[apps]] name = "billing" models = "notes.apps.billing.models" migrations = "notes.apps.billing.migrations" routes = "notes.apps.billing.routes:routes" prefix = "/billing" requires = [] # notes/apps/billing/models.py from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import db from hinoki.orm import Model , field , pk from hinoki.utils import utc_now @db . ordered_by ( "-created_at" ) class Invoice ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) reference : str = field ( max_length = 40 , unique = True ) paid : bool = False created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now , index = True ) # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema , derive from .models import Invoice class InvoiceIn ( Schema ): reference : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 40 )] @derive ( Invoice ) class InvoiceOut ( Schema ): ... billing_staff is an Access policy declared once in notes/security.py ( the billing policies ). notes/main.py stays as hinoki new wrote it: the application it declares binds every routes list named in hinoki.toml ( Register routes ). The manifest prefix and the group prefix join, and a "/" path means the group prefix itself: hinoki routes --path /billing GET /billing/invoices StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.api.list_invoices POST /billing/invoices StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.api.create_invoice GET /billing/invoices/{invoice_id} StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.api.get_invoice Best practices ¶ One RouteGroup per resource. State access= , atomic=True and the errors every action shares on the group. atomic=True on a group covers POST , PUT , PATCH and DELETE ; reads stay outside a transaction. Keep handlers thin. Validate with a Schema , call the model or a function in operations.py , and return XOut.from_model(...) . A handler never returns a model. Write paths relative to the app. The app's prefix lives only in hinoki.toml . Never repeat /billing in code. Paginate every list : pagination= , a PageParams parameter and Page[...] . Declare what you raise. Every APIError an action can raise belongs in its errors= (or the group's). A missing row from Model.aget is answered as errors.NotFound ( 404 not_found ). List the group in routes.py . An action is served only when its group is in the list that hinoki.toml names. Group defaults and overrides ¶ An action inherits the group's options and may override them. InvoiceSummary is a Schema with one field, open: int : # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . get ( "/summary" , access = None ) # public on purpose async def summary () -> InvoiceSummary : return InvoiceSummary ( open = await Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . acount ()) Option On the group On the action access= Default for every action Replaces it; access=None makes the action public atomic= Applies to POST , PUT , PATCH , DELETE atomic=True / False decides for this action, any method errors= Added to every action Merged with the group's A public action must also be listed in except_ of Actions.require_access in notes/rules.py , for example except_=["notes.api.health", "notes.apps.billing.api.summary"] , or the application refuses to start ( HNK-ACC-001 ). The rule exists so that public endpoints are a written decision. Actions.require_permissions ( HNK-ACC-002 ) only checks actions that have a policy, so it needs no entry. Compose with other decorators ¶ Put the HTTP decorator outermost. The group records the function it receives when @invoices.get(...) runs, so a decorator above it would not be served: # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . get ( "/export" ) @audited # your decorator, written with functools.wraps async def export_invoices () -> InvoiceExport : ... A wrapped function runs in an asyncio task. The native handler lane needs a plain async def . Test it ¶ A test builds its own application from the same routes list, so it needs neither the manifest nor a server. Mount the list at the manifest prefix to check the final paths, and pass the project's settings when the test sends requests: atomic=True needs the database they declare. # tests/billingroutestest.py from hinoki import Hinoki , Mount from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.apps.billing.routes import routes from notes.security import billing_staff from notes.settings import ProjectSettings def test_writes_are_staff_only_and_atomic () -> None : app = Hinoki ( include = [ Mount ( "/billing" , routes )]) found = app . resolve ( "POST" , "/billing/invoices" ) assert found is not None route , _ = found assert ( route . access , route . atomic ) == ( billing_staff , True ) async def test_anonymous_callers_are_refused () -> None : app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , include = [ Mount ( "/billing" , routes )]) async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : reply = await client . get ( "/billing/invoices" ) assert reply . status == 401 The handlers are plain functions, so a unit test can also await get_invoice(invoice_id) inside use_database(...) . Tests that reach the database need a disposable one; see testing . Pitfalls ¶ Symptom Cause Fix The route is missing from hinoki routes The group is not in routes.py , or the app has no routes key in hinoki.toml Add it to routes: list[Includable] Paths read /billing/billing/... The prefix is in code and in hinoki.toml Keep the app prefix in hinoki.toml only ValueError on RouteGroup("/invoices/") A prefix starts with / and does not end with one RouteGroup("/invoices") TypeError: unknown action options A misspelled keyword on a group action Use the option names listed in Requests and responses RuntimeError: a RouteGroup cannot change after it is included An action is added after the group is included Declare every action at import time RegistrationError: a RouteGroup must declare at least one action An empty group in routes.py Remove it or add an action RegistrationError: a RouteGroup can be included only once The group is listed twice in one application List it once; mount the list, not each group RegistrationError: … replaces=... only works inside an API class replaces= on a group action Remove it; it belongs to classes ValueError: … already declares an HTTP route Two HTTP decorators on one function One decorator per function RegistrationError: 1 rule violation(s) naming HNK-ACC-001 A public action not listed in notes/rules.py Add it to except_ , or give it a policy

docs.text: Installation ¶ Hinoki is pre-alpha and installs from a source checkout. You need: Python 3.12 or newer uv 0.9 or newer a stable Rust toolchain from rustup Install from source ¶ git clone https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki cd hinoki uv sync --locked uv run hinoki version uv sync --locked builds the Rust extension and installs the development tools. The last command confirms the installation: hinoki 0.0.1 Not on PyPI The hinoki name on PyPI belongs to an unrelated legacy package: do not install Hinoki by name. A project created with hinoki new points uv at this checkout in pyproject.toml ( [tool.uv.sources] ), so uv sync never fetches that package. Next: the Quick start creates and serves a project.

docs.text: Glossary ¶ One word, one meaning. "Schema" has four meanings in this field, so the docs keep the word for one of them. The four schemas ¶ Write Meaning Schema (code font) The Hinoki class for typed, validated request and response data: class InvoiceIn(Schema) . Always capitalised and in code font; say "a response Schema ". table state, migration state What the migration planner records about the tables ( migrations/NNNN-name.state.json ). Never "the database schema". OpenAPI document The generated /openapi.json . Its components.schemas entries are "OpenAPI schema objects". JSON Schema The standard the OpenAPI document uses to describe bodies, always by its name. Names ¶ Name Origin Hinoki 檜, the Japanese cypress of temples: fragrant, durable wood. Kiso Hinoki's Rust server, named after the Kiso Valley (Nagano, Japan), known for its hinoki forests such as Akasawa. Projects and apps ¶ Term Meaning manifest hinoki.toml : the project's application, its apps, their prefixes and dependencies. project application The Hinoki object named by project.application ( notes.main:app ); the one a server process serves. app A package listed under [[apps]] : models, migrations and a routes.py . Not a second Hinoki object. app prefix The path an app's routes are mounted under, set only in hinoki.toml ( /billing ). target module:attribute naming an app, such as notes.main:app . Commands use project.application from hinoki.toml when it is omitted. Code ¶ Term Meaning Model A class mapped to a table. Without @db.table , the name is <app>_<plural> : notes.apps.billing.models.Invoice → billing_invoices . A column reaches a client only through a Schema . action One declared endpoint ( @http.get , @invoices.post , ...): a function or an API class method. route group A RouteGroup : functions under one path prefix with shared access= , atomic= and errors= . Access The access policy of an action: an authentication provider and required permissions. Caller Who is making the request, as resolved by the provider.

docs.text: Guides ¶ One page per task. Start with data and endpoints, then add access, rules and runtime concerns as you need them. New to Hinoki? Take the tutorial or the quick start first. Data ¶ Configure a database : choose the backend, set the URL or connection fields, keep credentials secret. Define models : columns, primary keys, column types, table names and write-time validators. Model options : indexes, composite uniqueness, default order, update timestamps and names, as decorators. Relations : foreign keys, one-to-one, many-to-many association models and explicit loading. Query and write rows : filters, pagination, reusable queries, creates, updates and bulk writes. Lifecycle hooks : react to a model's own writes and inspect its changed columns. Migrations : plan, review, apply and check migrations for every app. Schemas : declare the data that crosses the API boundary and convert it to and from rows. Scalar field types : enums, literals, dates, decimals, bytes, addresses, secrets and paths. Collections and unions : sets, tuples, dictionaries, unions, discriminated unions, TypedDicts and dataclasses. Validate input : constraints, normalization, field and object checks, and input reshaping. Schemas from models : derive a Schema from a Model and convert rows with from_model . Time and utilities : UTC time, the application timezone, test clocks and update timestamps. Endpoints ¶ Function-based APIs : the default pattern: plain functions grouped by a RouteGroup that states access, transactions and errors once. Class-based APIs : API classes for @crud resources with hooks, inheritance and resources you ship to others. Register routes : how routes.py and hinoki.toml build the route map, with Mount , include= in tests and hinoki routes . Requests and responses : what an action receives (path, query, body, forms, XML, files) and how its result is checked. Generate CRUD routes : list, retrieve and write actions from a model, with access and ownership rules. Errors : malformed requests, authentication failures and declared application errors. Middleware : typed Middleware around an action or the whole app, identical on Kiso and Granian. Pagination : page-number pagination with PageNumberPagination . Parsers and renderers : other body formats in and out. OpenAPI document : the OpenAPI 3.1 document generated from routes, signatures and Schema declarations. Security and checks ¶ Authentication and access : providers resolve a Caller ; Access policies check permissions. Hosts, CORS and HTTPS : restrict the host names an app answers to, which browser origins may read it, browser security headers, HTTPS redirects and trusted proxies. Rules : typed promises about your application, checked with a stable ID, a location and an explanation. Runtime ¶ Application modules : resources that live as long as a worker, such as a database pool. Transactions : atomic=True on actions, db.atomic in application code. Settings : typed, immutable settings from the environment, dotenv and TOML, with redacted secrets. Serve an application : hinoki dev while you work, hinoki serve in production, on Kiso (the default) or Granian. Kiso server : what Hinoki's Rust server runs natively, its limits, workers and signals, reload and reverse-proxy behaviour. Test an application : test through the whole stack with ASGIClient , against a disposable database, from the test hinoki new generates. Command line : every hinoki command, the short forms inside a project and the explicit forms outside one. Create a project : the interactive hinoki new flow, its options and what the generated project contains. Inspect an application : check rules, list routes, export the OpenAPI document, show settings and diagnose the environment. Interactive shell : an async-capable prompt with the app's settings and models. Typing : what a type checker catches in handlers, decorators and Schema construction. Integrations ¶ Add an admin : staff pages for your models, with a sign-in page, users and per-model permissions. Customize the admin : columns, hooks, bulk actions, templates and themes. Expose actions over MCP : selected actions as tools for a remote MCP client. Development MCP : a server that describes your app to a coding agent; it can run requests against the app only when you enable --scenarios . Build with a coding agent : a project, rules and tools ready for an agent, and where its authority ends. Operating ¶ Sync and async code : the event loop, the bounded sync pool and which style each surface accepts. Benchmarks : retained measurements with their environment, method and limits. Native CRUD orientation run : a workload-specific measurement of generated CRUD. Concepts and project ¶ Concepts : how models, Schema classes, actions, workers and rules fit together. Request lifecycle : the order of routing, access, binding, handler, commit and response. Structure an application : layers, where each concern lives, and why. Glossary : one word, one meaning. Use other libraries : what owning Schema and Model means, and the extension points. Reference : public names, signatures and docstrings. Status : what works today and what does not yet. Documentation versions : how dev and release docs are published. Troubleshooting : common errors by their message. Toolchain and CI : local and CI commands for contributors.

docs.text: Inspect an application ¶ These commands load the application, report and exit. None of them serves requests, opens a database or writes files (except openapi --output ): uv run hinoki doctor uv run hinoki routes Each accepts --format json for scripts. On a colour terminal the reports use ✔ ok, ▲ warning, ✘ failed and – skipped; piped output, NO_COLOR and TERM=dumb give plain text. Diagnose a project with doctor ¶ uv run hinoki doctor uv run hinoki doctor --format json With no target, doctor uses project.application from hinoki.toml . If there is no manifest or default target, it reports environment checks and marks app checks as skipped. An explicit TARGET names another app ( module:app ). Loading it imports your Python code, so module-level code may have its own side effects. Hinoki does not start app or module lifespans, run hooks, start a server, run architecture rules, connect to a database, or write files. The report covers manifest validity, Python/native extension and optional Granian availability, route registration, configured typed settings, and in-memory OpenAPI generation. An app with no settings object reports that check as skipped; a custom non- Settings object is a warning. JSON output has schema_version: 1 and stable check IDs. Settings values and exception messages are not included. Exit status is 0 when no diagnostic failed, 1 for invalid manifest or app diagnostics, and 2 when a requested target cannot be loaded. Warnings and skipped checks remain visible. Database connectivity and applied migration state are intentionally separate: use hinoki migrations status for the live ledger and hinoki migrations plan --check for model-to-file drift. Check the rules with check ¶ uv run hinoki check uv run hinoki check --phase static Option Effect Default --rules MODULE:ATTRIBUTE the RuleSet to run the application's rules= --package PACKAGE package for the static import checks; repeat for several the package that contains the target --phase startup\|static run one phase both --waivers PATH waiver file; must exist the app's waivers= , else hinoki-rules.toml at the project root ( which file ) --format text\|json human or versioned JSON output text --allow-effects also run checks declared effectful (files, network, database) off Exit status is 0 when no rule fails, 1 for violations and 2 when the target or the checks cannot run. An application with no rules passes with 0 rule(s) and a warning on standard error, since nothing was checked. What each rule checks, and how to read and waive a result, is in Rules . List routes with routes ¶ uv run hinoki routes GET /billing/invoices StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.api.list_invoices POST /billing/invoices StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.api.create_invoice GET /billing/invoices/{invoice_id} StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.api.get_invoice GET /health public notes.api.health Each row is method, path, access (the provider and its permissions, or public ) and handler, sorted by path. The handler is the action's rule subject, the name that except_ and waivers match: an action of an API class is named after the class it is mounted on, even when it inherits the method. --path keeps paths that start with the prefix, --method one method; no match prints no routes match and exits 1: uv run hinoki routes --path /billing --method GET GET /billing/invoices StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.api.list_invoices GET /billing/invoices/{invoice_id} StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.api.get_invoice --lanes adds, per route, whether Kiso runs the handler natively ( native ) or through the Python pipeline ( python ), with the reason. The access log's lane field means something narrower: a request for a native route here still logs python unless Rust runs a generated CRUD plan for it. JSON always has method , path , handler , access , status , lane and lane_reason . Export the OpenAPI document with openapi ¶ uv run hinoki openapi --output openapi.json uv run hinoki openapi --check openapi.json uv run hinoki openapi --breaking-against openapi-baseline.json The command builds the app without serving it or opening a database; it works even when openapi_url is disabled. With no file option it prints deterministic JSON (sorted keys, two-space indentation and a trailing newline). --output FILE writes those bytes. --check FILE compares parsed JSON, so formatting differences do not count as drift. Exit status is 0 when the file matches or is written, 1 when its JSON differs, and 2 when the target cannot load or the check file is missing or invalid JSON. --output and --check cannot be used together. --breaking-against BASELINE compares the generated document with an earlier OpenAPI JSON file (the released version) and prints one breaking: … line per change that would break an existing client. Reported: a removed operation or success response, new or newly required request input, a removed response property, a changed type, and a request enum that narrows or a response enum that widens. Additions are compatible and are not reported. Exit status is 0 when nothing breaks, 1 when something does, and 2 when the target cannot load or the baseline is missing or not a JSON object. It cannot be combined with --output or --check . The comparison reads the documents only; it does not check behavior that an OpenAPI document does not describe. Run --check in CI to catch an OpenAPI document that drifted from the code, and --breaking-against with the last released document before a release. See OpenAPI for what the document contains. Show settings with settings ¶ uv run hinoki settings uv run hinoki settings --format json uv run hinoki settings --example The target is an application with typed settings or a settings class ( notes.settings:ProjectSettings ). Each value is shown with where it came from; settings.Secret values are redacted. --prefix , --dotenv and --toml replace the sources the class declares. --example prints a .env.example with defaults and types, leaving required fields blank and commenting out optional values with no printable default (secrets, unset values). See Settings . Report versions with version ¶ uv run hinoki version --verbose The default prints hinoki X.Y.Z . --verbose adds the Python version, platform, native extension path and Granian version; Granian is reported as not installed when its optional package is absent. Use --format json for machine-readable output. Details the binding does not expose, including its bundled SQLite library version, are omitted rather than inferred. Errors and edge cases ¶ A target that does not import prints an error: line with the import failure ( error: cannot load TARGET: … for routes and openapi ) and exits non-zero (2 for check , routes and openapi ). Importing the target runs your module-level code; keep import-time side effects out of it. openapi options --output , --check and --breaking-against exclude each other. doctor without hinoki.toml still checks the environment and marks the application checks skipped. See also ¶ Rules OpenAPI Troubleshooting Command line

docs.text: Kiso, Hinoki's Rust server ¶ Kiso is the HTTP server inside Hinoki's native extension, written in Rust on hyper, tokio and rustls. It is what hinoki dev and hinoki serve run unless you choose Granian, and it can answer many requests without entering Python. hinoki serve --workers 4 # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): server : settings . ServerSettings = settings . ServerSettings ( server = "kiso" , workers = 4 ) --server kiso selects it explicitly when a project defaults to Granian. Choose Granian instead when you need an ASGI wrapper around the application ( Serve an application ). What is native and what still runs in Python ¶ The listener, HTTP/1.1 parsing, connection and header limits, body framing and its limits and timeouts, route matching, the request ID, and the answers that need no application code run on the native runtime without taking the Python interpreter lock. Without host, CORS or HTTPS-redirect policies, a request the native layer can answer by itself is answered there: unknown paths and methods ( 404 , 405 with Allow ), oversized request lines or headers, 503 while the worker is not ready or the in-flight limit is reached, and malformed requests. When one of those policies is active, the Rust classifier checks it first and then answers unmatched requests itself, with the same CORS headers as the Python pipeline. The response carries the same security headers, request ID, CORS and HSTS policy as one produced by the application. The lifespan, handwritten handlers and their database calls still use Python. The OpenAPI document and the documentation pages and assets are built once at startup by the same Python code and answered by the Rust classifier for GET and HEAD (other methods continue to route lookup), with the same status, headers, request ID, CORS and security headers; they cross into Python only when a request target is not plain ASCII. Host allow-list checks, CORS preflight answers and HTTPS redirects run in the Rust classifier before docs and route lookup, with the same response order and headers as the Python pipeline. For matched routes that continue through the Python pipeline, Kiso also percent-decodes the captured path values and passes them to Python; an invalid UTF-8 escape is carried as an error marker and reported at the same point where the pipeline previously decoded it. Python still applies str , int , UUID, bool and custom converters, and owns authentication, hooks, body/query binding, handlers, error translation and response assembly. For an eligible public GET , DELETE , POST , PUT , PATCH or QUERY function, Kiso skips Python route matching and request binding. It accepts parameters from the path and query string annotated str , int , float , bool or UUID with the built-in converter, and query parameters whose default has exactly that type. Rust decodes provided values, converts them with the same rules as the Python converters (an invalid value gives the same 422 ), validates the full query, negotiates Accept , and prepares the handler arguments. An absent optional query uses its declared default, including when a wrapper observes the keyword arguments; an empty value is still an explicitly supplied empty string. Missing required or repeated query parameters use the same validation response as the Python pipeline. Error translation and Response creation remain in Python; JSON encoding uses Hinoki's Rust encoder, and Rust finalizes the response headers and suppresses the body for HEAD . Those final headers include the CORS headers for the request's Origin , on successful and error answers alike, exactly as the Python pipeline adds them; an answer that sets its own Access-Control-Allow-Origin keeps its CORS headers. An async handler runs in its ordinary asyncio task, unless it qualifies for the native handler lane ; a sync handler uses the bounded executor. If a sync handler returns an awaitable, Hinoki awaits it on the same request task after the executor call completes. An integer longer than 18 digits is left to the Python pipeline, which applies Python's own integer limits. A body method is eligible with exactly one Schema body parameter and only built-in parsers ( JSONParser , FormParser , TextParser , BytesParser , exact types without overrides; a custom parser or a JSONParser.prepare override uses the Python pipeline). The route's parser is chosen from the Content-Type after the body is read, so an unlisted type is the same 415 . Its body is read from the native connection only when the handler's turn comes, after content negotiation, with the same limits, and is then decoded and validated by the Rust decoder and validator. The failures keep the order and the answers of the Python pipeline: a declared length above the limit or a body read failure first, then a malformed query string, then the content type ( 415 ) and malformed JSON ( 400 ), then one 422 listing every path, query and body problem in declaration order. A refusal before the body is read closes the connection, as on the Python pipeline. The automatic path does not accept several body parameters, file or Request parameters, custom parsers, multipart uploads, defaults on path parameters, custom response headers or custom renderers. The built-in JSONRenderer , HTMLRenderer , TextRenderer and XMLRenderer , alone or several on one route, are eligible: Rust negotiates Accept (including 406 ) and Python renders with the chosen one, exactly as on the Python pipeline. A subclass of a built-in renderer or one with extra attributes is custom. A route with an access policy stays eligible, with at most one Caller principal parameter: Python authenticates the request before anything else, so the order of the answers ( 400 , invalid_query , 401 / 403 ) matches the Python pipeline, and the body is still read only after authentication succeeds. When that access policy uses an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth , Rust also answers the refusals itself ( 401 with the challenge, or 403 ) without crossing into Python, and hands the admitted caller to the handler. A route with a rate_limit policy is eligible too: Python asks the policy, with the same client address as the Python pipeline (the forwarded client when the TCP peer is a trusted proxy, otherwise the peer) and the authenticated caller, right after authentication and before negotiation, the body and validation, so a refused client gets the same 429 or 503 without the server reading its body. A route with atomic=True stays eligible: the handler runs inside the same transaction as on the Python pipeline, the commit follows the encoding of the answer, and any error or timeout rolls back before it is translated. Host restrictions, CORS and HTTPS redirects are checked natively and do not make an otherwise eligible route fall back. Every other route uses the full Python request pipeline for binding, validation, error translation and response assembly. The request body is read natively only when that pipeline asks for it, after authentication, so an unauthenticated client cannot make the server buffer a body. Handlers themselves remain Python code; this is not an application written in Rust, and no performance figure is claimed here. A Query[Schema] parameter of a GET or DELETE is eligible too (Python converts and validates the query string, reporting errors in the pipeline order; it does not combine with a body). A Form[Schema] or XML[Schema] body is eligible too: the text is converted and validated as described in Form bodies and XML bodies . The native handler lane ¶ An async def handler that only talks to the database through the ORM can run without an asyncio task: Kiso drives its coroutine itself, runs each database wait on the native runtime and sends the answer from there. Hinoki decides this once per route at worker startup, by reading the handler's own source. A route takes the lane when: it is a GET , DELETE , POST , PUT , PATCH or QUERY that is eligible for the native path above (a body method takes one Schema body and built-in parsers); the function is a plain async def , not wrapped by a decorator; every await in it is an ORM call on a Model class: a read: Model.aget(...) , Model.aget_or_none(...) , or Model.filter(...) / Model.all() with filter , order_by , limit and offset , ending in aget , afirst , acount or aexists , or awaited directly; a write: acreate , aupdate , aupdate_where , adelete , abulk_create , abulk_update , abulk_delete , or aupdate / adelete ending a filter(...) chain. A write counts only on a model that overrides none of the write hooks ( before_save , before_create , after_create , after_save ) or the methods the write calls ( insert , asave , from_schema and the like); asave , aupdate_from and aupdate_within on an instance stay on asyncio. These keep a route in an asyncio task: async with , async for , yield , async comprehensions, local names that shadow a model, and any other await ( asyncio.sleep , an HTTP client, another coroutine). Guards and bodies. A guarded route ( access , rate_limit , Query[Schema] or several renderers) is served the same way, and so is a body method: its guards run first inside the driven coroutine, in the order of the asyncio path (credentials, then the rate limit, then the body and the request values), and the body is read on the native runtime. Class APIs. A handler of a class API takes the lane when the class keeps the stock constructor (no __init__ or __new__ of its own in the class or its bases) and adds no response_headers . The instance is built per request, as on the asyncio path; a class that builds itself with application code stays on asyncio. The constructor is read once at startup. Transactions. An atomic=True route runs its handler inside a transaction opened, committed or rolled back on the native runtime, and an error is translated only after the rollback, as on the asyncio path. Invalid requests. A request Rust already finds invalid (a bad path encoding, an invalid path or query parameter, an unacceptable Accept ) stays on the asyncio path. Moving to asyncio. A provider or policy that awaits something only asyncio can run (a custom provider calling an HTTP service, a rate limit store on the thread pool) moves the request to an asyncio task at that point, once, with what is left of the timeout. A transaction already open goes with it, so later savepoints still nest and the rollback is unchanged. The same happens if a write hook is added to a model after startup and awaits asyncio. hinoki routes --lanes shows the choice, and hinoki.runtime logs the reason for every route at debug level. The behaviour is the same on both paths: status, headers, body, error translation, the request ID and the request_timeout (a 504 ). An error from a driven handler, and a failure of a generated CRUD action, is translated in place when no error handler you registered can match it; an exception one of your handlers matches is translated in an asyncio task, because the handler may await. Each request has its own context, so request_id and the database are the ones of that request. The handler's steps after its first run on the event-loop thread, so a task it starts still finds the loop. If a driven handler awaits something only asyncio can run (a database backend without native waits), it is moved to an asyncio task at that point and continues with what is left of the request timeout. At shutdown, running handlers are cancelled like request tasks. What it assumes: model classes and their ORM methods are not replaced after startup. Set server.native_dispatch = false to keep every handler in an asyncio task. No performance figure is claimed here. hinoki routes --lanes shows, per route, whether Kiso runs it natively and, if not, why ( Inspect an application ). Generated CRUD ¶ Generated CRUD plans can also execute public create ( POST ), update ( PATCH ) and delete actions in Rust. These routes use the native path only when their model and schemas are supported and they have no assignment rule or custom CRUD hook (an owner is allowed only with identity_key = caller_id , a text non-key column outside the update schema, on any supported database), and their access policy, if any, uses an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth . Rust reads and validates the bounded request body, runs the database transaction, fetches the written row where the response requires it, and encodes the response before commit. Writes continue to completion if the client disconnects. A unique-constraint violation returns 409 Conflict by default; a registered application error handler takes precedence. Routes that are ineligible or become stale use the ordinary Python CRUD pipeline. Plans are selected automatically at worker startup and checked once per second; a changed plan is disarmed until the worker restarts. This path adds no public setting. The measured phase 1 path is documented in the native CRUD orientation run . It is a single-host, workload-specific measurement and does not establish general or production performance. Limits ¶ HTTP/1.1, plus HTTP/2 over TLS when server.http2 is on (see below). No WebSocket or other protocol upgrades: an Upgrade header is ignored and the request is answered as plain HTTP, and the server never answers 101 . There is no cleartext HTTP/2 (neither prior knowledge nor Upgrade: h2c ). A request line plus headers larger than execution.max_header_bytes , or a query longer than execution.max_query_bytes , is refused ( 431 , 414 ). A body larger than execution.max_body_bytes is refused with 413 , by Content-Length before any byte is read or, for chunked bodies, as soon as the total passes the limit. A client that sends nothing for body_read_timeout seconds (10 by default, never more than half of execution.request_timeout ) gets 408 , and so does one that trickles data: the whole body must arrive within six times body_read_timeout . A client that does not finish its request headers within header_read_timeout seconds (10 by default) is disconnected; the same timer closes idle keep-alive connections. TLS is optional: set server.tls_cert_file and server.tls_key_file (PEM; the key may be PKCS#8, PKCS#1 or SEC1) and Kiso speaks HTTPS with rustls (TLS 1.2 and 1.3, the library's default cipher suites, no client certificates, ALPN http/1.1 , or h2 then http/1.1 with server.http2 ). The files are read once at start, so a renewed certificate needs a restart (a rolling restart of the workers is enough). A plaintext client on a TLS port gets a TLS alert, never an answer, and the handshake must finish within header_read_timeout . Requests over TLS have the scheme https , so the HSTS policy applies. Granian takes the same two settings (the framework asks it for TLS 1.2 and up and HTTP/1.1 only, as Kiso does, unless server.http2 is on). A trusted proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto overrides the scheme, http included, on both servers. The handshake and the request head each have their own header_read_timeout , so a slow client can hold a connection slot for up to twice that time. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, leave them unset and list the proxy in trusted_proxies instead. HTTP/2 is opt-in: set server.http2 = true together with the TLS files (it is a settings error without them, on both servers). The server then offers ALPN h2 and http/1.1 and serves each connection with the protocol it negotiated; a client that offers only http/1.1 , or no ALPN, still gets HTTP/1.1. Requests reach the application unchanged, with http_version 2 in the ASGI scope; the :authority pseudo-header becomes the Host and wins over a host header that differs. Limits are fixed, not settings: 32 concurrent streams per connection (the 33rd is refused), a 64 KiB stream window, header lists bounded by execution.max_header_bytes and at most 100 header lines per request ( cookie fields count once; more is answered 431 ), and the h2 library's rapid-reset protections. A connection counts as one slot of max_connections , but every stream in flight uses backend capacity (the in-flight limit and the queue) like a request of its own, so size those limits for connections times 32. The server also drops a connection on which more than 100 streams end before their response completed (client resets) within a fixed 10-second window; it is closed without a GOAWAY . The count is per connection, not per client: a client can pass about twice the bound across a window boundary, and a new connection starts from zero. A connection with no open stream for header_read_timeout is closed gracefully ( GOAWAY ; a stream opened in the race with the GOAWAY is accepted and then cut when the shutdown timeout ends). A response that sends no data for write_timeout seconds (a client that keeps its flow-control window at zero, or stopped reading) also gets the connection a GOAWAY : hyper cannot reset one stream from outside, so the other streams have the shutdown timeout to finish and the stalled one is cut with the connection. Progress is tracked per response, so opening new streams does not hide a stalled one. Keep-alive pings every 30 seconds drop a peer that stopped answering. Set write_timeout above 32 x 16 KiB divided by the slowest client bandwidth you expect to serve: HTTP/2 shares the window between streams unevenly, so on a slow link each of 32 concurrent downloads can wait that long between two chunks and be taken for stalled while bytes still flow. A request with several host headers and no :authority is refused with 400 . A client that trickles the head of one stream while others are open is not bounded by header_read_timeout . On stop the server sends GOAWAY , lets streams in flight finish, and aborts what is left after the shutdown timeout. Not provided: cleartext HTTP/2 (h2c), server push, and WebSocket or CONNECT over HTTP/2. Granian with server.http2 negotiates HTTP/2 itself ( http mode auto ), under its own limits. A client that stops reading a response for write_timeout seconds (30 by default) is disconnected; any progress restarts the timer. max_connections (10000 by default) bounds open connections. Requests waiting for the application are bounded by an in-flight limit and a queue; beyond them the answer is 503 . Requests with ambiguous framing (for example Content-Length together with Transfer-Encoding , repeated lengths, or a bare line feed in the head) are refused with 400 and the connection is closed. On start, Kiso names itself on stderr before the listening on ... line (which stays on stdout, where tools wait for it): its version, the mode ( serve or dev , which reloads on file changes), the worker count, the scheme, whether the access log is on and whether the native handler lane is on. In a terminal (and with NO_COLOR unset) it is the same box hinoki new draws, titled Kiso (no image, on any terminal), with the tagline and the version, then the facts, broken into rows that fit the box; otherwise it is one plain line, for example Kiso 0.0.1 (Hinoki's Rust server): serve, 4 workers, http, access log off, native lane on . The access log is one line per answered request, written to stderr by Kiso: 127.0.0.1:52341 - "GET /items?limit=5 HTTP/1.1" 200 OK 3.2ms . The time is how long the server took to decide the answer, not including writing it to the client, and the line is printed for every answer, including the ones the server gives itself ( 404 , 429 , 503 ). When stderr is a terminal (and NO_COLOR is unset) the line is coloured in the style of a development console: INFO: in green, the request in bold, the status by class (2xx green, 3xx cyan, 4xx yellow, 5xx red) and the time dimmed. Control characters in the target are shown as \xNN . Other formats and filters: server.access_log_format = "json" writes one JSON object per line instead, for a log pipeline: {"time":"2026-11-19T19:56:25.881Z","peer":"127.0.0.1:52341","method":"GET","path":"/items","query":"limit=5","http_version":"1.1","status":200,"duration_ms":3.2,"lane":"python"} . time is RFC 3339 UTC. lane says where the request was first routed: early for an answer from the transport or the classifier, native for a generated CRUD plan that Rust executes, and python for every request handed to the Python side, including handlers on the native handler lane , so it can differ from what hinoki routes --lanes shows. route is the pattern that matched, e.g. /items/{id} , so requests can be grouped without parsing paths (absent when no route matched). Quotes and control characters are escaped. server.access_log_format = "logger" hands each request to the Python hinoki.access logger instead of writing to stderr, so your own handlers, formatters and filters (see your own loggers ) decide where it goes; each record carries the JSON fields as record.access . Kiso queues up to 4096 records and a logging thread passes them to Python in batches, taking the GIL once per batch; when the logger falls behind, new records are dropped rather than slowing requests. Setting a format turns the log on, in serve too, unless access_log is false . access_log_skip = ["/health", "/static/*"] leaves noisy paths out and access_log_slow_ms = 100 keeps only slow answers; failures (status 400 and up) are always logged. A client that disconnects does not cancel its running handler; the handler finishes and its answer is discarded. A WSGI callable ( --interface wsgi ) runs in Python threads behind this listener, not on the native lane: see WSGI on Kiso for what applies to it. An answer Kiso cannot send as given (an informational status, a header name or value HTTP does not allow, an unreadable content-length ) becomes a bare 500 , and the reason is written to stderr, for example kiso: error: the response cannot be sent (invalid header "x-evil"); answering 500 instead . The access log records the 500 . A streamed body that is shorter or longer than its content-length is cut off with an error line on stderr and the connection is closed (HTTP/1.1) or the stream reset (HTTP/2), so the client never mistakes it for a complete answer. The access log keeps the status of the head here, because it is written when the head is decided. Workers, signals and restarts ¶ With one worker hinoki serve runs the server in its own process. With several workers (and always under hinoki dev ) it starts a supervisor that opens the listening socket once (honouring backlog ), starts each worker as a fresh process that imports the target and builds the application, and passes the socket down. Workers share the one socket, so connections are spread by the operating system's accept; Hinoki does not balance them. Databases and pools open inside each worker's lifespan, never in the supervisor. SIGTERM , SIGINT (Ctrl-C) or SIGHUP stops accepting, lets running requests finish for up to lifecycle.shutdown_timeout , runs the lifespan shutdown and exits. A worker still running five seconds after that is killed. A second signal kills the workers immediately. Once the stop begins the supervisor closes its own copy of the socket, so a client that connects while the workers drain is refused. --workers must be 1 to 256 ( 0 uses server.workers ). A worker that exits on its own, whether it failed to start or crashed, is not restarted: the supervisor stops the other workers and exits with a non-zero status. Restart policy belongs to the process manager (systemd, a container runtime) that runs hinoki serve . The listening socket is opened before the lifespan startup of a supervised worker finishes, so connections wait in the backlog until a worker accepts them. With one worker the socket is opened after a successful startup. If the supervisor is killed without a chance to clean up, its workers notice within a second of finishing their startup and stop. The workers' copy of the listening socket is not inherited by processes a handler starts. A socket that cannot be opened (address in use, a bad port or host) is reported as error: cannot listen on HOST:PORT: ... with exit status 2, with one worker or several. Reload with hinoki dev ¶ The supervisor watches the project directory ( *.py , *.toml and .env files; .venv , .git and caches are ignored) and, on a change, stops the worker gracefully and starts a new one on the same socket, so a client connecting during the restart waits instead of being refused. If the new code fails to import or start, the error is printed (a short error: cannot load ... line for a missing module or name, a traceback for other failures), waiting for changes follows, and the next edit starts the worker again; connections wait in the meantime. The host, port, backlog and the choice of server are read once when hinoki dev starts: change them and restart the command. The other server settings (limits, trusted_proxies , runtime_threads ) are read again by every restarted worker. The watcher ignores .venv but not a virtual environment with another name, such as venv/ : keep it outside the project directory or it triggers reloads. The first import of the target happens in the command itself, so an error there stops it with a message instead of waiting. dev needs watchfiles (the hinoki[server] extra) and uses one worker. Behind a reverse proxy ¶ server.trusted_proxies works as described in Hosts, CORS and HTTPS : the native layer matches the TCP peer against it for the request ID and the HSTS and scheme policy of its own answers, and the request pipeline resolves the forwarded scheme and client address of the requests it handles from the same peer. The rate limit of a natively served route resolves its client the same way, so RateLimitContext.client is the same on both lanes. Points to know: Entries are IP addresses or CIDRs. An IPv6 address with a zone id such as fe80::1%lo0 is refused when settings load, for either server (earlier versions loaded it and the ASGI path matched it; Kiso cannot take it). On a listener bound to :: that also accepts IPv4 (the default on many systems, for example Linux with bindv6only=0 and macOS), an IPv4 peer appears as ::ffff:a.b.c.d . A plain IPv4 entry such as 10.0.0.5 or 10.0.0.0/8 then never matches, and the proxy is treated as untrusted. That fails closed, and the ASGI path behaves the same. Either bind an IPv4 host ( --host 0.0.0.0 ) or list the mapped form, for example ::ffff:10.0.0.0/104 . A request ID that a trusted proxy sent and Hinoki refused is logged as ignored invalid request ID from trusted proxy ; for requests answered natively the warning is aggregated once a second with a count. Errors and edge cases ¶ A build whose native extension has no Kiso fails --server kiso with an error that says so. A socket that cannot be opened is reported as error: cannot listen on HOST:PORT: ... with exit status 2 . A worker that exits on its own is not restarted: restart policy belongs to your process manager. See also ¶ Serve an application Request lifecycle Native CRUD orientation run

docs.text: Kiso is the HTTP server inside Hinoki's native extension, written in Rust on hyper, tokio and rustls. It is what hinoki dev and hinoki serve run unless you choose Granian, and it can answer many requests without entering Python. hinoki serve --workers 4 # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): server : settings . ServerSettings = settings . ServerSettings ( server = "kiso" , workers = 4 ) --server kiso selects it explicitly when a project defaults to Granian. Choose Granian instead when you need an ASGI wrapper around the application ( Serve an application ).

docs.text: Generated CRUD plans can also execute public create ( POST ), update ( PATCH ) and delete actions in Rust. These routes use the native path only when their model and schemas are supported and they have no assignment rule or custom CRUD hook (an owner is allowed only with identity_key = caller_id , a text non-key column outside the update schema, on any supported database), and their access policy, if any, uses an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth . Rust reads and validates the bounded request body, runs the database transaction, fetches the written row where the response requires it, and encodes the response before commit. Writes continue to completion if the client disconnects. A unique-constraint violation returns 409 Conflict by default; a registered application error handler takes precedence. Routes that are ineligible or become stale use the ordinary Python CRUD pipeline. Plans are selected automatically at worker startup and checked once per second; a changed plan is disarmed until the worker restarts. This path adds no public setting. The measured phase 1 path is documented in the native CRUD orientation run . It is a single-host, workload-specific measurement and does not establish general or production performance.
docs.title: Generated CRUD

docs.text: HTTP/1.1, plus HTTP/2 over TLS when server.http2 is on (see below). No WebSocket or other protocol upgrades: an Upgrade header is ignored and the request is answered as plain HTTP, and the server never answers 101 . There is no cleartext HTTP/2 (neither prior knowledge nor Upgrade: h2c ). A request line plus headers larger than execution.max_header_bytes , or a query longer than execution.max_query_bytes , is refused ( 431 , 414 ). A body larger than execution.max_body_bytes is refused with 413 , by Content-Length before any byte is read or, for chunked bodies, as soon as the total passes the limit. A client that sends nothing for body_read_timeout seconds (10 by default, never more than half of execution.request_timeout ) gets 408 , and so does one that trickles data: the whole body must arrive within six times body_read_timeout . A client that does not finish its request headers within header_read_timeout seconds (10 by default) is disconnected; the same timer closes idle keep-alive connections. TLS is optional: set server.tls_cert_file and server.tls_key_file (PEM; the key may be PKCS#8, PKCS#1 or SEC1) and Kiso speaks HTTPS with rustls (TLS 1.2 and 1.3, the library's default cipher suites, no client certificates, ALPN http/1.1 , or h2 then http/1.1 with server.http2 ). The files are read once at start, so a renewed certificate needs a restart (a rolling restart of the workers is enough). A plaintext client on a TLS port gets a TLS alert, never an answer, and the handshake must finish within header_read_timeout . Requests over TLS have the scheme https , so the HSTS policy applies. Granian takes the same two settings (the framework asks it for TLS 1.2 and up and HTTP/1.1 only, as Kiso does, unless server.http2 is on). A trusted proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto overrides the scheme, http included, on both servers. The handshake and the request head each have their own header_read_timeout , so a slow client can hold a connection slot for up to twice that time. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, leave them unset and list the proxy in trusted_proxies instead. HTTP/2 is opt-in: set server.http2 = true together with the TLS files (it is a settings error without them, on both servers). The server then offers ALPN h2 and http/1.1 and serves each connection with the protocol it negotiated; a client that offers only http/1.1 , or no ALPN, still gets HTTP/1.1. Requests reach the application unchanged, with http_version 2 in the ASGI scope; the :authority pseudo-header becomes the Host and wins over a host header that differs. Limits are fixed, not settings: 32 concurrent streams per connection (the 33rd is refused), a 64 KiB stream window, header lists bounded by execution.max_header_bytes and at most 100 header lines per request ( cookie fields count once; more is answered 431 ), and the h2 library's rapid-reset protections. A connection counts as one slot of max_connections , but every stream in flight uses backend capacity (the in-flight limit and the queue) like a request of its own, so size those limits for connections times 32. The server also drops a connection on which more than 100 streams end before their response completed (client resets) within a fixed 10-second window; it is closed without a GOAWAY . The count is per connection, not per client: a client can pass about twice the bound across a window boundary, and a new connection starts from zero. A connection with no open stream for header_read_timeout is closed gracefully ( GOAWAY ; a stream opened in the race with the GOAWAY is accepted and then cut when the shutdown timeout ends). A response that sends no data for write_timeout seconds (a client that keeps its flow-control window at zero, or stopped reading) also gets the connection a GOAWAY : hyper cannot reset one stream from outside, so the other streams have the shutdown timeout to finish and the stalled one is cut with the connection. Progress is tracked per response, so opening new streams does not hide a stalled one. Keep-alive pings every 30 seconds drop a peer that stopped answering. Set write_timeout above 32 x 16 KiB divided by the slowest client bandwidth you expect to serve: HTTP/2 shares the window between streams unevenly, so on a slow link each of 32 concurrent downloads can wait that long between two chunks and be taken for stalled while bytes still flow. A request with several host headers and no :authority is refused with 400 . A client that trickles the head of one stream while others are open is not bounded by header_read_timeout . On stop the server sends GOAWAY , lets streams in flight finish, and aborts what is left after the shutdown timeout. Not provided: cleartext HTTP/2 (h2c), server push, and WebSocket or CONNECT over HTTP/2. Granian with server.http2 negotiates HTTP/2 itself ( http mode auto ), under its own limits. A client that stops reading a response for write_timeout seconds (30 by default) is disconnected; any progress restarts the timer. max_connections (10000 by default) bounds open connections. Requests waiting for the application are bounded by an in-flight limit and a queue; beyond them the answer is 503 . Requests with ambiguous framing (for example Content-Length together with Transfer-Encoding , repeated lengths, or a bare line feed in the head) are refused with 400 and the connection is closed. On start, Kiso names itself on stderr before the listening on ... line (which stays on stdout, where tools wait for it): its version, the mode ( serve or dev , which reloads on file changes), the worker count, the scheme, whether the access log is on and whether the native handler lane is on. In a terminal (and with NO_COLOR unset) it is the same box hinoki new draws, titled Kiso (no image, on any terminal), with the tagline and the version, then the facts, broken into rows that fit the box; otherwise it is one plain line, for example Kiso 0.0.1 (Hinoki's Rust server): serve, 4 workers, http, access log off, native lane on . The access log is one line per answered request, written to stderr by Kiso: 127.0.0.1:52341 - "GET /items?limit=5 HTTP/1.1" 200 OK 3.2ms . The time is how long the server took to decide the answer, not including writing it to the client, and the line is printed for every answer, including the ones the server gives itself ( 404 , 429 , 503 ). When stderr is a terminal (and NO_COLOR is unset) the line is coloured in the style of a development console: INFO: in green, the request in bold, the status by class (2xx green, 3xx cyan, 4xx yellow, 5xx red) and the time dimmed. Control characters in the target are shown as \xNN . Other formats and filters: server.access_log_format = "json" writes one JSON object per line instead, for a log pipeline: {"time":"2026-11-19T19:56:25.881Z","peer":"127.0.0.1:52341","method":"GET","path":"/items","query":"limit=5","http_version":"1.1","status":200,"duration_ms":3.2,"lane":"python"} . time is RFC 3339 UTC. lane says where the request was first routed: early for an answer from the transport or the classifier, native for a generated CRUD plan that Rust executes, and python for every request handed to the Python side, including handlers on the native handler lane , so it can differ from what hinoki routes --lanes shows. route is the pattern that matched, e.g. /items/{id} , so requests can be grouped without parsing paths (absent when no route matched). Quotes and control characters are escaped. server.access_log_format = "logger" hands each request to the Python hinoki.access logger instead of writing to stderr, so your own handlers, formatters and filters (see your own loggers ) decide where it goes; each record carries the JSON fields as record.access . Kiso queues up to 4096 records and a logging thread passes them to Python in batches, taking the GIL once per batch; when the logger falls behind, new records are dropped rather than slowing requests. Setting a format turns the log on, in serve too, unless access_log is false . access_log_skip = ["/health", "/static/*"] leaves noisy paths out and access_log_slow_ms = 100 keeps only slow answers; failures (status 400 and up) are always logged. A client that disconnects does not cancel its running handler; the handler finishes and its answer is discarded. A WSGI callable ( --interface wsgi ) runs in Python threads behind this listener, not on the native lane: see WSGI on Kiso for what applies to it. An answer Kiso cannot send as given (an informational status, a header name or value HTTP does not allow, an unreadable content-length ) becomes a bare 500 , and the reason is written to stderr, for example kiso: error: the response cannot be sent (invalid header "x-evil"); answering 500 instead . The access log records the 500 . A streamed body that is shorter or longer than its content-length is cut off with an error line on stderr and the connection is closed (HTTP/1.1) or the stream reset (HTTP/2), so the client never mistakes it for a complete answer. The access log keeps the status of the head here, because it is written when the head is decided.
docs.title: Limits

docs.text: With one worker hinoki serve runs the server in its own process. With several workers (and always under hinoki dev ) it starts a supervisor that opens the listening socket once (honouring backlog ), starts each worker as a fresh process that imports the target and builds the application, and passes the socket down. Workers share the one socket, so connections are spread by the operating system's accept; Hinoki does not balance them. Databases and pools open inside each worker's lifespan, never in the supervisor. SIGTERM , SIGINT (Ctrl-C) or SIGHUP stops accepting, lets running requests finish for up to lifecycle.shutdown_timeout , runs the lifespan shutdown and exits. A worker still running five seconds after that is killed. A second signal kills the workers immediately. Once the stop begins the supervisor closes its own copy of the socket, so a client that connects while the workers drain is refused. --workers must be 1 to 256 ( 0 uses server.workers ). A worker that exits on its own, whether it failed to start or crashed, is not restarted: the supervisor stops the other workers and exits with a non-zero status. Restart policy belongs to the process manager (systemd, a container runtime) that runs hinoki serve . The listening socket is opened before the lifespan startup of a supervised worker finishes, so connections wait in the backlog until a worker accepts them. With one worker the socket is opened after a successful startup. If the supervisor is killed without a chance to clean up, its workers notice within a second of finishing their startup and stop. The workers' copy of the listening socket is not inherited by processes a handler starts. A socket that cannot be opened (address in use, a bad port or host) is reported as error: cannot listen on HOST:PORT: ... with exit status 2, with one worker or several.
docs.title: Workers, signals and restarts

docs.text: The supervisor watches the project directory ( *.py , *.toml and .env files; .venv , .git and caches are ignored) and, on a change, stops the worker gracefully and starts a new one on the same socket, so a client connecting during the restart waits instead of being refused. If the new code fails to import or start, the error is printed (a short error: cannot load ... line for a missing module or name, a traceback for other failures), waiting for changes follows, and the next edit starts the worker again; connections wait in the meantime. The host, port, backlog and the choice of server are read once when hinoki dev starts: change them and restart the command. The other server settings (limits, trusted_proxies , runtime_threads ) are read again by every restarted worker. The watcher ignores .venv but not a virtual environment with another name, such as venv/ : keep it outside the project directory or it triggers reloads. The first import of the target happens in the command itself, so an error there stops it with a message instead of waiting. dev needs watchfiles (the hinoki[server] extra) and uses one worker.
docs.title: Reload with hinoki dev

docs.text: server.trusted_proxies works as described in Hosts, CORS and HTTPS : the native layer matches the TCP peer against it for the request ID and the HSTS and scheme policy of its own answers, and the request pipeline resolves the forwarded scheme and client address of the requests it handles from the same peer. The rate limit of a natively served route resolves its client the same way, so RateLimitContext.client is the same on both lanes. Points to know: Entries are IP addresses or CIDRs. An IPv6 address with a zone id such as fe80::1%lo0 is refused when settings load, for either server (earlier versions loaded it and the ASGI path matched it; Kiso cannot take it). On a listener bound to :: that also accepts IPv4 (the default on many systems, for example Linux with bindv6only=0 and macOS), an IPv4 peer appears as ::ffff:a.b.c.d . A plain IPv4 entry such as 10.0.0.5 or 10.0.0.0/8 then never matches, and the proxy is treated as untrusted. That fails closed, and the ASGI path behaves the same. Either bind an IPv4 host ( --host 0.0.0.0 ) or list the mapped form, for example ::ffff:10.0.0.0/104 . A request ID that a trusted proxy sent and Hinoki refused is logged as ignored invalid request ID from trusted proxy ; for requests answered natively the warning is aggregated once a second with a count.
docs.title: Behind a reverse proxy

docs.text: A build whose native extension has no Kiso fails --server kiso with an error that says so. A socket that cannot be opened is reported as error: cannot listen on HOST:PORT: ... with exit status 2 . A worker that exits on its own is not restarted: restart policy belongs to your process manager.

docs.text: Add middleware ¶ A middleware runs around an action. It is Hinoki's own typed interface, so it behaves the same on Kiso and on Granian: you do not wrap the ASGI application, and an application served by Kiso can use it. # notes/middleware.py from hinoki.http import Middleware , MiddlewareRequest , Next , Response class Tenant ( Middleware ): async def __call__ ( self , request : MiddlewareRequest , call_next : Next ) -> Response : if "x-tenant" not in request . headers : return Response ( 400 , "missing x-tenant" , content_type = "text/plain" ) response = await call_next () return response . with_header ( "x-served-by" , "tenant" ) Declare it on an action, or for the whole application: # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki , http from .middleware import Tenant @http . get ( "/items" ) async def items () -> list [ str ]: return [] app = Hinoki ( include = [ items ], middleware = [ Tenant ()]) RouteGroup actions take the same option. The application's middleware runs first, then the action's, in the order listed; each one returns what the next one returned unless it answers itself. What a middleware sees ¶ MiddlewareRequest is the head of the request: method , path , the matched route template in route (for example /items/{item_id} , safe to use as a metrics label), lower-case headers , the raw query string, client , scheme and request_id . It has no body and cannot change the request: headers is a read-only mapping, so authentication and the action see the headers the client sent. class Forge ( Middleware ): async def __call__ ( self , request : MiddlewareRequest , call_next : Next ) -> Response : request . headers [ "authorization" ] = "Bearer x" # TypeError: a 500 return await call_next () A middleware that needs to pass data on should answer itself or add response headers instead. The Response a middleware returns is checked like one a handler returns, also when it is built with Response.raw(status, body, headers) from encoded parts: a framing or server header ( content-length , transfer-encoding , connection , x-request-id ), an invalid name or a line break in a value is a ValueError , so the request answers 500 instead of a corrupt response. call_next() returns a Response with the action's answer. An error the action raised is already an HTTP answer, and an atomic=True transaction is already rolled back, so a middleware that reads the database after call_next() sees the state after the rollback. Call call_next() at most once (a second call is a 500 ). A middleware that raises is translated like an action error; one that returns anything but a Response is a 500 . Security, CORS and request-id headers are added after the middleware returns. Order and what stays outside ¶ Hinoki answers what needs no action first: the ready check, request size limits, host, CORS preflight and HTTPS redirect policies, the startup probe and the documentation pages. The route is chosen. An unknown path ( 404 ) or method ( 405 ) never reaches a middleware. The application's middleware, then the action's. Authentication, rate limit, negotiation, body binding, the transaction and the handler. execution.request_timeout applies to the whole of it: when it expires the 504 is produced outside the middleware, which only sees the cancellation. Cost ¶ An action with middleware is served by Python for the whole request, so it leaves the native lane : hinoki routes --lanes shows lane_reason middleware . Actions without middleware keep their lane. A middleware that only needs to observe requests can use the access log instead, which does not change the lane. Errors and edge cases ¶ A middleware must have async def __call__ ; any other object is a TypeError when the application or the action is declared. Keep a middleware free of request state kept in globals: use the MiddlewareRequest it receives. See also ¶ Request lifecycle Serve an application Transactions
