docs.text: Migrations ¶ Hinoki compares each app's models with the migration state recorded in its migration package and writes SQL files you review and commit. Nothing changes a database until you run apply ; an application never migrates at startup. hinoki migrations plan billing hinoki migrations apply Commands run from the project, where hinoki.toml registers each app's models and migrations ( hinoki new , hinoki app create ). Prefix them with uv run or activate .venv . Plan a migration ¶ hinoki migrations plan # a project with one app hinoki migrations plan billing # one app of several hinoki migrations plan billing --name add-invoice-index plan writes two files into the app's migration package: 0001-create-table-billing-invoices.sql and its .state.json . The number is automatic; the slug comes from the first change ( create table billing_invoices ) unless --name replaces it. In a project with several apps, plan needs the app name; --check and --dry-run without one cover every app. Plan for the backend you deploy The SQL uses the dialect of the selected database : usually the application's own database setting. Point it at the production backend (a disposable database of the same kind) before planning. The state file is backend-neutral. Review before applying ¶ Read both files. Changes that can lose data are destructive and are not written unless you pass --allow-destructive : dropping a table or column, changing a type or constraint, adding a non-null column; a changed derived table name (renaming the class or moving its module), which is planned as a drop and a create. Pin the name with @db.table(...) ( table names ). hinoki migrations plan billing --dry-run hinoki migrations plan billing --allow-destructive --dry-run prints the plan, destructive operations included, and writes nothing. Changing a constraint on an existing column may need a hand-written migration. Apply and inspect ¶ hinoki migrations status hinoki migrations sql 0001 -create-table-billing-invoices hinoki migrations apply hinoki migrations apply billing Command Effect status [APP] lists applied and pending migrations (nothing when there are none); creates the ledger, and a SQLite file, if missing sql NAME prints one migration's SQL; add --app APP only when the name is ambiguous apply [APP] applies pending migrations of every app, or of APP and its prerequisites, in dependency order Which database ¶ plan , status and apply use the first of: --database URL ; the HINOKI_DATABASE_URL environment variable; the project's application ( project.application in hinoki.toml ): a DatabaseModule it passes in modules= or installs with app.install(...) , otherwise its database setting, read from its settings sources as the server reads them, for example NOTES_DATABASE__URL or .env ; local SQLite, sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 . The application is imported from the project root to read its settings, so .env and other relative settings files are the ones beside hinoki.toml , even from a subdirectory. Anything it prints while importing goes to standard error. No connection opens until the command needs one, and nothing is started. The command never falls back to another database: it stops with exit 2 when the application cannot be imported (the message names the missing module or attribute) or its settings cannot be loaded; it installs a database module of its own whose URL Hinoki cannot read; the application's database is in-memory SQLite ( sqlite://:memory: ), where nothing it migrates would survive. A --database sqlite://:memory: URL is refused with exit 1 instead, because SQLite needs a file URL there. Fix the application, or choose the database with --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL , which skip step 3 and never import the application. An application without a database still migrates the local SQLite default, but the server has none to use: declare database: settings.DatabaseSettings ( configure a database ). Outside a project ( --models / --dir ), step 3 is skipped. plan , status and apply print the chosen database and its source on standard error. Everything before the host (user and password) and the URL options are masked, and a URL that does not parse is not echoed: $ NOTES_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://notes:secret@db.internal/notes hinoki migrations status database: postgresql://***@db.internal/notes (from settings: ProjectSettings.database) A relative SQLite path from the settings or the default is anchored beside hinoki.toml , so migrations run from a subdirectory use the same file; a relative SQLite URL given with --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL stays relative to the current directory. The server and hinoki settings do not anchor: they resolve the path, and read .env , from the directory they start in, so start them from the project root. A connection failure prints error: database: … and exits 1 . A --database URL is visible in the process list and shell history: do not put a password in it. An older scaffold's root app keeps unprefixed ledger keys; apps from hinoki app create use namespaced keys, so accounts/0001-initial.sql and billing/0001-initial.sql are distinct records. Run apply once per deployment, from one process, never from every worker's startup ( settings ). Concurrent runs are serialized: each file runs in one transaction under a PostgreSQL advisory lock, a MySQL/MariaDB migration lock or SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE , and reads the ledger inside it. On SQLite a second runner waits at most the busy timeout (5 seconds), then fails as locked. Check migration drift ¶ hinoki migrations plan --check Exits 1 when any app has model changes without a migration file, destructive ones included, 0 otherwise, and 2 when the database whose dialect it plans for cannot be resolved ( which database ). It covers every app in dependency order ( plan billing --check : that app and its prerequisites), writes nothing and opens no connection. It imports every registered model and migration module and, unless --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL names the database, the project's application to read its database, so those imports must be safe in CI: HINOKI_DATABASE_URL = postgresql://ci@localhost/notes hinoki migrations plan --check status compares files with a live database instead. Apps and dependencies ¶ An app that references another app's models declares it in requires : # hinoki.toml [[apps]] name = "billing" models = "notes.apps.billing.models" migrations = "notes.apps.billing.migrations" requires = [ "accounts" ] hinoki app create billing asks for requires ; hinoki app add NAME --models MODULE registers an existing package. Each app's tables belong only to its own migration state. Cross-app migration safety ¶ Before planning billing , the referenced table and primary key must already be recorded in accounts ' migration state with a compatible type; plan and review accounts first. It does not need to be applied yet. A parent table or referenced column is never dropped while another app's recorded state still refers to it, in plan , --dry-run and --check ; --allow-destructive does not override this, and an all-app command fails without partial output. Remove and apply the child reference first, then plan the parent teardown in a separate deployment. --dry-run without an app previews every app, possibly against a prerequisite's not-yet-planned models: do not apply in that order. It cannot take --name . Backend behaviour ¶ Backend Behaviour SQLite rebuilds a table when ALTER TABLE cannot express the change safely; holds the pool, suspends foreign-key enforcement on reserved connections, runs PRAGMA foreign_key_check before commit and rolls back on invalid references PostgreSQL each migration runs in a transaction MySQL DDL commits implicitly: a failed migration may be partially applied (Hinoki says so). Check the schema and status before retrying; keep a backup MariaDB separate backend on the MySQL wire protocol; JSON is a text alias decoded by typed fields MySQL and MariaDB foreign keys are table-level constraints. For databases migrated by an older Hinoki, check SHOW CREATE TABLE : MySQL ignores inline REFERENCES , and MariaDB varies by version. Add a missing constraint with a reviewed manual migration; applied migrations are never rewritten. Automatic removal of a foreign-key column is refused on these backends. State files record logical types; files from older versions that recorded SQLite or MySQL type names are normalized, so switching the planner's backend is not reported as a type change. Without a manifest ¶ A project without hinoki.toml passes the models module and directory: hinoki migrations --dir app/migrations plan --models app.models These options cannot be combined with a manifest. Prefer adding one: the root app keeps its ledger keys, so existing history is not replayed. See also ¶ Configure a database CLI reference Define models

docs.text: Read both files. Changes that can lose data are destructive and are not written unless you pass --allow-destructive : dropping a table or column, changing a type or constraint, adding a non-null column; a changed derived table name (renaming the class or moving its module), which is planned as a drop and a create. Pin the name with @db.table(...) ( table names ). hinoki migrations plan billing --dry-run hinoki migrations plan billing --allow-destructive --dry-run prints the plan, destructive operations included, and writes nothing. Changing a constraint on an existing column may need a hand-written migration.
docs.title: Review before applying

docs.text: hinoki migrations status hinoki migrations sql 0001 -create-table-billing-invoices hinoki migrations apply hinoki migrations apply billing Command Effect status [APP] lists applied and pending migrations (nothing when there are none); creates the ledger, and a SQLite file, if missing sql NAME prints one migration's SQL; add --app APP only when the name is ambiguous apply [APP] applies pending migrations of every app, or of APP and its prerequisites, in dependency order
docs.title: Apply and inspect

docs.text: plan , status and apply use the first of: --database URL ; the HINOKI_DATABASE_URL environment variable; the project's application ( project.application in hinoki.toml ): a DatabaseModule it passes in modules= or installs with app.install(...) , otherwise its database setting, read from its settings sources as the server reads them, for example NOTES_DATABASE__URL or .env ; local SQLite, sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 . The application is imported from the project root to read its settings, so .env and other relative settings files are the ones beside hinoki.toml , even from a subdirectory. Anything it prints while importing goes to standard error. No connection opens until the command needs one, and nothing is started. The command never falls back to another database: it stops with exit 2 when the application cannot be imported (the message names the missing module or attribute) or its settings cannot be loaded; it installs a database module of its own whose URL Hinoki cannot read; the application's database is in-memory SQLite ( sqlite://:memory: ), where nothing it migrates would survive. A --database sqlite://:memory: URL is refused with exit 1 instead, because SQLite needs a file URL there. Fix the application, or choose the database with --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL , which skip step 3 and never import the application. An application without a database still migrates the local SQLite default, but the server has none to use: declare database: settings.DatabaseSettings ( configure a database ). Outside a project ( --models / --dir ), step 3 is skipped. plan , status and apply print the chosen database and its source on standard error. Everything before the host (user and password) and the URL options are masked, and a URL that does not parse is not echoed: $ NOTES_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://notes:secret@db.internal/notes hinoki migrations status database: postgresql://***@db.internal/notes (from settings: ProjectSettings.database) A relative SQLite path from the settings or the default is anchored beside hinoki.toml , so migrations run from a subdirectory use the same file; a relative SQLite URL given with --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL stays relative to the current directory. The server and hinoki settings do not anchor: they resolve the path, and read .env , from the directory they start in, so start them from the project root. A connection failure prints error: database: … and exits 1 . A --database URL is visible in the process list and shell history: do not put a password in it. An older scaffold's root app keeps unprefixed ledger keys; apps from hinoki app create use namespaced keys, so accounts/0001-initial.sql and billing/0001-initial.sql are distinct records. Run apply once per deployment, from one process, never from every worker's startup ( settings ). Concurrent runs are serialized: each file runs in one transaction under a PostgreSQL advisory lock, a MySQL/MariaDB migration lock or SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE , and reads the ledger inside it. On SQLite a second runner waits at most the busy timeout (5 seconds), then fails as locked.
docs.title: Which database

docs.text: hinoki migrations plan --check Exits 1 when any app has model changes without a migration file, destructive ones included, 0 otherwise, and 2 when the database whose dialect it plans for cannot be resolved ( which database ). It covers every app in dependency order ( plan billing --check : that app and its prerequisites), writes nothing and opens no connection. It imports every registered model and migration module and, unless --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL names the database, the project's application to read its database, so those imports must be safe in CI: HINOKI_DATABASE_URL = postgresql://ci@localhost/notes hinoki migrations plan --check status compares files with a live database instead.
docs.title: Check migration drift

docs.text: An app that references another app's models declares it in requires : # hinoki.toml [[apps]] name = "billing" models = "notes.apps.billing.models" migrations = "notes.apps.billing.migrations" requires = [ "accounts" ] hinoki app create billing asks for requires ; hinoki app add NAME --models MODULE registers an existing package. Each app's tables belong only to its own migration state.
docs.title: Apps and dependencies

docs.text: Before planning billing , the referenced table and primary key must already be recorded in accounts ' migration state with a compatible type; plan and review accounts first. It does not need to be applied yet. A parent table or referenced column is never dropped while another app's recorded state still refers to it, in plan , --dry-run and --check ; --allow-destructive does not override this, and an all-app command fails without partial output. Remove and apply the child reference first, then plan the parent teardown in a separate deployment. --dry-run without an app previews every app, possibly against a prerequisite's not-yet-planned models: do not apply in that order. It cannot take --name .
docs.title: Cross-app migration safety

docs.text: Backend Behaviour SQLite rebuilds a table when ALTER TABLE cannot express the change safely; holds the pool, suspends foreign-key enforcement on reserved connections, runs PRAGMA foreign_key_check before commit and rolls back on invalid references PostgreSQL each migration runs in a transaction MySQL DDL commits implicitly: a failed migration may be partially applied (Hinoki says so). Check the schema and status before retrying; keep a backup MariaDB separate backend on the MySQL wire protocol; JSON is a text alias decoded by typed fields MySQL and MariaDB foreign keys are table-level constraints. For databases migrated by an older Hinoki, check SHOW CREATE TABLE : MySQL ignores inline REFERENCES , and MariaDB varies by version. Add a missing constraint with a reviewed manual migration; applied migrations are never rewritten. Automatic removal of a foreign-key column is refused on these backends. State files record logical types; files from older versions that recorded SQLite or MySQL type names are normalized, so switching the planner's backend is not reported as a type change.
docs.title: Backend behaviour

docs.text: A project without hinoki.toml passes the models module and directory: hinoki migrations --dir app/migrations plan --models app.models These options cannot be combined with a manifest. Prefer adding one: the root app keeps its ledger keys, so existing history is not replayed.

docs.text: Lifecycle hooks ¶ A model can react to its own writes with before_save , before_create , after_create and after_save . Each is an ordinary method, def or async def , taking only self . A model without hooks pays nothing. # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) import logging log = logging . getLogger ( __name__ ) class Invoice ( Model ): ... # fields as in Define models def before_save ( self ) -> None : if self . was_changed ( "reference" ): self . reference = self . reference . strip () . upper () async def after_create ( self ) -> None : self . after_commit ( lambda : log . info ( "invoice %s created" , self . id )) Order ¶ Write Hooks insert ( acreate , insert , asave of a new instance) before_save , before_create , write, after_create , after_save update ( asave of a loaded instance, aupdate_from ) before_save , write, after_save before_* hooks may change the values about to be written. after_* hooks see the stored row (generated keys, database defaults, @db.timestamps() ). An update with no changed column after before_save writes nothing and skips after_save . To extend an inherited hook, call super() . Instance state ¶ Member Meaning is_new True until the row is written or loaded; still True inside the hooks of an insert is_dirty True for a new instance or when a column differs from the stored row changes {column: Change(old, new)} ; a new instance lists every column with old=UNSET was_changed("reference") whether one column differs; an unknown name raises FieldError Stored values are refreshed after the after_* hooks, so changes still shows this write's changes while they run. Transactions and after_commit ¶ With any hook defined, the write runs in a transaction (a savepoint inside an open one): an exception in a hook rolls the write back and reaches the caller. A hook that opens its own db.atomic() fails with DatabaseError ( nested atomic scopes (savepoints) must be opened by the task that owns the transaction ) when a sync write runs inside a sync handler's with db.atomic(): ; from async code it nests as a savepoint. after_* hooks run before the commit. Work that must happen only after it goes through self.after_commit(callback) , a sync or async callable without arguments. Callbacks run in order after the outermost commit; a rollback drops them; an exception in one is logged and does not undo the commit. See transactions . Limits ¶ Hooks belong to instances: QuerySet.aupdate , adelete , Model.aupdate , aupdate_where and raw SQL do not run them. Sync hooks run inline on the event loop: keep them short and use async def for I/O. is_new , is_dirty , changes , was_changed , after_commit and the four hook names are reserved field names. From a helper task of a transaction (the sync model methods of a sync handler), a hooked write joins that transaction; an error still rolls the whole transaction back. A hook assigned to the class after creation is used from the next write. Generated CRUD and the admin's create and edit forms save through the same methods, so hooks run there too; deletes run none ( CRUD ). See also ¶ Query and write rows Transactions

docs.text: Model options ¶ Options that describe a model beyond its columns are decorators, read top to bottom like action decorators. There is no nested class Meta ; only names stay class keywords. # notes/apps/billing/models.py from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import db from hinoki.orm import Model , OnDelete , field , foreign_key , pk from hinoki.utils import utc_now # Customer is the model declared earlier in this file (see Models). @db . unique ( "customer_id" , "reference" ) @db . indexed ( "customer_id" , "created_at" ) @db . ordered_by ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) @db . timestamps () class Quote ( Model , label = "Quote" , plural = "Quotes" ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) customer_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Customer , on_delete = OnDelete . RESTRICT , related_name = "quotes" ) reference : str = field ( max_length = 40 ) created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) Option Form Effect single-column index field(index=True) CREATE INDEX on one column composite or foreign-key index @db.indexed("a", "b") CREATE INDEX on the columns, in order composite uniqueness @db.unique("a", "b", name=None) UNIQUE (a, b) , named with name= ; one column uses field(unique=True) default order @db.ordered_by("-created_at", "id") order of queries without order_by ; - is descending update timestamp @db.timestamps() refreshes updated_at on every ORM update table name @db.table("quotes") (optional) replaces the derived <app>_<models> name app part of the name app="sales" (class keyword, optional) replaces <app> ; ignored with an explicit table display names label= , plural= (class keywords, optional) replace the derived singular and plural Every option decorator is reached through from hinoki import db . The same objects are also importable from hinoki.orm , which keeps older imports such as from hinoki.orm import unique, timestamps working. Composite uniqueness ¶ @db.unique("a", "b") adds UNIQUE (a, b) to the table; it needs two or more distinct columns. A single column uses field(unique=True) . @db . unique ( "customer_id" , "reference" , name = "uq_quotes_customer_reference" ) class Quote ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) customer_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Customer , on_delete = OnDelete . RESTRICT ) reference : str = field ( max_length = 40 ) Without name= the backend names the constraint. With it, the migration renders CONSTRAINT "uq_quotes_customer_reference" UNIQUE (...) on PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB, so the constraint keeps a stable, chosen name in the database. A name is a letter or underscore followed by up to 62 letters, digits or underscores, compared without case (as MySQL and MariaDB do). Planning refuses a name already used by another constraint, a table, or an index or foreign key that Hinoki names, among the planned models and, in a project with hinoki.toml , in every app. Only a table model can name a constraint: on an abstract model name= raises RegistrationError , because every table inheriting it would repeat the name. Unnamed constraints are inherited as usual. Changing the constraints or their names on an existing table is not planned on PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB (write that migration by hand). SQLite rebuilds the table; a rename alone is not destructive, while changed columns are reported as destructive because existing rows may violate them. Indexes ¶ Use field(index=True) for one ordinary column and @db.indexed(...) for a composite index. A foreign_key has no index= option: index it with @db.indexed("customer_id") , or with a composite index that starts with it. The optional HNK-DB-002 rule ( Models.require_foreign_key_index ) checks this. index= takes True or False ; a primary key or unique column is already indexed and refuses index=True . field(index=True) and @db.indexed("column") on the same column produce one index. Names are ix_<table>_<columns>_<digest> , cut to the backend limit (63 bytes on PostgreSQL, 64 on MySQL and MariaDB); the digest keeps indexed("a_b") and indexed("a", "b") apart. Adding or removing an index is a non-destructive migration. Default order ¶ @db.ordered_by(...) orders every query that has no order_by , lists and pages included. An explicit order_by replaces it; counts and bulk updates ignore it. End with a unique column ( "-id" ) so pages are stable. Update timestamps ¶ @db.timestamps() sets a declared, non-nullable updated_at: datetime on every ORM update statement, including asave and abulk_update . @db.timestamps("modified_at", clock=my_clock) names another column or injects a clock. The parentheses are required: a bare @db.timestamps raises RegistrationError . See utilities . Names ¶ Leave the table name derived for new models. Pin it with @db.table(...) when the model has migration history and its class or module may change: a changed derived name is planned as a guarded drop and create, never a rename. Naming the table twice with different names ( @db.table twice, or with table= ) is an error naming both. Use label= / plural= for irregular or localized nouns. See table and display names . Rules for all options ¶ Column names are checked when the decorator runs; a typo fails at import with the model and the unknown names. Apply options before the model is used: the migration planner, the query layer and the admin read them from the class. Options of abstract bases are inherited; a decorator on the subclass replaces that kind of option. A table model does not pass its options to a subclass. Not yet Partial and expression indexes, and soft delete, are not available. See also ¶ Define models Migrations

docs.text: Schemas from models ¶ A Schema can take its fields and constraints from a Model with @derive(Model, ...) . Response handlers convert rows explicitly with from_model . # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py from hinoki import Schema , derive from .models import Invoice @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "reference" ,)) class InvoiceIn ( Schema ): ... @derive ( Invoice , exclude = ( "customer_id" ,)) class InvoiceOut ( Schema ): customer_name : str @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "reference" , "paid" ), partial = True ) class InvoicePatch ( Schema ): ... @derive ( Invoice ) class InvoiceRow ( Schema ): ... Option Effect @derive(Invoice) every column only=("a", "b") exactly these columns exclude=("a",) every column except these partial=True every selected field optional ( UNSET when absent) partial=("a",) only the named fields optional Column types, maximum lengths, defaults and nullability carry over. Annotations in the class body add or override fields; methods and checks are kept. Relations are not derived: declare nested shapes explicitly. Derivation takes every column by default, so use only or exclude when a column is private. These fail when the class is declared, with RegistrationError : unknown columns, a non-model, only together with exclude , an empty only=() , partial names outside the selection, a class that is not a Schema , and a second @derive . ( exclude=() selects every column.) The older model= class keyword ( class InvoiceOut(Schema, model=Invoice) ) still derives every column; prefer @derive(Invoice) . Combining it with @derive(...) without a model emits DeprecationWarning . Inherit from a derived schema ¶ A subclass inherits its base's fields; only and exclude cannot remove them. A derivation that would leave out a column the base declares fails closed: @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "reference" ,)) # RegistrationError: inherited field 'id' class ReferenceOnly ( InvoiceRow ): ... Derive the narrower schema from Schema instead. A selection that keeps or widens the inherited columns is allowed. Convert rows ¶ Return a Schema , never a Model : # notes/apps/billing/api.py from uuid import UUID from hinoki import RouteGroup , errors from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageNumberPagination , PageParams from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceOut invoices = RouteGroup ( "/invoices" , access = billing_staff ) def to_out ( invoice : Invoice ) -> InvoiceOut : return InvoiceOut . from_model ( invoice , customer_name = invoice . customer . name ) @invoices . get ( "/" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_invoices ( page : PageParams ) -> Page [ InvoiceOut ]: rows = await Invoice . all () . select_related ( "customer" ) . apaginate ( page ) return rows . map ( to_out ) @invoices . get ( "/ {invoice_id} " , errors = ( errors . NotFound ,)) async def get_invoice ( invoice_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceOut : invoice = await Invoice . filter ( id = invoice_id ) . select_related ( "customer" ) . aget () return to_out ( invoice ) from_model(row, **extra) reads the attributes the schema needs; extra fills fields the model lacks, such as customer_name . A missing attribute raises AttributeError . from_models(rows, **extra) converts a list; extra is shared by every row. For a page, Page.map(InvoiceOut.from_model) . Relations must be loaded first ( select_related ); nothing is fetched lazily. An invalid stored value (longer than the schema allows) is the server's fault: it becomes 500 internal_error , logged with the ValidationError , never a client 422. Returning a model A handler annotated with one concrete Schema still converts a single returned Model of the derived class at runtime, but type checkers reject it and the HNK-API-001 rule ( Actions.forbid_model_responses ) reports it. Lists or pages of models, models of another class, and plain dict values are 500 internal_error unless the action sets validate_response=False . A subclass instance is sent with the declared fields only. See the response check . See also ¶ Schemas Validate input Generate CRUD routes : read= , create= and update= take these schemas

docs.text: Return a Schema , never a Model : # notes/apps/billing/api.py from uuid import UUID from hinoki import RouteGroup , errors from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageNumberPagination , PageParams from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceOut invoices = RouteGroup ( "/invoices" , access = billing_staff ) def to_out ( invoice : Invoice ) -> InvoiceOut : return InvoiceOut . from_model ( invoice , customer_name = invoice . customer . name ) @invoices . get ( "/" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_invoices ( page : PageParams ) -> Page [ InvoiceOut ]: rows = await Invoice . all () . select_related ( "customer" ) . apaginate ( page ) return rows . map ( to_out ) @invoices . get ( "/ {invoice_id} " , errors = ( errors . NotFound ,)) async def get_invoice ( invoice_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceOut : invoice = await Invoice . filter ( id = invoice_id ) . select_related ( "customer" ) . aget () return to_out ( invoice ) from_model(row, **extra) reads the attributes the schema needs; extra fills fields the model lacks, such as customer_name . Relations must be loaded first ( select_related ); nothing is fetched lazily. An invalid stored value (longer than the schema allows) is the server's fault: it becomes 500 internal_error , logged with the ValidationError , never a client 422. Returning a model A handler annotated with one concrete Schema still converts a single returned Model of the derived class at runtime, but type checkers reject it and the HNK-API-001 rule ( Actions.forbid_model_responses ) reports it. Lists or pages of models, models of another class, and plain dict values are 500 internal_error unless the action sets validate_response=False . docs.text: Define models ¶ A Model maps a Python class to one table. Annotated fields are the columns; indexes, ordering and other options are decorators . A model never opens a connection on import and never loads a relation implicitly. # notes/apps/billing/models.py from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import db from hinoki.orm import Model , OnDelete , field , foreign_key , pk from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Customer ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) email : str = field ( max_length = 254 , unique = True ) @db . indexed ( "customer_id" , "created_at" ) @db . ordered_by ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) class Invoice ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) customer_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Customer , on_delete = OnDelete . RESTRICT , related_name = "invoices" ) reference : str = field ( max_length = 40 , unique = True ) paid : bool = False created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) The tables are billing_customers and billing_invoices . Changing a model never changes the database: create the tables with hinoki migrations plan billing and hinoki migrations apply ( migrations ). Declare columns ¶ Declaration Column name: str required, not null note: str \| None = None nullable, optional in the constructor paid: bool = False default value id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4) the primary key email: str = field(max_length=254, unique=True) bounded text, unique created_at: datetime = field(default_factory=utc_now, index=True) factory default, single-column index customer_id: UUID = foreign_key(Customer, on_delete=...) a reference ( relations ) field() takes unique , index , max_length , default , default_factory , constraints and validators . The annotation gives the type and nullability. One primary key. pk() declares it; pass default or default_factory when the constructor may omit it. A nullable key ( int | None ) raises RegistrationError when the class is defined. Keyword-only constructor. Invoice(reference="INV-1", customer_id=c.id) . Indexes. field(index=True) indexes one column; it cannot be combined with unique=True or pk() , which are already indexed. A foreign_key has no index= option: index it with @db.indexed(...) , or a composite index that starts with it, as Invoice does ( model options ). Composite uniqueness is @db.unique("a", "b") ; there is no nested class Meta . Column types ¶ Python type Stored as Read back as str , int , float , bool the backend's text, integer, float and boolean types the same type UUID , datetime native on PostgreSQL; text on SQLite UUID , datetime dict[...] , list[...] JSON (JSON text on SQLite, text alias on MariaDB) decoded by the annotation bytes BYTEA on PostgreSQL, blob on SQLite bytes date , time ISO text ( time with microseconds, no timezone) date , time timedelta whole microseconds, bigint timedelta Enum subclass its value: bigint when every value is an integer, else text the member IPv4Address , IPv6Address , IPv4Network , IPv6Network text the ipaddress object; writes accept only that class Decimal exact, per backend (below) Decimal A stored value that does not read back as its annotation raises FieldError . date and timedelta compare and order by value. A set, tuple, Literal , plain union or Any column has no SQL type: the migration planner reports no SQL type . SQLite's contains folds ASCII case only. Decimal columns ¶ Backend Column Filters and ordering PostgreSQL numeric = , ne , in , isnull , gt , gte , lt , lte , order_by MySQL, MariaDB decimal(65,30) the same; read back with scale 30 ( Decimal("1.5") returns as Decimal("1.500…0") , equal in value) SQLite text (its exact spelling) = , ne , in , isnull only; 12.3 and 12.30 differ; range filters and order_by raise FieldError # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) from decimal import Decimal class Price ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) amount : Decimal # inside an async operation # every backend cheap = await Price . filter ( amount = Decimal ( "9.99" )) # not SQLite ordered = await Price . filter ( amount__gte = Decimal ( "5" )) . order_by ( "amount" ) A filter value is a Decimal , an int or a numeric string; a float , a bool , NaN , an infinity or contains raises FieldError . decimal(65,30) bounds MySQL and MariaDB to 35 digits before the point; PostgreSQL numeric is unbounded. A table that already stores a Decimal as text on PostgreSQL or MySQL needs a reviewed migration that changes the column type. A generated CRUD list whose @db.ordered_by names a Decimal column takes the Python path on SQLite, where that ordering is refused. Table and display names ¶ Hinoki derives the table name <app>_<models> and display names from the class. Model Module Table Labels Invoice notes.apps.billing.models billing_invoices Invoice / Invoices LineItem notes.apps.billing.models billing_line_items Line item / Line items Note notes.models or notes.models.note notes_notes Note / Notes APIKey notes.models notes_api_keys API key / API keys The app is the package that holds the models module; a module without a models segment uses its own last name. The plural is a small English rule: consonant + y → ies ; s , x , z , ch , sh → es ; otherwise s . It does not know irregular nouns ( Person → persons ). Override Form app part of the name class Invoice(Model, app="accounts") whole table name (never prefixed) @db.table("invoices") display names class Person(Model, label="Person", plural="People") Pin the table name with @db.table(...) when a model already has migration history and you rename the class or move its module: a changed derived name is planned as a drop and a create, which the destructive-migration guard stops; it is never a rename. The optional HNK-DB-001 rule ( Models.require_explicit_table ) requires every matching model to pin it. Names must be portable ASCII of at most 63 characters. A derived name that is rejected ( sqlite_… , hinoki_migrations , non-ASCII such as class Café ) does not stop the class from being defined: @db.table("cafes") can still name it. Without one, the error is raised when the model is first used (query, write, migration plan, project or admin registration, or a foreign key to it). Model field constraints and validators ¶ field() can also check values before every ORM write. Use constraints=Field(...) for built-in checks and validators=(...) for synchronous application rules: # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) from hinoki import Field def no_padding ( value : str ) -> None : if value != value . strip (): raise ValueError ( "surrounding whitespace is not allowed" ) class Product ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) sku : str = field ( max_length = 32 , constraints = Field ( min_length = 3 , pattern = r "[A-Z0-9-]+" ) ) price : float = field ( constraints = Field ( gt = 0 )) name : str = field ( max_length = 120 , validators = ( no_padding ,)) When. Immediately before inserts and ORM updates, filtered bulk updates included; never on construction, assignment or reads. Invalid declarations fail when the class is created. Checks. String and list lengths, patterns, membership and numeric bounds. A JSON column ( dict[...] , list[dict[...]] ) takes no built-in checks; validators still run on it. Failure. ModelValidationError , before any SQL, with details holding each field's path , code and message . In a request it becomes the standard 422 response; the admin shows the messages. Validators are synchronous, raise ValueError to refuse, perform no I/O and do not change the value. Rules about other rows, permissions or current state belong in an operation. These checks protect CLI, admin and direct ORM writes; a Schema still validates HTTP input first ( validate input ). Database constraints remain authoritative. Share fields: abstract models and mixins ¶ An abstract model has no table: it is not migrated, cannot be queried and only exists to be subclassed. # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) class Keyed ( Model , abstract = True ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) @db . timestamps () @db . ordered_by ( "-updated_at" ) class Tracked ( Model , abstract = True ): created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now , index = True ) class Article ( Keyed , Tracked ): title : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) Article has created_at , updated_at , id and title , is ordered by -updated_at , indexes updated_at and refreshes it on every update. Tracked.all() raises ModelError . abstract=True is not inherited; an abstract model needs no primary key, a table model needs exactly one, its own or inherited. Options from abstract bases are inherited: all @db.unique and @db.indexed , and the order and timestamp column of the first base that sets one. A decorator on the subclass replaces that kind of option. A field(index=True) index belongs to its column and is dropped when a subclass redeclares the column without it. Constraint names are not inherited: an abstract model cannot use @db.unique(..., name=...) . Plain mixins (non-model classes) contribute annotated fields and methods; ClassVar annotations are not fields. Type checkers do not see mixin fields as constructor arguments: prefer an abstract model. Conflicting types. Two bases giving one field different types are refused unless the class redeclares the field. Subclassing a table model copies its columns into a separate, unrelated table; no join, no shared rows, no inherited options. Column order follows dataclass rules: model bases (last listed first), then mixins, then the class's own fields. A foreign key in an abstract model needs a per-subclass reverse name; see relations . docs.text: Own resources with modules ¶ A module owns something that lives as long as a worker or a command run: a connection pool, a client, a thread pool. It opens the resource at startup, provides it to the rest of the application and closes it when the run ends. Nothing is opened at import time. # notes/passwords.py from collections.abc import AsyncIterator from contextlib import asynccontextmanager from hinoki import Module , ModuleContext from hinoki.crypto import PasswordHasher class Passwords ( Module ): name = "passwords" @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan ( self , ctx : ModuleContext ) -> AsyncIterator [ None ]: hasher = PasswordHasher () ctx . provide ( PasswordHasher , hasher ) try : yield finally : hasher . close () Install it on the application: # notes/main.py app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , title = "Notes" , rules = project_rules , modules = [ Passwords ()], ) Each worker runs lifespan up to yield before it answers requests, and the finally block when it stops, even if a later module fails to start. Use what a module provides ¶ ctx.provide(Type, value) registers a value under its type; ctx.get(Type) returns it (or raises LookupError ) and ctx.find(Type) returns None instead. The value is reachable from: Where How Another module's lifespan ctx.get(PasswordHasher) , with requires = (Passwords,) A startup or shutdown hook ctx.get(PasswordHasher) A management command context.get(PasswordHasher) , with requires = (Passwords,) A rate-limit policy context.resource(PasswordHasher) # notes/commands.py from argparse import ArgumentParser , Namespace from hinoki.crypto import PasswordHasher from hinoki.management import Command , CommandContext from notes.passwords import Passwords class HashPassword ( Command ): name = "hash-password" help = "print the Argon2id hash of a password" requires = ( Passwords ,) def add_arguments ( self , parser : ArgumentParser ) -> None : parser . add_argument ( "password" ) async def handle ( self , context : CommandContext , args : Namespace ) -> None : print ( await context . get ( PasswordHasher ) . hash ( args . password )) With commands=[HashPassword] on the application, hinoki manage hash-password s3cret starts only Passwords (and what it requires), runs the command and closes it. Request handlers do not receive module values as parameters; the database is the exception, because model methods find the worker's Database themselves. The database module ¶ A database: settings.DatabaseSettings field on your settings class is enough: Hinoki installs DatabaseModule (from hinoki.db ) before any declared module, so a module with requires = (DatabaseModule,) can call ctx.get(Database) in its lifespan. Declaring DatabaseModule , or a subclass of it, in modules= replaces the automatic one; modules that require DatabaseModule still start after it. See database connection ownership . Declare modules ¶ modules= accepts instances and classes. An instance is the plain choice; a class is built with its from_settings(settings) classmethod, which you override to read your settings (the default raises TypeError and says so). requires decides the order: dependencies start first and stop last. An empty or duplicate name , a missing requirement, a cycle, or a type provided twice fails startup with ModuleGraphError . A module whose class extends a required class satisfies that requirement. Keep lifespan bounded (it shares lifecycle.startup_timeout ), fail fast when a required service is unavailable, and close what you own in finally . Startup and shutdown hooks ¶ For an action at the edge of a worker's life that owns no resource, such as warming a cache, logging the build or flushing a counter, list functions on the application instead of writing a module ( ProjectSettings here declares a database field, so the database module is installed): # notes/main.py import logging from hinoki import Hinoki , ModuleContext from hinoki.db import Database from notes.settings import ProjectSettings log = logging . getLogger ( "notes" ) async def warm_cache ( ctx : ModuleContext ) -> None : await ctx . get ( Database ) . fetch ( "SELECT 1" ) def say_goodbye ( ctx : ModuleContext ) -> None : log . info ( "worker stopping" ) app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , on_startup = [ warm_cache ], on_shutdown = [ say_goodbye ] ) A hook takes the worker's ModuleContext ( ctx.settings , ctx.get(Type) , ctx.tasks ). It is async def , or a plain def that runs on the bounded sync executor like a sync handler. Model methods reach the worker's database inside a hook as they do inside a request. Pass hooks as a list or tuple when constructing Hinoki ; the app's on_startup and on_shutdown tuples are read-only. Hooks must be callables, not async generators, and must return None . A plain def may instead return an awaitable, which Hinoki awaits; use async def when the hook needs to await work directly. Startup hooks Shutdown hooks Run Once per worker, after every module has started, in the listed order Once per worker, before background tasks, the sync executor and the modules are closed, in the listed order Time limit Share lifecycle.startup_timeout with the modules Each has its own lifecycle.shutdown_timeout Requests Answered 503 not_ready until the last hook returns Answered 503 not_ready from the moment shutdown begins A hook fails or times out Startup fails: later hooks do not run, no shutdown hook runs, the modules already started are closed, and the server is told that startup failed. The log has the traceback; the message names the hook ( startup hook 'warm_cache' failed to start: TimeoutError ) It is logged and reported as a shutdown error; the remaining hooks and the module cleanup still run Shutdown hooks run only after a startup that completed, and a shutdown hook is not the finally of a startup hook. Use this rule to choose: a resource you own is a module (its lifespan closes it even when a later step of startup fails); an action is a hook . A plain def hook that is still running when its time limit passes cannot be interrupted; it keeps its executor thread until it returns. Hooks run where the application serves requests: under hinoki dev / serve and any ASGI server, on the first request of each WSGI worker, and in the test clients . hinoki manage commands, check , routes and migrations do not run them. Scripts outside the server ¶ For app maintenance tasks, declare a management command and list its required module classes in Command.requires . Hinoki starts only those modules and their dependencies for one command run, so a database module is opened and closed without starting the HTTP server or unrelated modules. Standalone scripts outside Hinoki's server or management-command runner have no module lifespan. Open their own Database and close it explicitly; do not import a module-global pool. The blog seed script demonstrates this pattern. Errors and edge cases ¶ ctx.get for a type nobody provided raises LookupError: <Type> was not provided ; declare the providing module in requires . A module class without from_settings in modules= fails at construction: pass an instance instead. hinoki check , routes and migrations do not start modules or run hooks. See also ¶ Settings : where a module reads its configuration. Command line : running management commands. Sync and async : where sync hooks run.

An instance is the plain choice; a class is built with its from_settings(settings) classmethod, which you override to read your settings (the default raises TypeError and says so). requires decides the order: dependencies start first and stop last. An empty or duplicate name , a missing requirement, a cycle, or a type provided twice fails startup with ModuleGraphError . A module whose class extends a required class satisfies that requirement. Keep lifespan bounded (it shares lifecycle.startup_timeout ), fail fast when a required service is unavailable, and close what you own in finally .
docs.title: Declare modules

docs.text: For an action at the edge of a worker's life that owns no resource, such as warming a cache, logging the build or flushing a counter, list functions on the application instead of writing a module ( ProjectSettings here declares a database field, so the database module is installed): # notes/main.py import logging from hinoki import Hinoki , ModuleContext from hinoki.db import Database from notes.settings import ProjectSettings log = logging . getLogger ( "notes" ) async def warm_cache ( ctx : ModuleContext ) -> None : await ctx . get ( Database ) . fetch ( "SELECT 1" ) def say_goodbye ( ctx : ModuleContext ) -> None : log . info ( "worker stopping" ) app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , on_startup = [ warm_cache ], on_shutdown = [ say_goodbye ] ) A hook takes the worker's ModuleContext ( ctx.settings , ctx.get(Type) , ctx.tasks ). It is async def , or a plain def that runs on the bounded sync executor like a sync handler. Model methods reach the worker's database inside a hook as they do inside a request. Pass hooks as a list or tuple when constructing Hinoki ; the app's on_startup and on_shutdown tuples are read-only. Hooks must be callables, not async generators, and must return None . A plain def may instead return an awaitable, which Hinoki awaits; use async def when the hook needs to await work directly. Startup hooks Shutdown hooks Run Once per worker, after every module has started, in the listed order Once per worker, before background tasks, the sync executor and the modules are closed, in the listed order Time limit Share lifecycle.startup_timeout with the modules Each has its own lifecycle.shutdown_timeout Requests Answered 503 not_ready until the last hook returns Answered 503 not_ready from the moment shutdown begins A hook fails or times out Startup fails: later hooks do not run, no shutdown hook runs, the modules already started are closed, and the server is told that startup failed. The log has the traceback; the message names the hook ( startup hook 'warm_cache' failed to start: TimeoutError ) It is logged and reported as a shutdown error; the remaining hooks and the module cleanup still run Shutdown hooks run only after a startup that completed, and a shutdown hook is not the finally of a startup hook. Use this rule to choose: a resource you own is a module (its lifespan closes it even when a later step of startup fails); an action is a hook . A plain def hook that is still running when its time limit passes cannot be interrupted; it keeps its executor thread until it returns. Hooks run where the application serves requests: under hinoki dev / serve and any ASGI server, on the first request of each WSGI worker, and in the test clients . hinoki manage commands, check , routes and migrations do not run them.
docs.title: Startup and shutdown hooks

docs.text: For app maintenance tasks, declare a management command and list its required module classes in Command.requires . Hinoki starts only those modules and their dependencies for one command run, so a database module is opened and closed without starting the HTTP server or unrelated modules. Standalone scripts outside Hinoki's server or management-command runner have no module lifespan. Open their own Database and close it explicitly; do not import a module-global pool. The blog seed script demonstrates this pattern.
docs.title: Scripts outside the server

docs.text: ctx.get for a type nobody provided raises LookupError: <Type> was not provided ; declare the providing module in requires . A module class without from_settings in modules= fails at construction: pass an instance instead. hinoki check , routes and migrations do not start modules or run hooks.

docs.text: Create a project ¶ hinoki new creates a working project: an application with a health route, typed settings, architecture rules, a test and instructions for AI agents. From the Hinoki checkout: uv run hinoki new Answer the questions ¶ In a terminal, hinoki new asks for everything the command line leaves out: Question Answers Default Project name lower-case letters and digits, single underscores between words, starting with a letter none Parent directory any path . (here) Database none ; sqlite (local file in .hinoki/ ); postgresql (also writes .env.example ) none Server kiso (Hinoki's own Rust server: native handler lane, access log); granian (general-purpose ASGI server: runs any ASGI app) kiso Agent instructions and MCP config? yes / no yes Agent skills? yes / no no Initialize a git repository? yes / no yes Install dependencies (uv sync)? yes / no yes Create an app now? yes / no yes App name (only after yes) the same rule as the project name; an invalid name is asked again core Each answer collapses into a summary line. When the files are written, the command lists the key ones, creates the app you named with the same code as hinoki app create (and registers it in hinoki.toml ), runs git init and uv sync with a timer, and ends with the next commands to type. When no app was created, the summary says how to add one. Nothing is written until the last answer, so Ctrl-C, Esc or end of input cancels cleanly (exit 130). Create a project without questions ¶ Every question has a flag. --no-input never asks and uses the defaults for what is missing, which suits scripts and CI (without a terminal no question is asked either): uv run hinoki new notes --no-input --database sqlite --git --install Option Effect NAME the package name; required with --no-input --dir PATH parent directory; the project is PATH/NAME --database none\|sqlite\|postgresql see Choose a database --server kiso\|granian see Choose a server --agent-files / --no-agent-files write AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md and .mcp.json --skills / --no-skills also write the agent skills under .claude/skills --git / --no-git run git init ; no commit is made. Without a prompt: off --install / --no-install run uv sync . Without a prompt: off --app NAME also create this app and register it, without asking. The name is checked before anything is written --no-app create no app and do not ask about one; the two flags exclude each other --hinoki SOURCE where the project installs Hinoki from; see below What you get ¶ notes/ ├── hinoki.toml project registry: application, routes, apps ├── hinoki-rules.toml rule waivers (an example, commented out) ├── pyproject.toml dependencies, pytest, Ruff ├── README.md ├── AGENTS.md agent instructions (with CLAUDE.md and .mcp.json) ├── notes/ │ ├── main.py the application │ ├── api.py the health endpoint │ ├── routes.py the routes hinoki.toml points to │ ├── settings.py typed settings (NOTES_ variables and .env) │ └── rules.py architecture rules └── tests/ └── healthtest.py one test, no database needed hinoki.toml names the application, so project commands find it on their own. notes/main.py binds the routes the manifest lists with include=manifest_routes() : project.routes first, then each app's routes under its prefix . # hinoki.toml [project] application = "notes.main:app" routes = "notes.routes:routes" The project package holds no models and registers no app. Models live in apps: The last question of hinoki new (or --app billing ) creates the first one; uv run hinoki app create billing adds more later. Either way it writes notes/apps/billing/ and adds the [[apps]] entry for it ( hinoki app create ). Run it ¶ cd notes uv run pytest uv run hinoki dev Run uv sync first if you answered no to installing. The application answers on http://127.0.0.1:8000/health , with its documentation at /docs . Choose a database ¶ sqlite and postgresql add one field to notes/settings.py : class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings Its value comes from NOTES_DATABASE__<FIELD> variables (two underscores between the group and the field) in the environment or in .env ; keep .env out of git. With no value set it is the SQLite file .hinoki/local.sqlite3 . postgresql also writes .env.example with a placeholder URL; copy it to .env and fill it in: # .env.example NOTES_DATABASE__URL = postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/notes none declares no field, and a request that queries a model fails with no database is active . Add the field above when you add models. Configure a database lists the URL forms and the connection fields. No database is created or contacted. Create the tables with hinoki migrations apply once you have models. Choose a server ¶ kiso needs no configuration. granian writes settings.toml with [server] server = "granian" , which the settings class reads. Either way, NOTES_SERVER__SERVER and --server on dev and serve override the choice. Serve an application compares the two. Where Hinoki comes from ¶ This repository's pre-alpha Hinoki framework is not published on PyPI; the hinoki name belongs to an unrelated legacy package. The generated pyproject.toml therefore names this repository as the source under [tool.uv.sources] : Given Source written --hinoki /path/to/checkout that checkout, editable --hinoki https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki@REV (or git+https://... ) that repository, pinned to REV when given nothing, running from a source checkout the checkout you ran it from nothing, any other installation the public repository, default branch Checkout paths and Git source values are escaped as TOML strings. How it looks in a terminal ¶ On a colour, UTF-8 terminal (macOS and Linux) the prompts sit on a guide rail and answer to keys: type a name (backspace edits, Ctrl-U clears), move through the database and server lists with ↑/↓ or pick one by number, and switch yes/no with ←/→ or y / n ; Enter confirms. Each answered prompt collapses into one summary line. The run then lists the key files it created, times git init and uv sync (with a spinner while they run) and ends with the next commands. Ghostty, kitty, iTerm2 and WezTerm show the Hinoki logo as an inline image; other terminals show a text wordmark. Elsewhere the prompts are numbered lists and [Y/n] questions answered with Enter. Output that is piped, NO_COLOR and TERM=dumb give plain ASCII with no escape sequences. HINOKI_ANIMATE=0 (or CI ) turns off the tagline animation and the spinner; HINOKI_IMAGES=0 (or running inside tmux/screen) uses the text wordmark. When the terminal reports a light background through COLORFGBG , darker shades of the same colours are used. Ctrl-C or Esc cancels before anything is written (exit status 130); so does the end of input. Errors and edge cases ¶ The name must be lower-case letters and digits, with single underscores between words ( my_shop , api_v1 ), starting with a letter, and not hinoki , a Python keyword or a standard-library module such as json , which would shadow imports in the project. A refused name is asked again; with --no-input the command exits 2. An app name follows the same rule. A refused name is asked again; --app with a bad name exits 2 before anything is written. If the project is written but the app cannot be created, the error is printed, the project stays and the exit status is 2. PATH/NAME must not exist or must be empty; nothing is overwritten. git or uv missing or failing prints a warning and keeps the project. Nothing else is installed or run. See also ¶ Installation Quick start Command line Test an application

docs.text: OpenAPI document ¶ Hinoki.openapi() builds an OpenAPI 3.1 document from the routes registered with the app. Paths, parameters, request bodies, response schemas, declared errors and supported authentication schemes come from the action declarations and type annotations. Generate the document from the application without starting a server: hinoki openapi --output openapi.json hinoki openapi --check openapi.json hinoki openapi --breaking-against openapi-baseline.json --output writes stable, sorted JSON. --check compares parsed JSON with a committed file, so whitespace-only changes do not report drift. --breaking-against compares with an earlier document (the released one) and prints one breaking: … line per change that would break an existing client. The three options are exclusive. The command opens no database and works even when openapi_url is disabled. See inspect an application for output and exit status. Serve the document and viewers ¶ All three URLs are disabled by default. Set openapi_url to serve JSON; add docs_url for the bundled Swagger UI or redoc_url for ReDoc. A project created with hinoki new already sets the first two: # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.project import manifest_routes from notes.rules import project_rules from notes.settings import ProjectSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , include = manifest_routes (), rules = project_rules , openapi_url = "/openapi.json" , docs_url = "/docs" , redoc_url = "/redoc" , ) The corresponding docs.openapi_url , docs.docs_url and docs.redoc_url settings provide the same defaults. A viewer requires openapi_url . Hinoki(...) arguments override settings; passing None disables a page. The packaged viewers work without a CDN. The generated OpenAPI document, Swagger UI, ReDoc and their assets answer HEAD with the same status and representation headers as GET , without a response body. Each request still has its own request ID in the configured response header ( x-request-id by default). QUERY operations ¶ The document is OpenAPI 3.1, which has no field for the QUERY method (OpenAPI 3.2 adds query ). An action declared with @http.query is therefore written under the path item's x-query extension field, with the same operation object as any other method: operation ID, parameters, request body, responses and security. The document stays valid 3.1. Tools that only read the standard method fields do not see these operations: Swagger UI and ReDoc do not list them, and a client generator skips them unless it is told about x-query . The application MCP and explain_action read the field. What is generated ¶ A unique operationId is derived from the handler's qualified name. If names collide, Hinoki appends a numeric suffix. The first line of the handler docstring becomes summary ; the remaining lines become description . Path, query and pagination parameters come from the bound handler signature. Body fields and successful response fields come from Schema annotations. Parser and renderer media types supply the content types. Typed UploadedFile parameters generate a multipart/form-data request body with binary file properties. Repeated files use an array of binary items; optional single-file bindings are not required in the body or property list. Text keys read dynamically through request.POST are not inferred or listed. A declared errors=(...) adds response entries for those APIError classes. Request binding and schema validation errors are documented as 422 where the action has request inputs. access=... adds a security requirement when its authentication provider supplies an OpenAPI scheme. Authentication responses are included in the operation. Admin HTML routes marked hide_from_docs are omitted. A dict[str, X] field becomes type: object with additionalProperties (the value schema), propertyNames (the key schema) and minProperties / maxProperties from its declared entry limits. The framework bounds on client input (1000 entries, 256-character keys) are not part of the document because components describe responses too; see dictionary fields . date , time and timedelta fields become type: string with format: date , time and duration . A Decimal field becomes type: string , format: decimal and a pattern for its text form, with ge / le / gt / lt as minimum / maximum / exclusiveMinimum / exclusiveMaximum ; max_digits and decimal_places are not written, nor is a Decimal field's multiple_of . An int field's multiple_of becomes multipleOf . IP address and network fields become type: string with format: ipv4 , ipv6 , ipv4network or ipv6network . A Path field becomes type: string with format: path , and a SecretStr field type: string with format: password and writeOnly: true . A bytes field becomes type: string , format: byte and contentEncoding: base64 , and its decoded-size limits are not written either, since they count bytes rather than characters. See dates, durations, decimals and bytes . An Enum or Literal field becomes type: string or type: integer with an enum list of the values (the member values, never the names), inline in the property; a nullable one is wrapped in anyOf with null . See enums and literals . A set[X] or frozenset[X] field becomes an array with uniqueItems: true , tuple[X, ...] an array of X , and a fixed tuple[X, Y] an array with prefixItems , items: false and equal minItems / maxItems . See sets and tuples . A plain union such as int | str becomes anyOf of its variants, and Any or object an unconstrained schema ( {} ). See plain unions and Any . Discriminated unions declared as Schema fields become OpenAPI oneOf schemas with a discriminator and explicit tag-to-component mapping. Variant tag fields appear as required string enums; the runtime uses the same tags to select exactly one branch. List items, nested fields and nullable unions retain that structure. For route input and response documentation, put the union inside a wrapper Schema ; bare union return annotations are rejected instead of producing an incomplete schema. The return value is also checked against the annotation at runtime ( details ). oneOf : - $ref : "#/components/schemas/Cat" - $ref : "#/components/schemas/Dog" discriminator : propertyName : type mapping : cat : "#/components/schemas/Cat" dog : "#/components/schemas/Dog" See Collections and unions: discriminated unions for the Python declarations and validation behavior. For file binding syntax, limits and the in-memory boundary, see upload files . Add a useful docstring to each handler because it is the source for operation text: @http . get ( "/tasks/ {task_id} " ) async def get_task ( task_id : UUID ) -> TaskOutput : """Read one task. Returns the task visible to the authenticated caller. """ ... Current limits ¶ Per-action tags , deprecated , a caller-supplied operation_id and include_in_schema controls are not implemented. Response bodies are generated from annotations; every action's return value is checked against its annotation at runtime, and an annotation that cannot be checked stops the app at startup ( details ). See project status for other API boundaries.

For file binding syntax, limits and the in-memory boundary, see upload files . Add a useful docstring to each handler because it is the source for operation text: @http . get ( "/tasks/ {task_id} " ) async def get_task ( task_id : UUID ) -> TaskOutput : """Read one task. Returns the task visible to the authenticated caller. """ ...

docs.text: Per-action tags , deprecated , a caller-supplied operation_id and include_in_schema controls are not implemented. Response bodies are generated from annotations; every action's return value is checked against its annotation at runtime, and an annotation that cannot be checked stops the app at startup ( details ). See project status for other API boundaries.
docs.title: Current limits

docs.text: Pagination ¶ An action opts into page-number pagination with pagination=PageNumberPagination() . A size you leave out comes from the application's pagination settings group; without settings the defaults are page_size=20 and max_page_size=100 . The framework parses and validates page and page_size , injects a PageParams value, and documents both query parameters in OpenAPI. The Billing app lists invoices a page at a time. The handler asks the model for one page, and Page.map() turns its rows into schemas: # notes/apps/billing/api.py from hinoki import RouteGroup from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageNumberPagination , PageParams from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceOut invoices = RouteGroup ( "/invoices" , access = billing_staff , atomic = True ) @invoices . get ( "/" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_invoices ( page : PageParams ) -> Page [ InvoiceOut ]: return ( await Invoice . all () . apaginate ( page )) . map ( InvoiceOut . from_model ) Pages are one-based. page_size defaults to the strategy's configured size and cannot exceed its maximum. Invalid values produce a validation response before the handler runs; page is limited to 1 000 000 000, and longer or larger values answer 422 with the code le . Page contains items , page , page_size , total and the computed pages . Empty result sets have zero pages; a page beyond the end has an empty items list. Page.map() converts each item while preserving the counts and requested page. Defaults for the whole application ¶ settings.AppSettings has a pagination group, set in code, in the environment or in TOML. With the project's settings class: # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" ): pass export NOTES_PAGINATION__PAGE_SIZE = 25 export NOTES_PAGINATION__MAX_PAGE_SIZE = 200 The application in notes/main.py reads them through Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings, ...) . Precedence, from strongest to weakest: a size set on the action's PageNumberPagination(...) , the application's pagination settings, then 20 and 100. Each size is resolved separately, so PageNumberPagination(page_size=10) keeps its 10 and takes its maximum from the settings. The result must satisfy 1 <= page_size <= max_page_size : invalid settings fail when they load, and an action whose own size does not fit the resolved other one (for example PageNumberPagination(max_page_size=10) under a settings page_size of 25) fails when it is included, naming the action. The generated OpenAPI parameters show the resolved values. Use the queryset's apaginate / paginate methods for database rows. They append the primary key as the last sort key (after any order_by ), so rows with equal sort values keep one position across pages. Page.of(rows, params) slices an in-memory sequence and counts that sequence; it is not a substitute for database pagination on large tables.

docs.text: Structure an application ¶ Opinionated, with reasons. Each practice below is enforced by the framework, checkable with an optional rule , or a convention left to review. The Tracker example shows them together: api → operations → models , row permission in the statements, the direction enforced by Imports.forbid , operations tested without HTTP. 1. Three layers, one direction ¶ HTTP layer actions (functions or API classes) shapes, status codes, access, atomic=True │ ▼ Operations plain async functions one business operation each; no HTTP types │ ▼ Persistence Model / QuerySet tables, relations, explicit loading HTTP layer turns a request into typed values ( Schema , path and query parameters, Caller ) and an operation's result into a response Schema . No business rules, no SQL. Operations hold the rules ("an editor may publish only their own draft"). They take plain arguments ( principal , a Schema , IDs), so an action, a CLI command, a test, an admin hook or an MCP tool can call them. An action that reads cookies or headers cannot be reused; an operation can. Persistence never imports the HTTP layer. Rule: Imports.forbid(source="notes.apps.billing.models", target="notes.apps.billing.api") , and the same for operations → api. Small apps may skip the middle layer. Add it when an action holds a rule another entry point needs. 2. Where each concern lives ¶ Actions are functions by default, grouped in a RouteGroup that states shared options once; an API class earns its place for crud(...) resources with hooks or inherited actions. Concern Put it Why Routes Each app's routes.py ; prefixes only in hinoki.toml ( register routes ). Convention One place to read the map; one source per path segment Authentication A provider ( BearerAuth , JWTAuth , …) returning a Caller One path for HTTP, admin and MCP Coarse permission access= on the action, or once on its RouteGroup . Public is the default : protect on purpose. Rule: Actions.require_access A forgotten policy is the most common hole Row permission (owner, tenant) The statement : scope aupdate / adelete by owner so check and write are one operation No check-then-write race; hidden rows look missing ( 404 ). If the API promises a distinct 403 , make the conditional write and its fallback explicit, and document what it reveals Input validation The Schema (types, constraints, patterns) Strict, no coercion, validated in Rust before your code runs Business rules Operations Testable without HTTP Transactions atomic=True on every write. Rule: Transactions.require_atomic Commit after the response is encoded; rollback before the error becomes HTTP Errors Raise APIError subclasses and declare them: errors=(InvoiceAlreadyPaid,) . Translate exceptions you cannot change once with @app.error_handler(...) The declaration feeds OpenAPI, MCP and ASGIClient(app, strict_errors=True) . A database UniqueViolation is already 409 unique_conflict . A returned Response commits the transaction Secrets Settings and the environment, never defaults Nothing to leak from the repository 3. Schema classes and models ¶ Models describe tables; Schema classes describe the API. Never return a model : respond with InvoiceOut.from_model(row) . Name classes by role: InvoiceIn (what a client may set), InvoicePatch (every field UNSET by default), InvoiceOut (what a client may see, often @derive(Invoice) ). Rules: Actions.forbid_model_responses() refuses a Model return type, also inside list , Page and unions; Schemas.forbid_exposure("password_hash", …) keeps columns out of responses through nesting and subclasses. Create from a Schema and add what only the server knows: await Post.acreate(data, author_id=principal.user.id) ; server values win. Update with await row.aupdate_from(patch) , which writes only what was sent. A server-assigned field does not exist in the input Schema at all; the keyword override is a second line of defence. Constraints and patterns belong on the Schema , in the Rust pattern syntax (whole value, no look-around). 4. Relations and queries ¶ Relations are never lazy. Load what the response shows ( select_related for single values, prefetch_related for collections) in the function that builds the response, so the cost is visible in one place. Paginate every list ( pagination= + PageParams + Page[...] ). Never return an unbounded list; never load a whole table to count or aggregate (use acount() , filters or SQL). Rule: Actions.require_pagination . Filter and order only by names you choose; never pass client-supplied column names to filter or order_by . 5. Sync and async ¶ Prefer async handlers. A sync handler runs on a bounded pool and uses the sync model methods; it must not block for long, and a full queue answers 503 overloaded . Password hashing has its own bounded pool. Never call blocking code from an async handler. See sync and async code . 6. Modules ¶ An application is a set of modules with explicit dependencies and a lifespan ( DatabaseModule , your own Module ). Importing a module registers and opens nothing. Resources are created once per worker, in its lifespan. Migrations are a deploy step, never run at startup or from every worker. A standalone script owns and closes its own short-lived connection. 7. Migrations ¶ hinoki migrations plan billing hinoki migrations apply plan writes reviewable SQL and a state file; destructive operations are flagged and need --allow-destructive , and a new NOT NULL column without a default is flagged. Review the SQL like code and apply it to a disposable database first. See migrations . 8. Testing ¶ Run database tests against disposable servers for each backend you support: HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL (PostgreSQL), HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL , HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL . Without a URL those tests are skipped: read the skip summary; one backend's green run is not conformance for another. Drive HTTP behaviour through the ASGI client (no sockets); test operations directly. For security code, use independent test vectors and inject the clock ( JWTAuth.now ). 9. Security defaults to keep ¶ HTTPS terminates somewhere you control ( Admin(secure_cookies=True) behind a proxy); access= on everything that is not public on purpose; CSRF on every cookie-authenticated form (the admin does it); a strict CSP; Argon2id passwords; JWT keys with a fixed algorithm and a kid ; no token, password or hash in logs or error bodies; uploads within the 1 MiB body limit; no real personal data in tests or fixtures. 10. Rules to turn on from day one ¶ hinoki new enables eight rules ( HNK-ACC-001 , HNK-ACC-002 , HNK-API-001 , HNK-API-002 , HNK-API-003 , HNK-TXN-001 , HNK-SCH-001 , HNK-SCH-002 ) and leaves the model rules HNK-DB-001 and HNK-DB-002 commented out until the first model exists. Turn those on then, and add Imports.forbid ( HNK-IMP-001 ) for the direction in section 1 . Waivers live in hinoki-rules.toml , are the owner's decision, carry a reason and a bounded target, and are never edited by tools or agents to pass a check. 11. Anti-patterns ¶ Returning a Model , or a dict built from one. A business rule inside an action that another entry point also needs. Response(4xx) from an atomic=True action: it commits. Client-supplied column names reaching filter or order_by . Applying migrations at startup; creating a pool at import. A broad waiver ( * ), or editing waivers to silence a rule. Catching Exception in an action to "keep going": let the framework translate it and roll back. app.include(...) in a project with hinoki.toml : list the routes in routes.py . 12. More than one service ¶ Split a system only for a reason you can name (independent deploys, different scaling, a team boundary); every split costs something the framework cannot hide. No joins, no shared transaction. A foreign key never crosses a service. Store the other service's ID as a plain value and treat its answers as snapshots. A write across two services is a sequence of calls that can half-fail: make each step idempotent and decide what a retry does before writing the code. Each service owns its tables. Others call its API, never its database. Its migrations belong to it and are applied by its deploy step ( section 7 ). The caller is a Caller too. Service-to-service calls authenticate like any client (a JWT with a service identity and narrow permissions); do not forward the end user's token unless the callee must act as that user. Wrap every remote call in an operation ( section 1 ) with a timeout and a failure you chose ( 502 or 503 ), never a client library's exception. Share contracts, not models. Publish the response Schema classes or the OpenAPI document; keep models private. A runnable two-service example and a client helper do not exist yet.
