docs.text: Scalar field types ¶ A Schema field can be str , int , float , bool , UUID , datetime , date , time , timedelta , Decimal , bytes , an Enum class, a Literal , an ipaddress type, Email , Url , Slug , SecretStr or Path ; optionally | None (accepts null ) or | Unset , and wrapped in Annotated[..., Field(...)] . Containers, unions and nested types are in collections and unions . Anything else raises RegistrationError when the class is created. Numbers ¶ JSON input is strict: a float is never an integer, and bool is never a number. A float field always holds a float : JSON 1 becomes 1.0 , and Reading(value=1).value is 1.0 , also inside lists, sets, tuples and dict[str, float] . A float variant of a plain union keeps the value it was given. Multiples ¶ Field(multiple_of=step) requires an int or Decimal to be an exact whole multiple of a positive step. It runs after the bounds and fails with multiple_of . A float field refuses multiple_of (float multiples are inexact): use Decimal . from decimal import Decimal from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema class Order ( Schema ): quantity : Annotated [ int , Field ( ge = 0 , multiple_of = 5 )] price : Annotated [ Decimal , Field ( multiple_of = Decimal ( "0.05" ), max_digits = 8 )] Order . validate ({ "quantity" : 10 , "price" : "9.95" }) # accepted Order . validate ({ "quantity" : 12 , "price" : "9.97" }) # two multiple_of errors Enums and literals ¶ An Enum , StrEnum or IntEnum class, or a Literal of strings or of integers, accepts only its values. The wire carries the value; validation returns the member. import enum from typing import Literal from hinoki import Schema class Status ( enum . StrEnum ): DRAFT = "draft" SENT = "sent" class Priority ( enum . IntEnum ): LOW = 1 HIGH = 3 class Ticket ( Schema ): channel : Literal [ "web" , "email" ] status : Status = Status . DRAFT priority : Priority = Priority . LOW ticket = Ticket . validate ({ "channel" : "web" , "status" : "sent" , "priority" : 3 }) assert ticket . status is Status . SENT and ticket . priority is Priority . HIGH assert ticket . dump () == { "channel" : "web" , "status" : "sent" , "priority" : 3 } Strict values. "3" , 3.0 and True are not 3 . A wrong type answers type ; a value outside the list answers one_of , and the message lists the accepted values, never member names. One kind. All values are str or all int (64-bit). A mixed enum or Literal , None inside a Literal (write Literal["a"] | None ), a Flag , an empty enum, an enum member inside a Literal and other value types raise RegistrationError . Field(...) constraints are refused: the type is the list. Construction takes members for an enum field and the listed values for a Literal ; dump() writes values, to_dict() keeps members. Text sources read an IntEnum or int Literal like an int . Models. An Enum column stores the value; a Literal column has no SQL type: use an enum or str / int in the model and the Literal in the Schema . OpenAPI: type string or integer with an inline enum list. Dates, durations, decimals and bytes ¶ These travel as JSON strings and validate identically on both lanes. import datetime as dt from decimal import Decimal from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema class Booking ( Schema ): day : dt . date opens : dt . time length : dt . timedelta price : Annotated [ Decimal , Field ( ge = 0 , max_digits = 8 , decimal_places = 2 )] receipt : Annotated [ bytes , Field ( max_length = 1024 )] booking = Booking . validate ( { "day" : "2026-03-14" , "opens" : "09:30:00+01:00" , "length" : "PT1H30M" , "price" : "19.90" , "receipt" : "aGVsbG8=" , } ) assert booking . length == dt . timedelta ( hours = 1 , minutes = 30 ) assert booking . dump ()[ "price" ] == "19.90" Type Accepted input Output Error code date YYYY-MM-DD , a real date in years 0001–9999 same text date time HH:MM:SS[.f…] (1–6 fraction digits) with Z or ±HH:MM isoformat() time ; time_tz without offset timedelta ISO 8601 [-]P[nD][T[nH][nM][n[.f…]S]] ; no years, months or weeks PT1H30M , -PT0.5S duration ; duration_range Decimal string -?(0\|[1-9][0-9]*)(\.[0-9]+)? or integer; no floats, booleans, exponents, NaN , infinities fixed-point string keeping the scale ( "0.10" ) decimal bytes standard padded base64, no whitespace, not URL-safe padded base64 bytes Times need an offset on the wire, like a datetime ; from_model() accepts naive values. A date field refuses a datetime . Decimal is exact. ge , le , gt , lt take an int or Decimal . max_digits (default 64, at most 1000) counts all digits, decimal_places those after the point; checked in the order max_digits , decimal_places , max_whole_digits , bounds, multiple_of . bytes size. Lengths count decoded bytes. Without max_length , client input is capped at 65 536 bytes ( hinoki.fieldtypes.MAX_BYTES_LENGTH ); model-derived fields are not capped. pattern matches the decoded bytes read as Latin-1. Output. The JSON encoder writes these values only inside Schema instances; a bare Decimal or bytes in a plain dict is a TypeError . OpenAPI: format date , time , duration , decimal (with a pattern ) and byte ( contentEncoding: base64 ). Internet addresses, Email , Url and Slug ¶ from ipaddress import IPv4Address , IPv4Network from hinoki import Email , Schema , Url class Allowlist ( Schema ): owner : Email homepage : Url | None = None source : IPv4Address subnet : IPv4Network | None = None rule = Allowlist . validate ( { "owner" : "ops@example.com" , "source" : "10.0.0.7" , "subnet" : "10.0.0.0/24" } ) assert rule . source == IPv4Address ( "10.0.0.7" ) IPv4Address , IPv6Address , IPv4Network , IPv6Network read strict ASCII text and become the object (codes ipv4 , ipv6 , ipv4network , ipv6network ). IPv4 refuses leading zeros, IPv6 refuses zone ids, networks refuse host bits ( 10.0.0.7/24 ). Field(...) is refused. A union such as IPv4Address | IPv6Address takes either. Email , Url and Slug are Annotated[str, Field(format=...)] shortcuts; Email checks syntax, not deliverability. They work as model columns. Models store addresses as text and check the class before a write. SecretStr and Path ¶ from pathlib import Path from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema , SecretStr class Account ( Schema ): password : Annotated [ SecretStr , Field ( min_length = 8 )] home : Path account = Account . validate ({ "password" : "correct horse" , "home" : "/srv/ann" }) assert account . password . get_secret_value () == "correct horse" assert account . dump () == { "password" : "**********" , "home" : "/srv/ann" } SecretStr shows ********** in repr , str , dump() and responses; only get_secret_value() returns the text, and errors never repeat it. Construction takes a SecretStr only. Path reads a non-empty string without NUL (at most 4096 characters without max_length ) and never touches the file system; code path . Both are served by the Python lane by design and have no model column type. OpenAPI: format: path ; a secret is format: password , writeOnly . See also ¶ Collections and unions Validate input OpenAPI

docs.text: Validate input ¶ A Schema validates in three stages: Rust checks types and Field(...) constraints, then @field_normalize canonicalizes values, then @field_check and @object_check reject what the rules forbid. All failures are returned together in errors.ValidationError.details , and a request answers 422. Built-in and custom validation ¶ # notes/apps/accounts/schemas.py from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Invalid , Schema , field_check , field_normalize , object_check Username = Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 3 , max_length = 32 , pattern = r "[a-z0-9_]+" )] class Registration ( Schema ): username : Username email : Annotated [ str , Field ( format = "email" , max_length = 254 )] password : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 12 , max_length = 128 )] confirmation : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 128 )] @field_normalize ( "email" ) def lowercase_email ( self , value : str ) -> str : return value . lower () @field_check ( "password" ) def reject_common_password ( self , value : str ) -> None : if value . lower () in { "password12345" , "qwerty123456" }: raise Invalid ( "common_password" , "choose a less common password" ) @object_check def passwords_match ( self ) -> None : if self . password != self . confirmation : raise Invalid ( "password_mismatch" , "passwords do not match" , path = "confirmation" ) Tool Runs Use for Field(...) first, in Rust lengths, pattern , numeric bounds, one_of , format ( email , url , slug , hex_color ) Field(strip=, lower=, upper=) before every other check trimming and case folding of str @field_normalize("f") after structural validation typed canonical form; the result is checked against the same constraints @field_check("f") after normalization rejecting one value @object_check after field checks rules across fields Checks raise Invalid(code, message, path=...) and return None ; a non- None return or an async method is a programming error. Normalizers are typed synchronous methods returning str ; they cannot reject input or rescue a value that failed structural validation. All three run for Schema.validate(...) , Schema(...) and from_model() . They never run on a Model : model writes have their own constraints and validators . No I/O and no side effects. Rules that depend on current data belong in an operation. Normalize text ¶ class Signup ( Schema ): handle : Annotated [ str , Field ( strip = True , lower = True , min_length = 3 , max_length = 32 )] Signup . validate ({ "handle" : " AbC " }) . handle # "abc" strip removes what str.strip() removes; lower and upper follow str.lower() / str.upper() . Constraints see the normalized text, and a custom normalizer receives it. Only str fields accept these options; lower and upper together, or a one_of value the normalization would change, raise RegistrationError . Results are the same on both lanes and for direct construction. The OpenAPI document describes the constraints, not the normalization. Reshape input with @before_validate ¶ from typing import Any from hinoki import before_validate class Profile ( Schema ): display_name : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 80 )] @before_validate @classmethod def accept_legacy_name ( cls , data : dict [ str , Any ]) -> dict [ str , Any ]: if "name" in data and "display_name" not in data : rest = { key : value for key , value in data . items () if key != "name" } return { ** rest , "display_name" : data [ "name" ]} return data assert Profile . validate ({ "name" : "Ada" }) . display_name == "Ada" Runs on the decoded mapping before structural validation, on this schema and every nested one, on both lanes; base-class hooks first. The data is untrusted: check types first. It is a shallow copy; replace nested values instead of mutating them. Synchronous, no I/O. Invalid(...) answers 422; KeyError , TypeError , ValueError , IndexError or AttributeError answer invalid_input , not 500. A plain union of schemas with such a hook is refused: use a discriminated union . On a plain method the decorator raises RegistrationError . Which lane runs what ¶ Types and Field(...) constraints are checked in Rust on the Python-object path and, for most schemas, on the GIL-free JSON path. The decorators are Python callables: they run only on values that passed the Rust stage. Checks of nested Schema values run through lists and dicts at any depth. Text that cannot be stored ¶ A string or dict key containing NUL ( \u0000 ) is refused with nul or key_nul on both lanes, after the length checks and before pattern : PostgreSQL cannot store NUL in text . A string that is not valid Unicode (a lone surrogate) is refused with type . See also ¶ Schemas Errors : the 422 response body Define models

docs.text: Schemas ¶ A Schema describes data that crosses the API boundary and validates it strictly. Models describe tables; a column reaches a client only when a Schema names it. # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py from datetime import datetime from typing import Annotated from uuid import UUID from hinoki import UNSET , Field , Schema , Unset class InvoiceIn ( Schema ): reference : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 40 )] class InvoicePatch ( Schema ): reference : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 40 )] | Unset = UNSET paid : bool | Unset = UNSET class InvoiceOut ( Schema ): id : UUID reference : str paid : bool created_at : datetime Validation, construction and JSON serialization run in Rust. Validate input ¶ data = InvoiceIn . validate ({ "reference" : "INV-1" }) No coercion. "1" is not 1 . Text sources are the explicit exception: Schema.validate_text() , Form[...] , Query[...] and XML[...] first convert text to the int , float and bool the fields declare. Unknown keys are refused unless the class ignores them . Every problem is reported with its path, up to 50, in errors.ValidationError.details ; a request answers 422. Constraints, normalization and custom checks are in validate input . Supported field types are in scalar field types and collections and unions . Partial updates ¶ Declare a field X | Unset = UNSET . A field the client did not send stays UNSET and is left out of dump() and to_dict() , so await invoice.aupdate_from(patch) writes only what was sent. Convert to and from rows ¶ # inside an async operation invoice = await Invoice . acreate ( data , customer_id = customer . id ) await invoice . aupdate_from ( patch ) out = InvoiceOut . from_model ( invoice ) outs = InvoiceOut . from_models ( rows ) Server keywords win over client values, and a Schema never carries the primary key. from_model(row, **extra) reads the expected attributes; relations must already be loaded. from_models(rows) converts a synchronous iterable to a list. See schemas from models . to_dict() returns Python values (UUID and datetime stay objects); dump() returns the JSON-compatible form. Both skip UNSET . Construct, change and project ¶ Schema(...) takes Python values ( UUID , aware datetime , nested Schema instances) and validates them immediately. Schema.validate(data) is the wire path: JSON-compatible input, aliases resolved, errors with wire names. from_model() validates too, but accepts the naive datetimes some drivers return. An instance is frozen. replace(**changes) returns a validated copy; an unknown name raises TypeError : card = InvoiceOut . validate ( payload ) paid = card . replace ( paid = True ) dump() projects to JSON-compatible data: out . dump ( exclude_unset = True ) out . dump ( include = { "id" , "reference" }) out . dump ( by_alias = False ) include and exclude take Python field names, top level only; exclusion wins. exclude_unset=True omits fields filled by defaults that the caller did not supply; explicit "" , None , 0 or False are kept. A custom __init__ makes it raise TypeError . With no options dump() honours custom dump() overrides; recursive options refuse a custom-dumped nested value. An override using the new options must accept the same keyword-only signature. Filtering a dump is not authorization and does not change the OpenAPI document: declare a Schema with only the fields the caller may see. dump and replace are reserved method names; a field with either name raises RegistrationError . Wire aliases ¶ # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py (continued) class CustomerOut ( Schema ): display_name : Annotated [ str , Field ( alias = "displayName" )] person = CustomerOut . validate ({ "displayName" : "Aki" }) assert person . dump () == { "displayName" : "Aki" } assert person . to_dict () == { "display_name" : "Aki" } The alias is the only accepted input key; sending both names is an error. dump() , validation errors and the OpenAPI document use wire names; a check's default path is translated, an explicit Invalid(path=...) is already a wire path. name: str = Field(alias="...") works too. Aliases are unique and cannot contain . , [ or ] . Models take no aliases. Document a field ¶ class TagOut ( Schema ): name : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 40 , description = "Tag label." , examples = ( "priority" ,)) ] legacy : Annotated [ str | None , Field ( deprecated = True )] = None description , examples and deprecated appear in the OpenAPI document next to the property and change nothing about validation. Computed fields ¶ from hinoki import computed_field class CustomerCard ( Schema ): first : str last : str @computed_field ( alias = "displayName" , description = "First and last name" ) def full_name ( self ) -> str : return f " { self . first } { self . last } " CustomerCard(first="Ada", last="Lovelace").dump() includes "displayName": "Ada Lovelace" . Computed values are output only: they follow the declared fields in dump() and responses (both lanes), are readOnly in OpenAPI, are left out of to_dict() , and a client that sends one gets an unknown-field error. The method takes only self and needs a return annotation; a name clash with a field is a RegistrationError . computed_fields() returns them; subclasses inherit them. Class configuration ¶ from hinoki import SchemaConfig , SchemaExtra class VendorEvent ( Schema , config = SchemaConfig ( extra = SchemaExtra . IGNORE )): event_id : str revision : int SchemaExtra.IGNORE discards unknown keys in decoded input and request bodies; declared fields stay strict, and ignored values are never stored or dumped. Constructor keywords and from_model(..., **extra) keep their strict signatures; each nested Schema uses its own configuration. The OpenAPI document marks the schema additionalProperties: true . Generic schemas ¶ from hinoki import http class Envelope [ T ]( Schema ): data : T count : int = 0 @http . get ( "/me" ) async def me () -> Envelope [ CustomerOut ]: return Envelope [ CustomerOut ]( data = CustomerOut ( display_name = "Ada" )) Envelope[CustomerOut] is a cached Schema subclass with its own OpenAPI component ( Envelope_CustomerOut_ ). The bare Envelope cannot validate or be a field; self-referencing generics and generic subclasses of generic schemas raise RegistrationError . See also ¶ Validate input Scalar field types Collections and unions Schemas from models Glossary : what "schema" means in these docs

docs.text: Serve an application ¶ From the project directory: hinoki dev hinoki serve hinoki dev reloads on every change while you work; hinoki serve runs without reload, with the workers your settings ask for. Both read the application from project.application in hinoki.toml . To run another application, pass its target: module:app , such as hinoki dev notes.main:app . A function callable without arguments that returns an application (a factory) is also accepted. On Kiso, when the application sets docs_url , hinoki dev prints the address of the documentation page under the listening on line, for example docs: http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs , with the address in the brand colour on a terminal that takes colour (plain text in a pipe, in CI or with NO_COLOR set); nothing is printed when docs_url is unset. hinoki serve prints it too when it runs a supervisor (more than one worker), but not with a single worker, which runs in the command's own process. Each worker imports the target, then opens what the application owns (database pool, modules) in its lifespan and closes it on shutdown. Importing your code never opens a connection. See database connection ownership . Choose a server ¶ Both commands run on Kiso , Hinoki's own Rust server, unless you choose Granian : Kiso (default) Granian What it is Hinoki's HTTP server in the native extension (Rust: hyper, tokio, rustls) A general-purpose ASGI server, installed with the server extra Runs on the native lane Eligible routes skip Python routing and binding ( details ) Every request goes through the ASGI pipeline Access log Kiso's own, with access_log_format , access_log_skip , server_timing Granian's Hinoki middleware Yes; the route runs in Python instead of the native lane Yes, identical ASGI wrapper around the app Not possible: there is no ASGI boundary Yes, run the wrapper with granian ( metrics ) WSGI --interface wsgi : Python threads behind Kiso's listener, not native ( WSGI ) --interface wsgi Choose per run with a flag, or per project in settings: hinoki serve --server granian # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): server : settings . ServerSettings = settings . ServerSettings ( server = "granian" ) hinoki new --server granian (or the server question of hinoki new ) writes the same choice to settings.toml ; NOTES_SERVER__SERVER=kiso overrides it for one environment. What Kiso runs natively, its limits, signals and proxy handling are on Kiso server . Set host, port and workers ¶ They come from the application's server settings group; flags override them: Setting Variable Default Flag server.host NOTES_SERVER__HOST 127.0.0.1 --host server.port NOTES_SERVER__PORT 8000 --port server.workers NOTES_SERVER__WORKERS 1 --workers (serve) server.runtime_threads NOTES_SERVER__RUNTIME_THREADS 1 server.backlog NOTES_SERVER__BACKLOG 1024 server.access_log NOTES_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG unset Unset logs in hinoki dev only (or whenever access_log_format is set); true or false decides for both server.access_log_skip NOTES_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG_SKIP unset Kiso only: comma-separated paths the log leaves out (health checks); exact, or a prefix when the entry ends with * server.server_timing NOTES_SERVER__SERVER_TIMING unset Kiso only: add a Server-Timing header ( kiso;dur=3.2;desc="native" : milliseconds the server took and the serving lane, with the same values as the access log's lane ); unset means hinoki dev only server.recent_requests NOTES_SERVER__RECENT_REQUESTS unset Kiso only: file that also receives each request as a JSON line, read by the recent_requests tool of hinoki mcp ; rotated near 1 MiB server.access_log_slow_ms NOTES_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG_SLOW_MS unset Kiso only: keep only answers at least this slow, in milliseconds server.access_log_format NOTES_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG_FORMAT unset Kiso only: pretty , plain , json or logger . Unset is pretty on a colour terminal and plain otherwise server.server NOTES_SERVER__SERVER kiso --server The connection limits and timeouts ( max_connections , header_read_timeout , body_read_timeout , write_timeout ), native_dispatch , the TLS files and http2 , and trusted_proxies are described under Kiso and in the settings table . Left unset, they are None in hinoki settings and Kiso applies its own defaults (for example 10000 connections and a 10-second header timeout), so that Granian can refuse the Kiso-only ones only when you set them. dev always runs one worker with reload. hinoki settings shows what is in effect ( Inspect an application ). Before serving a deployment, narrow allowed_hosts to the names it answers to ( NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS=app.example.com ). While it is the default * and debug is off, each worker logs allowed_hosts is '*' and debug is off: ... at startup, on every server. Settings that apply to one server only ¶ hinoki serve refuses a setting the chosen server cannot honour, by name, and exits with status 2; it never ignores it or falls back to the other server. Setting Kiso Granian host , port , workers , runtime_threads , backlog , access_log , trusted_proxies , request_id_header , trust_request_id , tls_cert_file , tls_key_file , http2 applied applied max_connections , header_read_timeout , body_read_timeout , write_timeout , native_dispatch , access_log_format , access_log_skip , access_log_slow_ms , recent_requests , server_timing applied when set refused when set If the native extension of a build has no Kiso, --server kiso fails with an error that says so. Optional startup probe ¶ Hinoki(startup_url="/health") reserves one public, fixed GET / HEAD endpoint and returns {"status":"ok"} after that worker's lifespan startup has completed. The setting is off by default. Its path must be a literal ASCII path; query strings, fragments, parameters, percent escapes and dot segments are rejected. It must not match an application route or an enabled OpenAPI/docs path. The endpoint is not an application route and does not appear in OpenAPI or generated CRUD/MCP tools. This is a startup probe , not a general readiness or liveness check. A 200 says that startup completed (and, on Kiso, its request wake reader was installed); it does not check database availability, downstream services, request capacity, or whether the Python event loop continues to make progress. It answers independently of the Python request queue when Kiso can apply the response directly. Before readiness it returns 503 not_ready ; during shutdown readiness is cleared before graceful draining begins. ASGI/Granian and WSGI answer it in the Python pipeline after host, CORS and HTTPS-redirect checks. Kiso checks host restrictions, answers CORS preflights and redirects plain HTTP requests on its Tokio thread before it considers the probe. GET and HEAD negotiate application/json and validate query syntax; other methods return 405 with Allow: GET, HEAD , unless CORS answers a preflight first. WSGI reads request bodies before the pipeline, so its body-size behavior differs from Kiso for a body sent to this GET / HEAD endpoint. WSGI also starts lazily on the first request and uses its adapter-level 503 if startup fails. Since WSGI exposes a decoded PATH_INFO rather than the raw request path, percent-encoded aliases may be indistinguishable from the literal probe path there. Other runners ¶ dev and serve are conveniences. The application is a plain ASGI app, so any ASGI server can run it directly; the server settings group is then ignored, because only hinoki serve applies it: granian --interface asgi notes.main:app Metrics and tracing ¶ Hinoki ships no metrics registry, exporter or tracing integration, and no health route besides the optional startup probe . On an ASGI server the application is a plain ASGI callable, so wrap it with the instrumentation you already use, or with a few lines of your own: # notes/metrics.py import time class Timing : """Report each request's method, status and duration to ``record``.""" def __init__ ( self , app , record ): self . app , self . record = app , record async def __call__ ( self , scope , receive , send ): if scope [ "type" ] != "http" : await self . app ( scope , receive , send ) return started , status = time . monotonic (), None async def watch ( message ): nonlocal status if message [ "type" ] == "http.response.start" : status = message [ "status" ] await send ( message ) try : await self . app ( scope , receive , watch ) finally : # status stays None when the request was aborted before a response began self . record ( scope [ "method" ], status , time . monotonic () - started ) from notes.main import app as notes_app app = Timing ( notes_app , record = my_metrics . observe ) # serve with any ASGI server What this measures is the time from the ASGI call to the last byte handed to the server, not what a client perceives. Keep method and status as labels; do not label by scope["path"] (it holds ids and has unbounded cardinality), the request ID (it is for correlating logs: logging.include_request_id adds it to each Hinoki log line) or the caller. Hinoki does not currently expose the matched route template to a wrapper, so per-route metrics need an application-level counter inside the handler or a gap report so a hook can be designed. Kiso has no ASGI boundary, so this wrapper does not apply to it and it has no instrumentation seam today. Use the server's own limits and access log and the request log of your proxy, or serve with Granian when you need to wrap the application. WSGI ¶ ASGI is the intended way to serve Hinoki. When a deployment can only run WSGI, wrap the application: # wsgi.py from hinoki.wsgi import WSGIAdapter from notes.main import app wsgi_app = WSGIAdapter ( app ) hinoki serve wsgi:wsgi_app --interface wsgi # Kiso hinoki serve wsgi:wsgi_app --interface wsgi --server granian # Granian --interface wsgi (or server.interface = "wsgi" on the application the WSGIAdapter wraps) tells hinoki serve that the target is a WSGI callable rather than a Hinoki application; the default is asgi . The target may be a WSGIAdapter or any (environ, start_response) callable, but not a factory and not a Hinoki application (the error names WSGIAdapter ). A project whose server.interface is wsgi refuses an ASGI target unless you pass --interface asgi . granian --interface wsgi wsgi:wsgi_app still works for a deployment that runs Granian directly. WSGI on Kiso ¶ Kiso owns the listener and calls the callable from a fixed pool of Python threads ( execution.sync_workers ) with a queue of execution.sync_queue waiting requests; beyond both the answer is 503 with Retry-After: 1 . This path is not native : the application, the environment and every response chunk are Python objects, and the request crosses the interpreter lock. Rust owns the sockets, TLS, the access log, the limits and the end of the response. Request body. Read in full before the call, up to execution.max_body_bytes : 413 above it, 408 if it stalls, 400 if malformed. Kiso therefore answers 413 for a body Granian's WSGI interface would pass on (Granian has no limit). Request path. A path whose decoded form holds a NUL byte or a . or .. segment ( %00 , %2e%2e , %2f included) answers 400 before the application is called. Request headers. Each becomes HTTP_* in the environment, and repeats are joined by a comma; repeated Cookie headers (one per cookie, as HTTP/2 clients send them) are joined by ; . A header whose name contains an underscore is dropped, because X_Foo and X-Foo would both become HTTP_X_FOO ; a client could otherwise pose as a header your proxy sets, such as Remote-User . Use dashes in custom header names. Response. Streamed: the head goes out with the first piece, a slow client slows the application down (a bounded buffer), and a client that leaves makes the next write fail and closes the iterable. An exception before the head answers 500 with an empty body and the traceback in the log; after it, the stream is reset instead of ending as complete. A header value with a line break or another control character is an error in start_response , so it answers 500 with the traceback too. A body shorter or longer than the Content-Length the application set closes the connection with an error line from Kiso. A close() of the iterable that raises after the whole body was sent is logged by the hinoki.runtime logger, and the response still ends normally. Timeout. execution.request_timeout bounds the time until the response starts ( 504 ) and, once it has started, the silence between two pieces of the body: an application that stays quiet longer has its stream reset and its iterable closed. A slow client does not count, only a slow application. A running sync call cannot be stopped; it keeps its thread until it returns. Applies: TLS and HTTP/2, access_log and access_log_format , server_timing , max_connections , header and body timeouts, --workers and graceful shutdown ( lifecycle.shutdown_timeout ). Does not apply: the native lane ( native_dispatch is refused), host, CORS and redirect policies of the server (a wrapped Hinoki application still applies its own), and trusted_proxies (refused: the client address is the TCP peer). Settings. A plain callable has no settings of its own, so server , execution and lifecycle come from the environment ( EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS , SERVER__WORKERS , ...); a bad value stops the command with status 2 . A WSGIAdapter uses its application's settings. Lifespan. A plain callable has none. A WSGIAdapter starts its application's modules when the worker starts, not on the first request, and stops them on a graceful stop. The adapter itself buffers its responses, so streaming reaches the client only from a plain callable. Its other specifics below apply on both servers. The adapter drives the same ASGI callable on a background event loop that it owns, so routing, binding, access, errors, limits and the OpenAPI document behave as under ASGI. Specifics: Startup is lazy under Granian (Kiso starts them with the worker). Modules (including the database pool) start on the first request of each worker process, so a pre-forking server can import the file in its master process. If startup fails, every request answers 503 with not_ready and the error is logged. Shutdown runs on WSGIAdapter.close() or, otherwise, at interpreter exit. A server that kills workers without exiting normally skips it, as it would any atexit hook. Async handlers run on the adapter's loop and sync handlers on the bounded executor, as under ASGI. Each WSGI server thread blocks for the duration of its request, so concurrency is the server's thread count rather than the event loop. Bodies are buffered. Request bodies are read up to max_body_bytes plus one byte, so an oversized upload still answers 413 . Responses are complete before they are sent; streaming responses are not available, and a client disconnect is not reported to the handler. Paths. The server decodes the path once and the adapter passes it on without decoding again, so a client's %2520 reaches the handler as %20 , as under ASGI. A percent-encoded slash ( %2F ) cannot be told apart from a real one in WSGI and is not available inside a path parameter. A bad Content-Length answers 400 . One protocol per process. Do not serve the same application object over ASGI and WSGI in one process; the adapter owns its own loop and module lifespan. Run two processes if you need both. The path is checked against Kiso and Granian ( --interface wsgi , with one and two workers) by a parity test, not against every WSGI server. Errors and edge cases ¶ error: X is neither an application nor a factory : the target names something else, for example an ASGI wrapper; run wrappers with granian . error: Granian is not installed; install the server extra : run uv sync in a generated project (it depends on hinoki[server] ), or use Kiso. hinoki dev reloads with watchfiles , also part of the server extra, on either server; without it dev exits with that message and serve still works. --workers outside the supported range is refused on Kiso; 0 means "use server.workers ". --interface wsgi with server.native_dispatch or server.trusted_proxies set on Kiso exits with status 2 and names the setting. --interface wsgi with a Hinoki application or a non-callable exits with an error that points to WSGIAdapter . A factory exits with status 2 : error: wsgi:create_app is a factory; for --interface wsgi name a WSGI callable, such as WSGIAdapter(app) from hinoki.wsgi . Build the application at import time instead, as in wsgi_app = WSGIAdapter(create_app()) . A Kiso-only setting under --server granian exits with status 2 and names the setting. See also ¶ Kiso server Settings Command line

docs.text: They come from the application's server settings group; flags override them: Setting Variable Default Flag server.host NOTES_SERVER__HOST 127.0.0.1 --host server.port NOTES_SERVER__PORT 8000 --port server.workers NOTES_SERVER__WORKERS 1 --workers (serve) server.runtime_threads NOTES_SERVER__RUNTIME_THREADS 1 server.backlog NOTES_SERVER__BACKLOG 1024 server.access_log NOTES_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG unset Unset logs in hinoki dev only (or whenever access_log_format is set); true or false decides for both server.access_log_skip NOTES_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG_SKIP unset Kiso only: comma-separated paths the log leaves out (health checks); exact, or a prefix when the entry ends with * server.server_timing NOTES_SERVER__SERVER_TIMING unset Kiso only: add a Server-Timing header ( kiso;dur=3.2;desc="native" : milliseconds the server took and the serving lane, with the same values as the access log's lane ); unset means hinoki dev only server.recent_requests NOTES_SERVER__RECENT_REQUESTS unset Kiso only: file that also receives each request as a JSON line, read by the recent_requests tool of hinoki mcp ; rotated near 1 MiB server.access_log_slow_ms NOTES_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG_SLOW_MS unset Kiso only: keep only answers at least this slow, in milliseconds server.access_log_format NOTES_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG_FORMAT unset Kiso only: pretty , plain , json or logger . Unset is pretty on a colour terminal and plain otherwise server.server NOTES_SERVER__SERVER kiso --server The connection limits and timeouts ( max_connections , header_read_timeout , body_read_timeout , write_timeout ), native_dispatch , the TLS files and http2 , and trusted_proxies are described under Kiso and in the settings table . Left unset, they are None in hinoki settings and Kiso applies its own defaults (for example 10000 connections and a 10-second header timeout), so that Granian can refuse the Kiso-only ones only when you set them. dev always runs one worker with reload. hinoki settings shows what is in effect ( Inspect an application ). Before serving a deployment, narrow allowed_hosts to the names it answers to ( NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS=app.example.com ). While it is the default * and debug is off, each worker logs allowed_hosts is '*' and debug is off: ... at startup, on every server.
docs.title: Set host, port and workers

docs.text: hinoki serve refuses a setting the chosen server cannot honour, by name, and exits with status 2; it never ignores it or falls back to the other server. Setting Kiso Granian host , port , workers , runtime_threads , backlog , access_log , trusted_proxies , request_id_header , trust_request_id , tls_cert_file , tls_key_file , http2 applied applied max_connections , header_read_timeout , body_read_timeout , write_timeout , native_dispatch , access_log_format , access_log_skip , access_log_slow_ms , recent_requests , server_timing applied when set refused when set If the native extension of a build has no Kiso, --server kiso fails with an error that says so.
docs.title: Settings that apply to one server only

docs.text: Hinoki(startup_url="/health") reserves one public, fixed GET / HEAD endpoint and returns {"status":"ok"} after that worker's lifespan startup has completed. The setting is off by default. Its path must be a literal ASCII path; query strings, fragments, parameters, percent escapes and dot segments are rejected. It must not match an application route or an enabled OpenAPI/docs path. The endpoint is not an application route and does not appear in OpenAPI or generated CRUD/MCP tools. This is a startup probe , not a general readiness or liveness check. A 200 says that startup completed (and, on Kiso, its request wake reader was installed); it does not check database availability, downstream services, request capacity, or whether the Python event loop continues to make progress. It answers independently of the Python request queue when Kiso can apply the response directly. Before readiness it returns 503 not_ready ; during shutdown readiness is cleared before graceful draining begins. ASGI/Granian and WSGI answer it in the Python pipeline after host, CORS and HTTPS-redirect checks. Kiso checks host restrictions, answers CORS preflights and redirects plain HTTP requests on its Tokio thread before it considers the probe. GET and HEAD negotiate application/json and validate query syntax; other methods return 405 with Allow: GET, HEAD , unless CORS answers a preflight first. WSGI reads request bodies before the pipeline, so its body-size behavior differs from Kiso for a body sent to this GET / HEAD endpoint. WSGI also starts lazily on the first request and uses its adapter-level 503 if startup fails. Since WSGI exposes a decoded PATH_INFO rather than the raw request path, percent-encoded aliases may be indistinguishable from the literal probe path there.
docs.title: Optional startup probe

docs.text: dev and serve are conveniences. The application is a plain ASGI app, so any ASGI server can run it directly; the server settings group is then ignored, because only hinoki serve applies it: granian --interface asgi notes.main:app
docs.title: Other runners

docs.text: Hinoki ships no metrics registry, exporter or tracing integration, and no health route besides the optional startup probe . On an ASGI server the application is a plain ASGI callable, so wrap it with the instrumentation you already use, or with a few lines of your own: # notes/metrics.py import time class Timing : """Report each request's method, status and duration to ``record``.""" def __init__ ( self , app , record ): self . app , self . record = app , record async def __call__ ( self , scope , receive , send ): if scope [ "type" ] != "http" : await self . app ( scope , receive , send ) return started , status = time . monotonic (), None async def watch ( message ): nonlocal status if message [ "type" ] == "http.response.start" : status = message [ "status" ] await send ( message ) try : await self . app ( scope , receive , watch ) finally : # status stays None when the request was aborted before a response began self . record ( scope [ "method" ], status , time . monotonic () - started ) from notes.main import app as notes_app app = Timing ( notes_app , record = my_metrics . observe ) # serve with any ASGI server What this measures is the time from the ASGI call to the last byte handed to the server, not what a client perceives. Keep method and status as labels; do not label by scope["path"] (it holds ids and has unbounded cardinality), the request ID (it is for correlating logs: logging.include_request_id adds it to each Hinoki log line) or the caller. Hinoki does not currently expose the matched route template to a wrapper, so per-route metrics need an application-level counter inside the handler or a gap report so a hook can be designed. Kiso has no ASGI boundary, so this wrapper does not apply to it and it has no instrumentation seam today. Use the server's own limits and access log and the request log of your proxy, or serve with Granian when you need to wrap the application.
docs.title: Metrics and tracing

docs.text: ASGI is the intended way to serve Hinoki. When a deployment can only run WSGI, wrap the application: # wsgi.py from hinoki.wsgi import WSGIAdapter from notes.main import app wsgi_app = WSGIAdapter ( app ) hinoki serve wsgi:wsgi_app --interface wsgi # Kiso hinoki serve wsgi:wsgi_app --interface wsgi --server granian # Granian --interface wsgi (or server.interface = "wsgi" on the application the WSGIAdapter wraps) tells hinoki serve that the target is a WSGI callable rather than a Hinoki application; the default is asgi . The target may be a WSGIAdapter or any (environ, start_response) callable, but not a factory and not a Hinoki application (the error names WSGIAdapter ). A project whose server.interface is wsgi refuses an ASGI target unless you pass --interface asgi . granian --interface wsgi wsgi:wsgi_app still works for a deployment that runs Granian directly.
docs.title: WSGI

docs.text: Kiso owns the listener and calls the callable from a fixed pool of Python threads ( execution.sync_workers ) with a queue of execution.sync_queue waiting requests; beyond both the answer is 503 with Retry-After: 1 . This path is not native : the application, the environment and every response chunk are Python objects, and the request crosses the interpreter lock. Rust owns the sockets, TLS, the access log, the limits and the end of the response. Request body. Read in full before the call, up to execution.max_body_bytes : 413 above it, 408 if it stalls, 400 if malformed. Kiso therefore answers 413 for a body Granian's WSGI interface would pass on (Granian has no limit). Request path. A path whose decoded form holds a NUL byte or a . or .. segment ( %00 , %2e%2e , %2f included) answers 400 before the application is called. Request headers. Each becomes HTTP_* in the environment, and repeats are joined by a comma; repeated Cookie headers (one per cookie, as HTTP/2 clients send them) are joined by ; . A header whose name contains an underscore is dropped, because X_Foo and X-Foo would both become HTTP_X_FOO ; a client could otherwise pose as a header your proxy sets, such as Remote-User . Use dashes in custom header names. Response. Streamed: the head goes out with the first piece, a slow client slows the application down (a bounded buffer), and a client that leaves makes the next write fail and closes the iterable. An exception before the head answers 500 with an empty body and the traceback in the log; after it, the stream is reset instead of ending as complete. A header value with a line break or another control character is an error in start_response , so it answers 500 with the traceback too. A body shorter or longer than the Content-Length the application set closes the connection with an error line from Kiso. A close() of the iterable that raises after the whole body was sent is logged by the hinoki.runtime logger, and the response still ends normally. Timeout. execution.request_timeout bounds the time until the response starts ( 504 ) and, once it has started, the silence between two pieces of the body: an application that stays quiet longer has its stream reset and its iterable closed. A slow client does not count, only a slow application. A running sync call cannot be stopped; it keeps its thread until it returns. Applies: TLS and HTTP/2, access_log and access_log_format , server_timing , max_connections , header and body timeouts, --workers and graceful shutdown ( lifecycle.shutdown_timeout ). Does not apply: the native lane ( native_dispatch is refused), host, CORS and redirect policies of the server (a wrapped Hinoki application still applies its own), and trusted_proxies (refused: the client address is the TCP peer). Settings. A plain callable has no settings of its own, so server , execution and lifecycle come from the environment ( EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS , SERVER__WORKERS , ...); a bad value stops the command with status 2 . A WSGIAdapter uses its application's settings. Lifespan. A plain callable has none. A WSGIAdapter starts its application's modules when the worker starts, not on the first request, and stops them on a graceful stop. The adapter itself buffers its responses, so streaming reaches the client only from a plain callable. Its other specifics below apply on both servers. The adapter drives the same ASGI callable on a background event loop that it owns, so routing, binding, access, errors, limits and the OpenAPI document behave as under ASGI. Specifics: Startup is lazy under Granian (Kiso starts them with the worker). Modules (including the database pool) start on the first request of each worker process, so a pre-forking server can import the file in its master process. If startup fails, every request answers 503 with not_ready and the error is logged. Shutdown runs on WSGIAdapter.close() or, otherwise, at interpreter exit. A server that kills workers without exiting normally skips it, as it would any atexit hook. Async handlers run on the adapter's loop and sync handlers on the bounded executor, as under ASGI. Each WSGI server thread blocks for the duration of its request, so concurrency is the server's thread count rather than the event loop. Bodies are buffered. Request bodies are read up to max_body_bytes plus one byte, so an oversized upload still answers 413 . Responses are complete before they are sent; streaming responses are not available, and a client disconnect is not reported to the handler. Paths. The server decodes the path once and the adapter passes it on without decoding again, so a client's %2520 reaches the handler as %20 , as under ASGI. A percent-encoded slash ( %2F ) cannot be told apart from a real one in WSGI and is not available inside a path parameter. A bad Content-Length answers 400 . One protocol per process. Do not serve the same application object over ASGI and WSGI in one process; the adapter owns its own loop and module lifespan. Run two processes if you need both. The path is checked against Kiso and Granian ( --interface wsgi , with one and two workers) by a parity test, not against every WSGI server.
docs.title: WSGI on Kiso

docs.text: error: X is neither an application nor a factory : the target names something else, for example an ASGI wrapper; run wrappers with granian . error: Granian is not installed; install the server extra : run uv sync in a generated project (it depends on hinoki[server] ), or use Kiso. hinoki dev reloads with watchfiles , also part of the server extra, on either server; without it dev exits with that message and serve still works. --workers outside the supported range is refused on Kiso; 0 means "use server.workers ". --interface wsgi with server.native_dispatch or server.trusted_proxies set on Kiso exits with status 2 and names the setting. --interface wsgi with a Hinoki application or a non-callable exits with an error that points to WSGIAdapter . A factory exits with status 2 : error: wsgi:create_app is a factory; for --interface wsgi name a WSGI callable, such as WSGIAdapter(app) from hinoki.wsgi . Build the application at import time instead, as in wsgi_app = WSGIAdapter(create_app()) . A Kiso-only setting under --server granian exits with status 2 and names the setting.

docs.text: Configure an application with settings ¶ Settings are typed, immutable classes. You declare the fields your application needs; Hinoki adds the groups every application has, reads values from the environment, .env and TOML once, and refuses to start when something is wrong. # notes/settings.py from typing import Literal from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings support_email : str = "support@example.com" stripe_key : settings . Secret | None = None theme : Literal [ "light" , "dark" ] = "light" notes/main.py passes the class with Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings) , which loads it while building the application. Your fields are then on app.settings , and modules read them as ctx.settings . Declare fields ¶ A field without a default is required. Use plain types ( str , int , bool , tuple[str, ...] , Literal[...] , X | None ), settings.Secret for anything confidential, and a settings.Settings subclass for a group of your own. Settings types live in the hinoki.settings namespace ( settings.AppSettings , settings.DatabaseSettings , settings.Secret , settings.Settings , settings.SettingsError ); name your loaded value app_settings so the namespace is not shadowed. settings.AppSettings brings the built-in groups: execution , lifecycle , logging , docs , server , pagination , cors , security and admin , plus timezone , debug and allowed_hosts (see Hosts, CORS and HTTPS ). docs.openapi_url , docs.docs_url and docs.redoc_url default to None ; the generated main.py sets them with Hinoki(...) arguments, which win over settings. Built-in fields and defaults ¶ Group Field Default Constraint or effect execution sync_workers 8 1 to 1024 worker threads execution sync_queue 64 0 or greater queued calls execution request_timeout 30.0 seconds Must be positive; request expiry returns 504 execution max_body_bytes 1048576 (1 MiB) 1 to 1073741824 bytes; larger request bodies return 413 execution max_query_bytes 8192 (8 KiB) 1 to 1048576 raw query-string bytes; larger queries return 414 execution max_header_bytes 32768 (32 KiB) 1 to 1048576 combined header bytes; larger headers return 431 lifecycle startup_timeout 30.0 seconds Must be positive lifecycle shutdown_timeout 10.0 seconds Must be positive logging level info debug , info , warning , error or critical logging format text text or json logging config unset module:attribute of a logging.config.dictConfig mapping (or a function returning one) for your own loggers, handlers and formatters logging include_request_id false Add the active request ID to Hinoki log records for request correlation docs title Hinoki API OpenAPI info title docs version 0.1.0 OpenAPI info version docs openapi_url None JSON document route; disabled when None docs docs_url None Swagger UI route; requires openapi_url docs redoc_url None ReDoc route; requires openapi_url server server kiso granian or kiso ; --server overrides it. See Kiso server server interface asgi asgi or wsgi : what hinoki serve calls (a Hinoki application or a WSGI callable); --interface overrides it. See WSGI pagination page_size 20 Page size an action's PageNumberPagination() leaves out; 1 to max_page_size . See Pagination pagination max_page_size 100 Largest page_size a client may ask for server host 127.0.0.1 Bind address used by hinoki dev/serve server port 8000 1 to 65535 server workers 1 1 to 256 ; dev uses one worker for reload server runtime_threads 1 Must be positive server backlog 1024 Must be positive server access_log unset One line per request on either server. Unset logs in hinoki dev only (or whenever access_log_format is set); true or false decides for dev and serve server access_log_skip unset Kiso only: paths the log leaves out, exact or a * prefix; failures are still logged server server_timing unset Kiso only: add a Server-Timing header with the time taken and the serving lane; unset means hinoki dev only, so browser developer tools show it server recent_requests unset Kiso only: file that also receives each request as a JSON line for hinoki mcp 's recent_requests tool; works with the access log off server access_log_slow_ms unset Kiso only: keep only answers at least this slow (ms); failures are still logged server access_log_format unset Kiso only (Granian refuses it): pretty , plain , json or logger (route to the hinoki.access Python logger). Unset is pretty on a colour terminal and plain otherwise server max_connections unset (10000) Kiso only: open-connection limit, 1 to 1000000 ; refused under Granian server header_read_timeout unset (10 seconds) Kiso only: time to receive request headers, and the keep-alive idle limit; refused under Granian server body_read_timeout unset (10 seconds) Kiso only: silence allowed while a body is read (at most half of execution.request_timeout ); refused under Granian server write_timeout unset (30 seconds) Kiso only: how long a response write may make no progress before the connection is closed; above 0 and at most 3600; refused under Granian server native_dispatch unset (on) Kiso only: run the async def handlers it can prove safe without an asyncio task (see the native handler lane ); false keeps every handler in an asyncio task; refused under Granian server tls_cert_file , tls_key_file unset PEM certificate chain and private key; both or neither, and both must exist. Serves HTTPS on either server; Kiso reads them once at start server http2 false Serve HTTP/2 over TLS (ALPN h2 , with http/1.1 as fallback); needs tls_cert_file and tls_key_file , otherwise refused when settings load. No cleartext HTTP/2; on either server server trusted_proxies empty IP addresses or CIDRs allowed to supply forwarded client/protocol metadata; an IPv6 zone id ( fe80::1%lo0 ) is refused when settings load, whichever server runs server request_id_header x-request-id HTTP header used for generated request IDs; other framework-owned names are refused server trust_request_id false Accept a validated inbound ID only from a peer in trusted_proxies cors origins empty Allowed browser origins ( scheme://host[:port] ), or the single entry * ; empty disables CORS cors methods GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, QUERY Methods a preflight allows cors headers authorization, content-type Request headers a preflight allows cors expose_headers empty Response headers a browser script may read cors credentials false Allow cookies and HTTP authentication; refused together with * cors max_age 600 seconds 0 to 86400 ; how long a browser may cache a preflight admin secret unset The server secret (32+ bytes, from the environment or *_FILE ) that keys the admin's CSRF tokens; an admin without its own secret= needs it admin session_hours 12 1 to 720 ; a signed-in admin session ends this long after sign-in, whatever else happens admin idle_minutes 120 1 to session_hours * 60 ; ... or this long after its last request admin min_password_length 12 8 to 128 ; the shortest password the admin's own users may have admin theme unset A built-in admin theme name ( studio , console , paper , bento ) used by an Admin without its own theme= ; an unknown name is refused when the settings load security redirect_https false Send known HTTP requests to HTTPS with 308 ; requires explicit allowed_hosts security hsts_seconds 0 0 to 63072000 ; emit HSTS only when the effective scheme is HTTPS security hsts_include_subdomains false Add includeSubDomains ; requires nonzero hsts_seconds security hsts_preload false Add preload ; requires subdomains and at least one year of HSTS security frame_options sameorigin settings.FrameOptions.DENY or .SAMEORIGIN security referrer_policy same-origin A supported settings.ReferrerPolicy enum value (top level) timezone UTC IANA timezone name used by app.now() (top level) debug false Adds exception details to 500 answers; development only (top level) allowed_hosts * Host names, .domain or * ; other Host values receive 400 settings.DatabaseSettings is an optional field you declare in your own settings class, not a settings.AppSettings group. Its url defaults to sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 ; max_size defaults to 10 connections per worker and must be at least 1 . Where values come from ¶ load is the only place configuration is read; Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings) calls it for you. Highest first: Source Example overrides= in code (tests) ProjectSettings.load(overrides={"theme": "dark"}) the process environment NOTES_THEME=dark a *_FILE variable (container secrets) NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/stripe the .env file the class names NOTES_THEME=dark in .env the TOML file the class names theme = "dark" in settings.toml the default in the class theme: ... = "light" Name a TOML file on the class with toml="settings.toml" (a project created with --server granian already does). Tables map to groups: [database] with max_size = 12 sets database.max_size . TOML cannot hold settings.Secret values or the database URL; keep those in the environment or *_FILE files. load(prefix=..., dotenv=..., toml=...) overrides what the class declared. A TOML file named on the class or passed to load must exist and parse (an empty file is fine); a missing .env is skipped. Relative .env and TOML paths resolve from the current directory, so start the server from the project root. Load the class yourself when module code needs a typed value before the application exists: # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.project import manifest_routes from notes.settings import ProjectSettings settings = ProjectSettings . load () app = Hinoki ( settings = settings , title = f "Notes ( { settings . theme } )" , include = manifest_routes () ) Variable names ¶ The variable is the prefix plus the field name in capitals; a group nests with a double underscore. Field Variable support_email NOTES_SUPPORT_EMAIL stripe_key NOTES_STRIPE_KEY database.url NOTES_DATABASE__URL execution.sync_workers NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS logging.format NOTES_LOGGING__FORMAT Values are converted strictly: integers are ASCII digits (no 1_000 , no 0x10 ), booleans are true/false/yes/no/on/off/1/0 , lists are comma separated (use tuple[str, ...] to keep them immutable), Literal[...] takes one of its choices, and an empty value for X | None means None . Mistakes fail at startup, all at once ¶ A variable that starts with your prefix and looks like one of your settings but names no field is an error (a typo guard; strict=False turns it off). It looks like a setting when its first word starts a field's variable ( NOTES_DATABASE_URL , NOTES_SERVER__PROT ) or when it is spelt close to one ( NOTES_THEMES ). Other variables that only share the prefix belong to another program and are ignored: systemd's JOURNAL_STREAM does not break a project whose prefix is JOURNAL_ . A missing required value, a bad number or a value that is not one of the choices is an error too, and every problem is listed together , with variable names and reasons but never values: invalid settings: NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS: must be an integer NOTES_DATABASE__MAX_SIZE: must be an integer NOTES_THEMES: unknown setting Keep secrets secret ¶ Declare them as settings.Secret (or settings.Secret | None ). A settings.Secret prints as *** in repr , str , logs, error messages, describe() and the settings command; you get the real text only with secret.reveal() , at the one place that needs it (where the payment client is built: app_settings.stripe_key.reveal() ). Put secrets in the environment, a secret manager that exports variables, or files : with Docker or Kubernetes secrets set NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/stripe ; the file's content (without the trailing newline) is the value. Only a regular file up to 64 KiB is read; setting both NOTES_STRIPE_KEY and NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE is an error. A .env file is for development; never commit it. Pickling or serialising a settings object stores its secrets in plain text, so don't. A validate() method you add to a group shows its message in errors, so never put a field's value in it. See what is in effect ¶ hinoki settings NOTES_DATABASE__URL environment *** NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS default 8 NOTES_STRIPE_KEY file *** NOTES_THEME .env dark The second column is where each value came from: override , environment , .env , toml , file or default . The command reads the prefix, .env and TOML file the class declares; --prefix , --dotenv and --toml override them. --format json prints the same for tools, and --example writes a ready .env.example : every variable with its default and type, required values blank to fill in, and the optional ones with no printable default (secrets such as the database URL, values that default to unset) commented out, so a copied file keeps their defaults: hinoki settings --example > .env.example Logging and your own loggers ¶ Declare loggers, handlers and formatters the way Django's LOGGING does, with a standard logging.config.dictConfig mapping, and point logging.config at it: # notes/logs.py LOGGING = { "version" : 1 , "formatters" : { "short" : { "format" : " %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s " }}, "handlers" : { "console" : { "class" : "logging.StreamHandler" , "formatter" : "short" }}, "loggers" : { "orders" : { "handlers" : [ "console" ], "level" : "INFO" }}, } NOTES_LOGGING__CONFIG = notes.logs:LOGGING The value may also name a function that returns the mapping. It is applied when each worker starts, right after Hinoki's own hinoki logger setup, with disable_existing_loggers off unless your mapping sets it. A mapping that configures the hinoki logger replaces Hinoki's handler on it. A target that cannot be imported or is not a mapping raises during startup. Kiso's access log is written by Kiso; set server.access_log_format = "logger" to route it through the hinoki.access logger. Database connection ownership ¶ A database: settings.DatabaseSettings field is all it takes: Hinoki installs DatabaseModule for it (a module declared in modules= replaces it). With nothing configured, the URL is the local SQLite file sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 , and the module creates its hidden directory and file when it starts. Configure a database covers the URL, the connection fields, TLS and each backend. The module opens a pool in each worker's startup lifespan, fails startup if the database is unreachable, and closes that worker's pool on shutdown. Nothing connects when modules or models are imported. Each worker owns its own pool, so budget replicas × workers × max_size against the server database's connection limit. One-off scripts have a different lifecycle: they open a short-lived Database themselves ( use the database from a script ). examples/blog/apps/blog/seed.py does so, applies migrations, inserts synthetic rows and closes the pool in finally . It is a one-time seed for a fresh disposable database, not a repeatable reset: cd examples export BLOG_DATABASE__URL = postgresql://app:password@localhost/blog uv run python -m blog.seed Use a disposable database for the example. The seed command is not a production migration mechanism and is not run at app startup. Errors and edge cases ¶ Setting both NOTES_STRIPE_KEY and NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE is an error; only a regular file up to 64 KiB is read. A variable with your prefix that looks like a setting (same first word, or a close spelling) but names no field is an error; other variables that only share the prefix, such as JOURNAL_STREAM , are ignored. Pass strict=False to load to turn the check off. The server group is applied by hinoki dev and hinoki serve , not by other ASGI servers ( Serving ). See also ¶ Hosts, CORS and HTTPS Own resources with modules Configure a database

See Kiso server server interface asgi asgi or wsgi : what hinoki serve calls (a Hinoki application or a WSGI callable); --interface overrides it. See WSGI pagination page_size 20 Page size an action's PageNumberPagination() leaves out; 1 to max_page_size . See Pagination pagination max_page_size 100 Largest page_size a client may ask for server host 127.0.0.1 Bind address used by hinoki dev/serve server port 8000 1 to 65535 server workers 1 1 to 256 ; dev uses one worker for reload server runtime_threads 1 Must be positive server backlog 1024 Must be positive server access_log unset One line per request on either server. Unset logs in hinoki dev only (or whenever access_log_format is set); true or false decides for dev and serve server access_log_skip unset Kiso only: paths the log leaves out, exact or a * prefix; failures are still logged server server_timing unset Kiso only: add a Server-Timing header with the time taken and the serving lane; unset means hinoki dev only, so browser developer tools show it server recent_requests unset Kiso only: file that also receives each request as a JSON line for hinoki mcp 's recent_requests tool; works with the access log off server access_log_slow_ms unset Kiso only: keep only answers at least this slow (ms); failures are still logged server access_log_format unset Kiso only (Granian refuses it): pretty , plain , json or logger (route to the hinoki.access Python logger). Unset is pretty on a colour terminal and plain otherwise server max_connections unset (10000) Kiso only: open-connection limit, 1 to 1000000 ; refused under Granian server header_read_timeout unset (10 seconds) Kiso only: time to receive request headers, and the keep-alive idle limit; refused under Granian server body_read_timeout unset (10 seconds) Kiso only: silence allowed while a body is read (at most half of execution.request_timeout ); refused under Granian server write_timeout unset (30 seconds) Kiso only: how long a response write may make no progress before the connection is closed; above 0 and at most 3600; refused under Granian server native_dispatch unset (on) Kiso only: run the async def handlers it can prove safe without an asyncio task (see the native handler lane ); false keeps every handler in an asyncio task; refused under Granian server tls_cert_file , tls_key_file unset PEM certificate chain and private key; both or neither, and both must exist. Serves HTTPS on either server; Kiso reads them once at start server http2 false Serve HTTP/2 over TLS (ALPN h2 , with http/1.1 as fallback); needs tls_cert_file and tls_key_file , otherwise refused when settings load. No cleartext HTTP/2; on either server server trusted_proxies empty IP addresses or CIDRs allowed to supply forwarded client/protocol metadata; an IPv6 zone id ( fe80::1%lo0 ) is refused when settings load, whichever server runs server request_id_header x-request-id HTTP header used for generated request IDs; other framework-owned names are refused server trust_request_id false Accept a validated inbound ID only from a peer in trusted_proxies cors origins empty Allowed browser origins ( scheme://host[:port] ), or the single entry * ; empty disables CORS cors methods GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, QUERY Methods a preflight allows cors headers authorization, content-type Request headers a preflight allows cors expose_headers empty Response headers a browser script may read cors credentials false Allow cookies and HTTP authentication; refused together with * cors max_age 600 seconds 0 to 86400 ; how long a browser may cache a preflight admin secret unset The server secret (32+ bytes, from the environment or *_FILE ) that keys the admin's CSRF tokens; an admin without its own secret= needs it admin session_hours 12 1 to 720 ; a signed-in admin session ends this long after sign-in, whatever else happens admin idle_minutes 120 1 to session_hours * 60 ; ... or this long after its last request admin min_password_length 12 8 to 128 ; the shortest password the admin's own users may have admin theme unset A built-in admin theme name ( studio , console , paper , bento ) used by an Admin without its own theme= ; an unknown name is refused when the settings load security redirect_https false Send known HTTP requests to HTTPS with 308 ; requires explicit allowed_hosts security hsts_seconds 0 0 to 63072000 ; emit HSTS only when the effective scheme is HTTPS security hsts_include_subdomains false Add includeSubDomains ; requires nonzero hsts_seconds security hsts_preload false Add preload ; requires subdomains and at least one year of HSTS security frame_options sameorigin settings.FrameOptions.DENY or .SAMEORIGIN security referrer_policy same-origin A supported settings.ReferrerPolicy enum value (top level) timezone UTC IANA timezone name used by app.now() (top level) debug false Adds exception details to 500 answers; development only (top level) allowed_hosts * Host names, .domain or * ; other Host values receive 400 settings.DatabaseSettings is an optional field you declare in your own settings class, not a settings.AppSettings group. Its url defaults to sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 ; max_size defaults to 10 connections per worker and must be at least 1 .

docs.text: load is the only place configuration is read; Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings) calls it for you. Highest first: Source Example overrides= in code (tests) ProjectSettings.load(overrides={"theme": "dark"}) the process environment NOTES_THEME=dark a *_FILE variable (container secrets) NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/stripe the .env file the class names NOTES_THEME=dark in .env the TOML file the class names theme = "dark" in settings.toml the default in the class theme: ... = "light" Name a TOML file on the class with toml="settings.toml" (a project created with --server granian already does). Tables map to groups: [database] with max_size = 12 sets database.max_size . TOML cannot hold settings.Secret values or the database URL; keep those in the environment or *_FILE files. load(prefix=..., dotenv=..., toml=...) overrides what the class declared. A TOML file named on the class or passed to load must exist and parse (an empty file is fine); a missing .env is skipped. Relative .env and TOML paths resolve from the current directory, so start the server from the project root. Load the class yourself when module code needs a typed value before the application exists: # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.project import manifest_routes from notes.settings import ProjectSettings settings = ProjectSettings . load () app = Hinoki ( settings = settings , title = f "Notes ( { settings . theme } )" , include = manifest_routes () )
docs.title: Where values come from

docs.text: The variable is the prefix plus the field name in capitals; a group nests with a double underscore. Field Variable support_email NOTES_SUPPORT_EMAIL stripe_key NOTES_STRIPE_KEY database.url NOTES_DATABASE__URL execution.sync_workers NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS logging.format NOTES_LOGGING__FORMAT Values are converted strictly: integers are ASCII digits (no 1_000 , no 0x10 ), booleans are true/false/yes/no/on/off/1/0 , lists are comma separated (use tuple[str, ...] to keep them immutable), Literal[...] takes one of its choices, and an empty value for X | None means None .
docs.title: Variable names

docs.text: A variable that starts with your prefix and looks like one of your settings but names no field is an error (a typo guard; strict=False turns it off). It looks like a setting when its first word starts a field's variable ( NOTES_DATABASE_URL , NOTES_SERVER__PROT ) or when it is spelt close to one ( NOTES_THEMES ). Other variables that only share the prefix belong to another program and are ignored: systemd's JOURNAL_STREAM does not break a project whose prefix is JOURNAL_ . A missing required value, a bad number or a value that is not one of the choices is an error too, and every problem is listed together , with variable names and reasons but never values: invalid settings: NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS: must be an integer NOTES_DATABASE__MAX_SIZE: must be an integer NOTES_THEMES: unknown setting
docs.title: Mistakes fail at startup, all at once

docs.text: Declare them as settings.Secret (or settings.Secret | None ). A settings.Secret prints as *** in repr , str , logs, error messages, describe() and the settings command; you get the real text only with secret.reveal() , at the one place that needs it (where the payment client is built: app_settings.stripe_key.reveal() ). Put secrets in the environment, a secret manager that exports variables, or files : with Docker or Kubernetes secrets set NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/stripe ; the file's content (without the trailing newline) is the value. Only a regular file up to 64 KiB is read; setting both NOTES_STRIPE_KEY and NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE is an error. A .env file is for development; never commit it. Pickling or serialising a settings object stores its secrets in plain text, so don't. A validate() method you add to a group shows its message in errors, so never put a field's value in it.
docs.title: Keep secrets secret

docs.text: hinoki settings NOTES_DATABASE__URL environment *** NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS default 8 NOTES_STRIPE_KEY file *** NOTES_THEME .env dark The second column is where each value came from: override , environment , .env , toml , file or default . The command reads the prefix, .env and TOML file the class declares; --prefix , --dotenv and --toml override them. --format json prints the same for tools, and --example writes a ready .env.example : every variable with its default and type, required values blank to fill in, and the optional ones with no printable default (secrets such as the database URL, values that default to unset) commented out, so a copied file keeps their defaults: hinoki settings --example > .env.example
docs.title: See what is in effect

docs.text: Declare loggers, handlers and formatters the way Django's LOGGING does, with a standard logging.config.dictConfig mapping, and point logging.config at it: # notes/logs.py LOGGING = { "version" : 1 , "formatters" : { "short" : { "format" : " %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s " }}, "handlers" : { "console" : { "class" : "logging.StreamHandler" , "formatter" : "short" }}, "loggers" : { "orders" : { "handlers" : [ "console" ], "level" : "INFO" }}, } NOTES_LOGGING__CONFIG = notes.logs:LOGGING The value may also name a function that returns the mapping. It is applied when each worker starts, right after Hinoki's own hinoki logger setup, with disable_existing_loggers off unless your mapping sets it. A mapping that configures the hinoki logger replaces Hinoki's handler on it. A target that cannot be imported or is not a mapping raises during startup. Kiso's access log is written by Kiso; set server.access_log_format = "logger" to route it through the hinoki.access logger.
docs.title: Logging and your own loggers

docs.text: A database: settings.DatabaseSettings field is all it takes: Hinoki installs DatabaseModule for it (a module declared in modules= replaces it). With nothing configured, the URL is the local SQLite file sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 , and the module creates its hidden directory and file when it starts. Configure a database covers the URL, the connection fields, TLS and each backend. The module opens a pool in each worker's startup lifespan, fails startup if the database is unreachable, and closes that worker's pool on shutdown. Nothing connects when modules or models are imported. Each worker owns its own pool, so budget replicas × workers × max_size against the server database's connection limit. One-off scripts have a different lifecycle: they open a short-lived Database themselves ( use the database from a script ). examples/blog/apps/blog/seed.py does so, applies migrations, inserts synthetic rows and closes the pool in finally . It is a one-time seed for a fresh disposable database, not a repeatable reset: cd examples export BLOG_DATABASE__URL = postgresql://app:password@localhost/blog uv run python -m blog.seed Use a disposable database for the example. The seed command is not a production migration mechanism and is not run at app startup.
docs.title: Database connection ownership

docs.text: Setting both NOTES_STRIPE_KEY and NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE is an error; only a regular file up to 64 KiB is read. A variable with your prefix that looks like a setting (same first word, or a close spelling) but names no field is an error; other variables that only share the prefix, such as JOURNAL_STREAM , are ignored. Pass strict=False to load to turn the check off. The server group is applied by hinoki dev and hinoki serve , not by other ASGI servers ( Serving ).
