docs.text: Explore an application in the shell ¶ hinoki shell opens Python with your application loaded and its database connected, so you can try queries against real data: uv run hinoki shell >>> await Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . acount () 3 >>> [ invoice . reference for invoice in await Invoice . all ()] ['INV-003', 'INV-002', 'INV-001'] >>> settings . database . url Secret('***') What is in the namespace ¶ Name Value app the application from hinoki.toml ( [project] application ) settings its validated settings model classes every concrete model of every registered app, by class name ( Invoice , Note , …) Two models with the same class name in different apps stop the shell before the prompt; select the modules you need with --models . A model may not be called app or settings . Await at the prompt ¶ The shell keeps one event loop for the session, so top-level await and multiline statements work. Use the async ORM methods ( acount() , aget() , awaiting a query): the synchronous ones are meant for def handlers and cannot block the shell's loop. Choose the application and models ¶ uv run hinoki shell --models notes.apps.billing.models uv run hinoki shell notes.main:app In a project the target defaults to project.application , and every registered app's models are loaded; repeat --models to load only some. Outside a project, pass a target ( module:app ); --models is then optional. What starts and what does not ¶ Each module the application installs, the database first, starts in dependency order and closes when the session ends. The application's on_startup and on_shutdown hooks do not run, so nothing sends mail or seeds data behind your back, and migrations are never applied: run hinoki migrations apply yourself. Unmanaged asyncio tasks are cancelled on exit; cleanup is bounded by the lifecycle.shutdown_timeout setting (10 seconds by default), and a task that ignores cancellation is abandoned at that deadline. Startup is bounded too: if a module suppresses cancellation while opening, the shell stops the loop and cannot guarantee that the module released what it had opened. Real data, your privileges Code at the prompt runs with your user's privileges against the configured database and can change it. Point the settings at a development database. How it looks ¶ On a colour terminal the shell opens with the Hinoki banner, a summary (the application title, the settings class and the loaded models) and a hinoki ❯ prompt. NO_COLOR , TERM=dumb , HINOKI_ANIMATE=0 and HINOKI_IMAGES=0 behave as for hinoki new ; without colour the shell prints Hinoki interactive shell; use Ctrl-D or Ctrl-C to exit. and Python's >>> / ... prompts. Errors and edge cases ¶ Without a terminal the shell exits 2: " hinoki shell requires an interactive terminal". Ctrl-D exits, Ctrl-C at the prompt exits, Ctrl-C during a cell interrupts that cell. exit() , quit() or raise SystemExit in a cell also end the session and close the app modules; the shell exits 0 whatever code is passed. A model module that does not import stops the shell with cannot load model module '…' ; a duplicate class name with model name 'Invoice' occurs in both '…' and '…' . Both exit 2. Outside a project without a target: pass TARGET outside a project with hinoki.toml . See also ¶ Models Own resources with modules Command line

docs.text: Project status ¶ Hinoki is pre-alpha. The public API and migration format may change; this repository is not published on PyPI. The hinoki project name currently belongs to an unrelated legacy package. Use this repository's source checkout for evaluation and test against disposable data. The documentation site separates current development docs from release-tagged versions. Until the first release, the site root points to the dev docs. Implemented and exercised ¶ The repository includes typed function and class endpoints, routes registered per app in routes.py , optional model-backed CRUD route generation, request binding and strict schemas, built-in and custom Schema validation, bounded typed multipart uploads, opt-in Model write constraints and validators, access policies and declared errors, optional architecture rules, settings and worker modules, SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB ORM backends with relations, querysets and file-based migrations, sync and async handlers, atomic writes ( atomic=True on actions, db.atomic as a block or decorator, sync and async), model lifecycle hooks with instance state and after-commit callbacks, bulk_create / bulk_update / bulk_delete and their abulk_* forms (one transaction each), a runtime check of every response against its return annotation (startup errors for annotations that cannot be checked), route-level rate limit policies supplied by the application, OpenAPI, parsers, renderers, development and application MCP, and an optional admin with four styles, its own users, sign-in page, per-model permissions and shared sign-in limits, and hinoki admin commands. The examples are the best way to see the pieces together: Notes for a small declared app, Tracker for layers, ownership and rules, and Blog for relations, auth and admin. Current boundaries ¶ SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB are supported ORM databases; SQLite is the local-development default. MySQL and MariaDB have separate real-server integration coverage in CI. SQL Server and Oracle are not supported. See the database guide for backend-specific TLS, migration and feature limits, including MariaDB JSON behavior. Hinoki does not open database connections at import or apply migrations automatically. Rate limits are policies a route names; the application owns their storage ( rate limit an action ). The admin's sign-in uses a per-worker window by default and DatabaseLoginWindow for a limit shared by every worker ( limit sign-in attempts ). There is no metrics exporter or tracing integration; see serving . The ASGI adapter and application handler calls run in Python, except for the Kiso native paths described below. The Rust extension provides path matching, selected query/header/cookie parsing, schema validation/serialization, cryptography and SQL ORM compilation/execution, and drives eligible generated CRUD writes and eligible async def ORM handlers. Built-in security settings add browser response headers, HSTS on effective HTTPS requests, and an opt-in 308 HTTPS redirect that requires explicit allowed hosts. Generated typing for some keyword-based ORM calls is less precise than model construction; see typing . Many-to-many links use an explicit model with two foreign keys and a composite uniqueness constraint. Implicit join models, direct collection access such as post.tags , and advanced relation paths are not available. End-to-end performance claims are not made without comparable retained measurements; see the benchmark report and its limits. The default server is Kiso, Hinoki's Rust HTTP server (Granian stays available with --server granian , and any other ASGI server can run the app). It serves serve and dev : HTTP/1.1, optional TLS and, with server.http2 over TLS, HTTP/2 (no h2c, server push or WebSocket upgrades), an access log (pretty, plain or JSON, with path exclusions and a slow floor), a startup banner naming Kiso, most request-pipeline work still runs in Python and so do handlers, except that an async def handler provably limited to ORM reads and stock writes ( atomic=True , guarded and body routes included) is driven from Rust without an asyncio task ( native handler lane ), and eligible public generated create , update and delete actions run their transaction in Rust ( generated CRUD ); no performance figure is claimed. Kiso applies host, CORS preflight and HTTPS-redirect policies natively before its optional startup_url probe; the probe reports startup completion, not general application or database health. See Kiso . The server adapter is ASGI. hinoki.wsgi.WSGIAdapter wraps an application for WSGI servers (buffered bodies, no streaming); verified with Granian only, see serving . Responses are sent complete: streaming responses, server-sent events and WebSockets are not available on any server. CORS is one application-wide policy in the cors settings group; there is no per-route CORS option. Application MCP has its own allowed-origin check. Cursor pagination is not available; pagination currently uses page numbers. Pagination page-size defaults are 20 and 100 ; the pagination settings group changes them for the whole app and an action's own PageNumberPagination values win. See pagination . OpenAPI generation creates operation IDs and reads summary/description from handler docstrings. Per-action tags , deprecated , custom operation_id and include_in_schema controls are not available. There is no maintained Docker image or deployment recipe. hinoki serve runs the app on Kiso by default, or on Granian with --server granian ; container packaging and process orchestration are application deployment choices. See the roadmap for project direction and contributing for local checks.

docs.text: Sync and async code ¶ Each worker runs one event loop. async def is the native style; a plain def handler or hook is fully supported and runs on a bounded thread pool, with the request's context and blocking ORM twins that never block the loop. Two actions added to the invoices group of function endpoints , answering with a one-field Schema : # notes/apps/billing/api.py (in the invoices group's module) class UnpaidCount ( Schema ): count : int @invoices . get ( "/unpaid/count" ) async def count_unpaid () -> UnpaidCount : # async: await the a... method return UnpaidCount ( count = await Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . acount ()) @invoices . get ( "/unpaid/count-sync" ) def count_unpaid_sync () -> UnpaidCount : # sync: the twin without the "a" return UnpaidCount ( count = Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . count ()) A name with the a prefix awaits the database ( aget , acreate , acount ); the same name without it is the blocking twin. A queryset is lazy until evaluated: await queryset is the async form of queryset.list() . Choose a style ¶ Prefer async def . Use def for code that is naturally blocking: a library without async support, or CPU work measured to be short. Never call blocking code from an async def . From a def , use the sync twin instead of calling an a... coroutine. CPU-heavy work belongs in a separate process, not in either pool. A sync ORM call made on the event loop raises, naming the a... method to use. What runs where ¶ Surface Async Sync Notes Action handlers async def def Sync runs on the executor CRUD hooks ( get_queryset , written_queryset , to_schema , store , change , remove ) async def def Same executor as handlers Auth providers ( authenticate , resolve , resolve_token , JWT resolve_claims ) async def def Sync hooks run on the executor Model writes and lookups acreate , aget , aget_or_none , aupdate , aupdate_where , adelete , asave , aupdate_from , abulk_create , abulk_update , abulk_delete The same names without a Sync calls work only inside a sync handler or hook served by Hinoki; both take returning=False ( queries ) QuerySet reads await qs , afirst , aget , acount , aexists , apaginate list , first , get , count , exists , paginate QuerySet writes aupdate , adelete update , delete Relations select_related , prefetch_related same Never lazy in either style Raw SQL ( Database.fetch , fetch_one , execute ) async none Async-only escape hatch Transactions atomic=True same The runtime owns it Atomic blocks async with db.atomic(): , @db.atomic on async def with db.atomic(): , @db.atomic on def Sync forms raise RuntimeError on the loop ( transactions ) Schema , Request , Response , parsers, renderers plain code same No I/O Password hashing await hasher.hash/verify hash_sync , verify_sync Async calls use their own bounded pool Error handlers ( app.error_handler ) async def def Run on the loop: no blocking calls Module lifespans async context manager none Resources belong to the worker's loop Startup and shutdown hooks async def hook(ctx) def hook(ctx) Hinoki(on_startup=..., on_shutdown=...) ; sync runs on the executor Admin hooks ( stats , check , save , remove ) async def none The admin runs on the loop Tests ASGIClient SyncClient Same behaviour Size the pool ¶ execution.sync_workers (default 8 ) threads serve sync handlers and hooks; execution.sync_queue (default 64 ) requests may wait for one. A full queue answers 503 overloaded with Retry-After . See settings . Errors and edge cases ¶ Sync hooks share the pool with sync handlers. A flood of bad credentials or slow hooks can fill the queue and turn legitimate sync work into 503 . Keep sync hooks short, reject malformed credentials before touching the database, and prefer async hooks. A sync auth hook runs before the action's transaction opens , so it is never part of it. Sync model calls work only inside the app's sync handlers and hooks. In a test body, use the async API (an async fixture) or your own connection, also with SyncClient . Async only: module lifespans, admin hooks, background tasks ( ctx.tasks.start_soon takes coroutines) and raw Database SQL. A sync error handler runs on the loop and must not call the ORM; its failure is treated as unhandled. SyncClient works only inside its with block and raises a timeout error after timeout seconds (default 60). The test suite exercises sync and async handlers, sync authentication hooks, ORM calls through both clients, mixed traffic and cancellation against a disposable database. docs.text: Test an application ¶ A project created with hinoki new already has a test that runs a request through the whole stack, without a network socket: # tests/healthtest.py from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.main import app async def test_health_answers_through_the_whole_stack () -> None : async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : reply = await client . get ( "/health" ) assert ( reply . status , reply . body ) == ( 200 , { "status" : "ok" }) Run it with uv run pytest . The generated pyproject.toml sets asyncio_mode = "auto" and collects files named *test.py . ASGIClient runs the application's startup (modules, database pool, startup hooks and rules ) when the block opens and its shutdown when it closes. A reply has status , headers , body (decoded JSON, or text) and raw bytes. Test protected actions ¶ token= sends Authorization: Bearer <token> , so a test exercises the real provider and policy: # tests/billingtest.py from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.main import app async def test_invoices_need_a_staff_token () -> None : async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : anonymous = await client . get ( "/billing/invoices" ) unknown = await client . get ( "/billing/invoices" , token = "not-a-token" ) assert anonymous . status == 401 assert unknown . status == 401 Use a disposable database ¶ The application reads its settings when its module is imported, so point the prefix variable at a throwaway database first. A conftest.py at the project root is imported before any test module: # conftest.py import os os . environ [ "NOTES_DATABASE__URL" ] = "sqlite://./.hinoki/test.sqlite3" This applies when the settings declare database: settings.DatabaseSettings . Create the tables once, with the same variable: NOTES_DATABASE__URL = sqlite://./.hinoki/test.sqlite3 uv run hinoki migrations apply When settings.toml sets engine and its connection fields, a URL conflicts with them ( set either url or engine with its fields, not both ). Override the fields instead, and clear the server-only ones SQLite refuses: # conftest.py import os os . environ . update ( NOTES_DATABASE__ENGINE = "sqlite" , NOTES_DATABASE__NAME = ".hinoki/test.sqlite3" , NOTES_DATABASE__HOST = "" , NOTES_DATABASE__USER = "" , ) Apply the migrations with the same variables, and pass the same keys under "database" to overrides= in the example below. When one test needs other settings, build a second application from the same routes instead of changing the shared one. This example only calls /health , so its new database needs no tables; to give a test migrated tables, copy them as below : # tests/exportstest.py from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.project import manifest_routes from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.settings import ProjectSettings async def test_health_with_its_own_database () -> None : settings = ProjectSettings . load ( overrides = { "database" : { "url" : "sqlite://./.hinoki/other.sqlite3" }} ) app = Hinoki ( settings = settings , include = manifest_routes ()) async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : assert ( await client . get ( "/health" )) . status == 200 Use synthetic rows and credentials, and never point test settings at production data. Give each test its own database ¶ The tests above share one file, so rows one test writes are still there in the next. To start every test from empty, migrated tables, copy the file you migrated above into the test's temporary directory and build the application on the copy: # tests/conftest.py import shutil from collections.abc import AsyncIterator from pathlib import Path import pytest from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.project import manifest_routes from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.settings import ProjectSettings TEMPLATE = Path ( ".hinoki/test.sqlite3" ) # migrated once with the command above @pytest . fixture async def client ( tmp_path : Path ) -> AsyncIterator [ ASGIClient ]: copy = tmp_path / "test.sqlite3" shutil . copyfile ( TEMPLATE , copy ) settings = ProjectSettings . load ( overrides = { "database" : { "url" : f "sqlite:// { copy } " }}) app = Hinoki ( settings = settings , include = manifest_routes ()) async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : yield client A test takes client as an argument; whatever it writes is gone in the next test, and the template file is never modified. Run migrations apply on the template again after you add a migration. The copy works for SQLite files only. Catch undeclared errors ¶ ASGIClient(app, strict_errors=True) fails the test when an action answers an HTTP error that is missing from its errors= declaration, so the OpenAPI document cannot drift from what the action really does. ASGIClient and SyncClient (for synchronous tests, below ) both have get , post , put , patch , delete , head , options and query (the HTTP QUERY method; its body goes in json= or body= , while the query= option of every call is the query string), plus request(method, path, ...) for any other method. Test file uploads ¶ ASGIClient and SyncClient accept data= and files= and build the multipart boundary and Content-Type header for you. Use a sequence of file tuples to send repeated field names in order: # tests/uploadtest.py async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : response = await client . post ( "/documents" , data = { "title" : "Report" }, files = [( "document" , "report.txt" , b "contents" , "text/plain" )], ) assert response . status == 201 Each file tuple is (field_name, filename, content_bytes, content_type) . Form data may be a mapping or an ordered sequence of (name, text) pairs; sequences retain repeated names. Do not pass json= or raw body= together with data= / files= ; the helper owns the multipart content type and boundary. The application enforces its configured complete-body and per-part limits. This helper sends complete in-memory bodies and does not model streaming uploads. Headers and hosts ¶ headers= accepts a mapping or a sequence of (name, value) pairs. Use pairs to send a repeated header; Hinoki's request header mapping joins repeated values with ", " . A client can add a default Host header to each request: # tests/headerstest.py async with ASGIClient ( app , host = "api.example.com" ) as client : response = await client . get ( "/health" , headers = [( "X-Trace" , "first" ), ( "X-Trace" , "second" )] ) The default remains no Host header. Set headers={"host": "other.example.com"} on a call to override the client's host. Because the clients run in-process, they do not log the startup warning about the default allowed_hosts = * that a served worker logs ( Hosts, CORS and HTTPS ). Synchronous tests and time ¶ SyncClient is available for synchronous test functions. It runs the app's lifespan and refuses unsafe nested use from a running event loop. For deterministic time, ManualClock is a thread-safe callable clock. It accepts and returns timezone-aware instants normalized to UTC; advance(seconds=...) and set(datetime) control its value. A naive datetime raises ValueError . Pass it to app.now(clock) or other code that accepts a Clock . Test the layers separately ¶ Keep business operations independent of Request and HTTP response types when practical. Test ownership and state transitions against a disposable database, then test route binding, access, status codes and error declarations through ASGIClient . Repository checks ¶ From the checkout, the documented gates are: uv run --locked ruff check . uv run --locked ruff format --check . uv run --locked mypy uv run --locked complexipy . --failed uv run --locked pytest --cov cargo fmt --all --check cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings cargo test --workspace uv run --locked --group docs mkdocs build --strict PostgreSQL-dependent Python and Rust tests require HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL ; without it those tests are skipped. Migration conformance tests for MySQL and MariaDB also require HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL and HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL , respectively. CI provides disposable real-server services. See toolchain and CI for the Rust complexity check, the pre-commit hooks and the packaging checks. See also ¶ Create a project : what the generated tests and settings contain. docs.text: Toolchain and CI ¶ All Python commands run through uv with the lock enforced; Rust through Cargo . CI runs the same commands. Setup ¶ uv sync --locked # creates .venv, builds the Rust extension (maturin), installs dev groups uv run --locked pre-commit install Requires: uv ≥ 0.9, a stable Rust toolchain (rustup) with rustfmt and clippy . The PyO3 extension build backend requires maturin ≥ 1.9.4; uv selects it from the isolated build-system requirement. Gates ¶ Gate Command Lock is current uv lock --check Lint (+ autofix) uv run --locked ruff check --fix . Format uv run --locked ruff format . Types + typing fixtures uv run --locked mypy Python cognitive complexity uv run --locked complexipy . --failed Rust cognitive complexity Install rust-code-analysis-cli 0.0.25, then run rust-code-analysis-cli -m -p crates -O json --pr -o /tmp/hinoki-rust-complexity && python scripts/check_rust_complexity.py /tmp/hinoki-rust-complexity Python tests + coverage uv run --locked pytest --cov Only the real-server tests uv run --locked pytest -m runtime Rust format / lints / tests cargo fmt --all --check · cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings · cargo test --workspace (see PyO3 setup below) All hooks uv run --locked pre-commit run --all-files Database tests ¶ The binding tests embed Python. Select the interpreter explicitly and add its shared-library directory when running the workspace suite locally: PYTHON = " $( uv run --locked python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)' ) " PYTHON_LIBDIR = " $( " $PYTHON " -c 'import sysconfig; print(sysconfig.get_config_var("LIBDIR"))' ) " PYO3_PYTHON = " $PYTHON " \ LD_LIBRARY_PATH = " $PYTHON_LIBDIR ${ LD_LIBRARY_PATH :+: $LD_LIBRARY_PATH } " \ cargo test --workspace CI sets these variables for the Rust job using its uv-managed Python 3.13. PostgreSQL-dependent tests in tests/dbtest.py , tests/transactiontest.py and crates/orm/tests/postgres.rs need a disposable server and run only when HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL is set; otherwise pytest reports them as skipped and Cargo prints SKIPPED . Migration conformance tests for MySQL and MariaDB use HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL and HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL ; test each supported backend separately and read the skip summary. A run without the PostgreSQL URL does not verify PostgreSQL behavior. Locally: docker run -d --name hinoki-test-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD = hinoki -e POSTGRES_DB = hinoki \ -p 127 .0.0.1:54399:5432 --tmpfs /var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17-alpine export HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL = postgres://postgres:hinoki@127.0.0.1:54399/hinoki uv run --locked pytest PYTHON = " $( uv run --locked python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)' ) " PYTHON_LIBDIR = " $( " $PYTHON " -c 'import sysconfig; print(sysconfig.get_config_var("LIBDIR"))' ) " PYO3_PYTHON = " $PYTHON " \ LD_LIBRARY_PATH = " $PYTHON_LIBDIR ${ LD_LIBRARY_PATH :+: $LD_LIBRARY_PATH } " \ cargo test --workspace docker rm -f hinoki-test-pg CI provides the same database as a service container. Never point the variable at a database with real data: tests create and drop tables. The Python and Rust suites include ORM/model tests. PostgreSQL-dependent tests run only with a disposable HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL ; migration conformance tests for MySQL and MariaDB also use HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL and HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL . CI provides disposable real-server services. The native CRUD differential test build enables the private sql-trace Cargo feature so it can compare SQL text, parameters and order for both request lanes; ordinary wheels are built without that feature. Build it into the environment with uv run --no-sync --with "maturin>=1.9.4,<2" maturin develop --manifest-path crates/bindings/Cargo.toml --features sql-trace . Without it those tests skip; set HINOKI_REQUIRE_SQL_TRACE=1 (CI does) to make a missing trace build fail them instead. The CI Rust job also runs cargo clippy -p hinoki-bindings --all-targets --features sql-trace -- -D warnings . Generated OpenAPI is validated with openapi-spec-validator inside the Python tests. The retained benchmark report has reproducible end-to-end measurements, but benchmark runs are separate from the default CI test gate. Decisions ¶ Python ≥ 3.12 , dev interpreter 3.13 ( .python-version ), CI 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14, abi3 wheels (smoke-tested in a clean 3.12 environment by the wheel CI job). Ruff is the only linter/formatter ( ruff check with --fix , then ruff format ), version pinned in pyproject.toml ( lint group) and in .pre-commit-config.yaml ; keep them equal when bumping. mypy --strict is the separate type check. No overlapping tools (no black, isort, flake8, pylint). maturin is the build backend ( python-source = "python" , extension hinoki.core ); uv rebuilds when Rust sources change ( tool.uv.cache-keys ). Cognitive complexity is capped at 15 for every Python function and Rust function/closure. CI runs pinned complexipy and rust-code-analysis-cli ; test and development code are included. Refactor over-budget functions instead of suppressing analyzer findings. Dependency groups: lint , typecheck , test , aggregated by dev . Granian is both the optional runtime server extra and a test dependency for server integration coverage. docs.text: The binding tests embed Python. Select the interpreter explicitly and add its shared-library directory when running the workspace suite locally: PYTHON = " $( uv run --locked python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)' ) " PYTHON_LIBDIR = " $( " $PYTHON " -c 'import sysconfig; print(sysconfig.get_config_var("LIBDIR"))' ) " PYO3_PYTHON = " $PYTHON " \ LD_LIBRARY_PATH = " $PYTHON_LIBDIR ${ LD_LIBRARY_PATH :+: $LD_LIBRARY_PATH } " \ cargo test --workspace CI sets these variables for the Rust job using its uv-managed Python 3.13. PostgreSQL-dependent tests in tests/dbtest.py , tests/transactiontest.py and crates/orm/tests/postgres.rs need a disposable server and run only when HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL is set; otherwise pytest reports them as skipped and Cargo prints SKIPPED . Migration conformance tests for MySQL and MariaDB use HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL and HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL ; test each supported backend separately and read the skip summary. A run without the PostgreSQL URL does not verify PostgreSQL behavior. Locally: docker run -d --name hinoki-test-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD = hinoki -e POSTGRES_DB = hinoki \ -p 127 .0.0.1:54399:5432 --tmpfs /var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17-alpine export HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL = postgres://postgres:hinoki@127.0.0.1:54399/hinoki uv run --locked pytest PYTHON = " $( uv run --locked python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)' ) " PYTHON_LIBDIR = " $( " $PYTHON " -c 'import sysconfig; print(sysconfig.get_config_var("LIBDIR"))' ) " PYO3_PYTHON = " $PYTHON " \ LD_LIBRARY_PATH = " $PYTHON_LIBDIR ${ LD_LIBRARY_PATH :+: $LD_LIBRARY_PATH } " \ cargo test --workspace docker rm -f hinoki-test-pg CI provides the same database as a service container. Never point the variable at a database with real data: tests create and drop tables. The Python and Rust suites include ORM/model tests. PostgreSQL-dependent tests run only with a disposable HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL ; migration conformance tests for MySQL and MariaDB also use HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL and HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL . CI provides disposable real-server services. The native CRUD differential test build enables the private sql-trace Cargo feature so it can compare SQL text, parameters and order for both request lanes; ordinary wheels are built without that feature. Build it into the environment with uv run --no-sync --with "maturin>=1.9.4,<2" maturin develop --manifest-path crates/bindings/Cargo.toml --features sql-trace . Without it those tests skip; set HINOKI_REQUIRE_SQL_TRACE=1 (CI does) to make a missing trace build fail them instead. The CI Rust job also runs cargo clippy -p hinoki-bindings --all-targets --features sql-trace -- -D warnings . Generated OpenAPI is validated with openapi-spec-validator inside the Python tests. The retained benchmark report has reproducible end-to-end measurements, but benchmark runs are separate from the default CI test gate.

docs.text: Run writes in transactions ¶ An action opts into a database transaction with atomic=True . The transaction opens for the request and commits only after the handler returns and the response body is encoded and rendered. Set it once on a RouteGroup and every write method of the group is atomic: # notes/apps/billing/api.py from uuid import UUID from hinoki import RouteGroup from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import AuditEvent , Invoice # AuditEvent: any model of yours from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut invoices = RouteGroup ( "/invoices" , access = billing_staff , atomic = True ) @invoices . post ( "/" , status = 201 ) # atomic: a write method in an atomic group async def create_invoice ( data : InvoiceIn ) -> InvoiceOut : invoice = await Invoice . acreate ( data ) await AuditEvent . acreate ( subject = invoice . reference , action = "created" ) return InvoiceOut . from_model ( invoice ) @invoices . post ( "/ {invoice_id} /remind" , status = 204 , atomic = False ) # writes nothing async def remind ( invoice_id : UUID ) -> None : ... On a single action, write @http.post("/invoices", atomic=True) . Hinoki checks the returned value against the response annotation before encoding it (see the response check ). What rolls back ¶ If the handler raises, response encoding/rendering fails, the request times out, or the task is cancelled, the transaction rolls back before the error response is translated. A value that does not match the response annotation is rejected as a 500 , and the transaction rolled back, unless the action opts out with validate_response=False . Do not send email or perform another irreversible side effect inside the transaction; arrange it after the transaction commits, or use an outbox owned by the application. RouteGroup(..., atomic=True) makes POST , PUT , PATCH and DELETE atomic by default; GET actions are not. An action opts out with atomic=False . A project created with hinoki new enforces Transactions.require_atomic() ( HNK-TXN-001 ), so a write that opts out stops hinoki check and startup until you record the decision. List the action in except_ in notes/rules.py : # notes/rules.py project_rules = RuleSet ( # ... the other rules Transactions . require_atomic ( except_ = [ "notes.apps.billing.api.remind" ]), ) A temporary exception goes in hinoki-rules.toml instead ( waivers ). Atomic blocks and functions in application code ¶ db.atomic ( from hinoki import db ) opens the same kind of scope in your own code, on the database that is current for the task: the one a request makes active, or the one set with hinoki.orm.use_database(...) . Use it as a block: # notes/apps/billing/operations.py from hinoki import db from .models import AuditEvent , Invoice async def mark_paid ( invoice : Invoice ) -> None : async with db . atomic (): invoice . paid = True await invoice . asave () await AuditEvent . acreate ( subject = invoice . reference , action = "paid" ) or as a decorator on an async def , with or without parentheses: # notes/apps/billing/operations.py @db . atomic async def settle_all () -> int : return await Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . aupdate ({ "paid" : True }, returning = False ) @db . atomic () async def reopen ( invoice_id : UUID ) -> None : await Invoice . aupdate ( id = invoice_id , paid = False ) Each call of a decorated function opens its own scope: returning commits, an exception rolls back and propagates. The wrapper keeps the function's name, docstring, signature and annotations ( functools.wraps ). In a sync handler, hook or helper, use the same API without await : with db.atomic(): as a block, or @db.atomic on a plain def . The sync model methods ( create , update , bulk_create , ...) inside it run in the same transaction: # notes/apps/billing/operations.py @db . atomic def settle_all_sync () -> int : return Invoice . update_where ({ "paid" : False }, { "paid" : True }) def mark_paid_sync ( invoice : Invoice ) -> None : with db . atomic (): invoice . paid = True invoice . save () The sync forms only work on a worker thread served by Hinoki, as the sync model methods do; on the event loop they raise RuntimeError (use async with there). A nested sync scope is a savepoint, like the async one. Raw Database.execute and fetch remain async-only (see sync and async ). db.atomic() is current_database().atomic() resolved when the block is entered or the function is called. When you hold a Database yourself (a script, a module lifespan, ctx.get(Database) ), call database.atomic() directly; it behaves the same. Database.migration() is the separate, exclusive scope used for migrations. Nesting and savepoints ¶ A scope opened while another scope of the same task is already open becomes a savepoint, whether it comes from atomic=True , async with , or a decorated function. An exception inside the inner scope rolls back only that savepoint; the outer transaction continues and commits when it ends. A decorated function called from an atomic=True action therefore joins the request's transaction as a savepoint rather than committing on its own. # notes/apps/billing/operations.py async def create_with_discount ( data : InvoiceIn , coupon_id : UUID ) -> Invoice : async with db . atomic (): invoice = await Invoice . acreate ( data ) try : async with db . atomic (): # SAVEPOINT await Coupon . aupdate ( id = coupon_id , used = True ) raise CouponExpired () except CouponExpired : pass # only the coupon update is undone return invoice # the invoice committed when the outer block ended A child task cannot share its parent's active transaction: opening a nested scope from another task raises DatabaseError . Decorated functions and routes ¶ A function decorated with @db.atomic can also be a route handler (put the HTTP decorator outermost). Binding, OpenAPI and the native server see the original signature, and the handler runs inside its own atomic scope. That scope covers the handler call only: it commits when the handler returns, before the response is encoded. atomic=True on the action is the declaration that also covers response encoding, and it is what HNK-TXN-001 ( Transactions.require_atomic ) reads: the rule does not inspect decorators, so an action that is only decorated with @db.atomic is still reported. Prefer atomic=True on actions and keep db.atomic for application code that the action calls. On the native server lane, a handler is still Python code: Rust calls the Python function, so a @db.atomic function behaves exactly as on the Python pipeline, including the rollback when it raises. After-commit callbacks ¶ Database.after_commit(callback) (for example current_database().after_commit(...) ) registers a sync or async callable without arguments to run after the outermost transaction commits, which is where email, queue publishing and cache invalidation belong. Callbacks run in registration order; a rollback of the transaction, or of the savepoint scope that registered them, drops them, and an exception in one is logged without undoing the commit. Calling it outside a transaction raises DatabaseError . Model hooks register through self.after_commit(callback) ; see lifecycle hooks . # notes/apps/billing/operations.py from hinoki.orm import current_database async def issue ( data : InvoiceIn ) -> Invoice : async with db . atomic (): invoice = await Invoice . acreate ( data ) current_database () . after_commit ( lambda : publish ( "invoice.issued" , invoice . id )) return invoice Errors and edge cases ¶ after_commit outside a transaction, or a nested scope opened from a child task, raises DatabaseError . The sync forms raise RuntimeError on the event loop. An action that is only decorated with @db.atomic is still reported by HNK-TXN-001 ; declare atomic=True . See also ¶ Rules : Transactions.require_atomic makes atomic writes a checked promise. Lifecycle hooks : self.after_commit in model hooks. Sync and async

docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Each section starts with the message or symptom you see. error: cannot load notes.main:app ¶ Run the command from the project directory (the one with hinoki.toml ) and check the module path and the attribute after the colon. Hinoki adds the current directory to the import path, but the module must still import cleanly: the text after the colon is the original exception. Settings report a missing or unknown variable ¶ Check the settings class's prefix= and the nested names: groups are joined with __ , as in NOTES_DATABASE__URL . Print every expected name with: hinoki settings --example settings.Secret values are shown redacted on purpose. The database connection fails at startup ¶ Each worker opens its pool during startup. Check the backend URL, network reachability and the server from the same environment as the worker, and the backend notes in configure a database . While debugging, use one worker and a small pool: total connections are replicas × workers × pool size. server.<name> is not supported by the granian server ¶ hinoki serve refuses a setting the chosen server cannot honour, and exits with status 2. Unset it or run on Kiso, the default. See settings that apply to one server only . cannot listen on HOST:PORT ¶ The address is in use, or the host or port is invalid. Stop the other process or pass another --port ; the command exits with status 2. Every request answers 400 disallowed_host or 503 not_ready ¶ 400 disallowed_host : the Host header is not in allowed_hosts . 503 not_ready : the worker has not finished starting, or has begun shutting down ( startup probe ). RelationNotLoaded ¶ Relations are never loaded lazily. Name the relation in the query that needs it: select_related("author") for a single row, prefetch_related("posts") for a collection. See relations . hinoki check reports unverifiable ¶ The rule could not establish its promise. Read the explanation and any fix: line. Some rules inspect only declarations; checks with side effects run only with hinoki check --allow-effects . Sync handlers answer 503 overloaded ¶ Sync handlers and sync hooks share a bounded pool and queue. Move database and network calls to async handlers, keep sync hooks short, or size the pool; see sync and async code . A migration is marked destructive ¶ Read the generated SQL and the data it removes, and test it against a disposable copy before passing --allow-destructive . See migrations . Report a problem ¶ Collect the environment without reading settings or opening a database: hinoki version --verbose --format json hinoki doctor hinoki doctor imports the project application but does not start it, run rules, connect to a database or write files. Include the Hinoki version, the command or route, the complete diagnostic and a minimal example; remove credentials and personal data first.

docs.text: Type checking Hinoki applications ¶ Hinoki's public APIs use Python annotations so a type checker can catch mistakes in handlers, decorators and schema construction. The repository is checked with mypy in strict mode; other checkers and IDEs have not been evaluated systematically. Run the project's check from its checkout: uv run --locked mypy In a project created by hinoki new , mypy is part of the dev dependency group: uv run mypy notes Typed surfaces ¶ Contract Result HTTP decorators Preserve a handler's parameter and return types. Invalid decorator options such as atomic="yes" are type errors. Schema classes Generated constructors check required, unknown and mistyped fields; Field(default_factory=...) preserves the value type. Application and route groups Hinoki.include , API classes and RouteGroup provide typed declarations. Unknown include items fail at app construction. Authentication context Annotate a parameter as Caller[User] to receive the typed caller and application user. Decorator composition User decorators should preserve signatures with functools.wraps , ParamSpec and TypeVar . For standalone handlers the final decorated function is dispatched. With RouteGroup , put the HTTP decorator outermost so it captures the final handler. ORM method signatures ¶ Model construction and common instance operations are typed. Some ORM methods that accept arbitrary model field names still have broad keyword signatures, so a checker may not catch a misspelled field passed to these methods: task = Task ( title = "Write docs" ) # constructor fields and values are checked await task . asave () Fields inherited from an abstract model are part of the checked constructor. Fields that come from a plain (non-model) mixin exist at run time but are not constructor arguments for a type checker; use an abstract model when you need them checked. Model.acreate(**values) and some filter/update keyword calls cannot currently verify each field name against the model class. Use the constructor plus asave() when you want field-level checking on insertion. This limitation does not affect runtime validation of model fields or database constraints. The return types of the write methods are checked: aupdate returns the model, aupdate_where and QuerySet.aupdate a list of it, and with a literal returning=False each returns int ( writes that do not read the row back ). A returning value that is a plain bool gives the union of both. acreate and insert return the model either way. Unpacking a dictionary into aupdate(**values) or update(**values) gives Any , because the dictionary could hold returning ; pass returning=True explicitly to keep the model type. The Python package includes typing metadata, and the compiled hinoki.core module has a matching stub. See the API reference for the public signatures.
docs.title: Typing

docs.text: Time and utilities ¶ Hinoki ships a few helpers where the framework defines the behaviour. Use the standard library for everything else. UTC time ¶ utc_now() returns a timezone-aware datetime in UTC; use it for field factories and application code. # notes/apps/billing/models.py from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field , pk from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Event ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) A clock is any callable returning an aware datetime ( hinoki.utils.Clock ). Code that depends on time accepts a clock; tests pass a fixed one. No process-wide patching is needed. utc_today(clock=utc_now) returns the date in UTC, independent of the machine's timezone: 2026-01-02 00:30+02:00 is 2026-01-01 . Test clocks ¶ # tests/clocktest.py from datetime import UTC , datetime from hinoki.testing import ManualClock def test_clock_moves () -> None : clock = ManualClock ( datetime ( 2026 , 1 , 1 , tzinfo = UTC )) first = clock () clock . advance ( seconds = 60 ) assert ( clock () - first ) . total_seconds () == 60 ManualClock stores UTC instants, accepts only aware values and works with app.now(clock) , utc_today(clock) and @db.timestamps(clock=...) . Application timezone ¶ # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): timezone : str = "Europe/Rome" app.now() returns an aware datetime in the settings' IANA timezone (default UTC ); an invalid name fails while settings load. Apps in one process can use different timezones; there is no Hinoki(timezone=...) . app.now(clock) takes a clock for tests. Model update timestamps ¶ # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) @db . timestamps () class Statement ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) title : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) @db.timestamps() sets the non-nullable updated_at: datetime column on every ORM update: Model.aupdate , aupdate_where , asave , aupdate_from , abulk_update , QuerySet.aupdate and their sync forms. One statement gives every row the same time; a value supplied for the column is replaced. @db.timestamps("modified_at", clock=my_clock) names another column or injects a clock; clock values must be aware and are stored in UTC. Creation uses the field factories. Raw SQL bypasses the decorator: use a database trigger if independent writers need database-authoritative times. Both columns are ordinary fields, visible to type checkers and migrations. Other common needs ¶ Need Use UUID identifiers uuid.uuid4() secret tokens secrets , or hinoki.crypto.random_token() for Hinoki authentication file system paths pathlib.Path configuration settings requests in tests hinoki.testing clients ( testing ) Hinoki has no slug, retry or environment helpers: their rules belong to the application. See also ¶ Model options Testing

docs.text: Restrict hosts, origins and HTTPS ¶ A new application answers any Host , sends no CORS headers, never redirects to HTTPS and trusts no proxy. That keeps development friction-free; before a deployment, name what it serves: # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): allowed_hosts : tuple [ str , ... ] = ( "api.example.com" ,) cors : settings . CorsSettings = settings . CorsSettings ( origins = ( "https://app.example.com" ,), ) security : settings . SecuritySettings = settings . SecuritySettings ( redirect_https = True , hsts_seconds = 31_536_000 , ) server : settings . ServerSettings = settings . ServerSettings ( trusted_proxies = ( "10.20.0.0/16" ,), ) Every field can also come from the environment, which is usually where a deployment sets them: NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS = api.example.com,.example.org NOTES_CORS__ORIGINS = https://app.example.com,http://localhost:5173 NOTES_SECURITY__REDIRECT_HTTPS = true Debug, allowed hosts and CORS ¶ These three are off or permissive by default, so an application behaves the same until you set them. debug ¶ With debug on, the 500 internal_error answer for an unhandled exception also carries a debug object: { "error" : "internal_error" , "request_id" : "5f0c…" , "debug" : { "exception" : "builtins.RuntimeError" , "message" : "the cache is cold" , "traceback" : [ "Traceback (most recent call last):\n" , "…" ] } } Declared errors, validation errors and the other framework answers are unchanged, and the exception is logged either way. Exception messages can contain data you would not publish, so keep debug off in a deployment; each worker logs a warning at startup while it is on. debug changes nothing else: it does not enable documentation pages, relax authentication or skip the host check, and hinoki dev does not set it. allowed_hosts ¶ The Host header of every request must match one entry: Entry Matches * (the default) Any host; nothing is checked api.example.com That host, on any port .example.org example.org and every subdomain 127.0.0.1 , ::1 That address ( [::1]:8000 in the header) Matching ignores case, the port and a trailing dot. The header must be exactly one host with an optional port; a request for another host, with two Host headers or without a usable one, receives 400 disallowed_host before routing, authentication and body reading; documentation routes are covered too. Entries are names: a scheme, port, path, non-ASCII text (write an international name in its ASCII IDNA form, xn--... ) or a partial wildcard such as *.example.com fails at load, and * cannot be mixed with other entries. A dot entry is as wide as it reads: .com allows every .com host. Set the list in a deployment that is reachable under more names than it should answer to. While allowed_hosts is * and debug is off, each worker logs a warning at startup (logger hinoki.runtime , shown with the default logging settings): every Host header is accepted, so links, redirects and cache keys built from it, such as a password-reset link, can name a host the client chose (Host header injection). Name the hosts the deployment serves to silence it, for example allowed_hosts=("app.example.com",) , or (".example.com",) for a domain and its subdomains ( NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS=app.example.com ). It is a warning, not an error, so the default keeps working in development; with debug on it is not logged, and the in-process test clients ( ASGIClient , SyncClient ) and the MCP run_scenario tool, which receive no network Host header, do not log it either. The in-process test clients send no Host header, so a test of an application with a restrictive list passes one: await client.get("/x", headers={"host": "api.example.com"}) . cors ¶ CORS is off while cors.origins is empty: no header is added and OPTIONS requests receive 405 . With origins configured: A request whose Origin is listed receives access-control-allow-origin with that origin and vary: origin , on every answer including errors, so a browser client can read a 401 or 422 body. credentials = true adds access-control-allow-credentials: true ; expose_headers is sent as access-control-expose-headers . A request from any other origin, or without an Origin , is served normally without the permission headers and still carries vary: origin , so a shared cache never hands one origin's answer to another; the browser refuses to hand the response to the page. CORS tells browsers what to allow. It is not authentication and does not stop a non-browser client. A preflight ( OPTIONS with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method ) is answered with 204 , the configured methods , headers and max_age , without reaching a route or its access policy. A preflight from an origin that is not listed receives 403 cors_origin_denied . Origins are compared exactly, in lower case as browsers send them: https://app.example.com and https://app.example.com:8443 are different origins, and a trailing slash or path is refused at load. Browsers leave a default port out of Origin , so list https://app.example.com , not https://app.example.com:443 . The single entry * answers every origin with access-control-allow-origin: * ; it cannot be combined with credentials , and browsers will not send cookies or HTTP authentication to it. The policy applies to the whole application, including the ASGI and WSGI adapters; there is no per-route CORS option. An answer that already sets access-control-allow-origin itself (a Response with that header) is sent as it is, without the policy's headers. Security headers and HTTPS ¶ Every HTTP response gets X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff , the configured X-Frame-Options and Referrer-Policy , including errors, OpenAPI/docs and admin responses. Defaults are SAMEORIGIN and same-origin , preserving the admin's existing referrer privacy default. These fields are owned by the app security policy: configured values replace same-named headers returned by a route. The choices are enums rather than arbitrary strings, and environment/TOML values must match the listed wire values exactly. FrameOptions provides deny and sameorigin . ReferrerPolicy provides no-referrer , no-referrer-when-downgrade , same-origin , origin , strict-origin , origin-when-cross-origin , strict-origin-when-cross-origin and unsafe-url . unsafe-url can disclose the full referring URL to another origin; use it only when that is intended. # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): security : settings . SecuritySettings = settings . SecuritySettings ( redirect_https = True , hsts_seconds = 31_536_000 , hsts_include_subdomains = True , frame_options = settings . FrameOptions . DENY , referrer_policy = settings . ReferrerPolicy . STRICT_ORIGIN , ) For configuration loaded from the environment, set NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS=api.example.com and NOTES_SECURITY__REDIRECT_HTTPS=true . A wildcard host policy cannot be combined with the redirect: Hinoki requires an explicit host allowlist before constructing an absolute Location , which avoids redirecting an attacker supplied Host value. The redirect is 308 , preserves the method and raw path/query, and runs before route lookup, authentication and body reading. A configured CORS preflight is answered before redirecting so browser preflight requests remain usable. HSTS defaults off. Hinoki emits it only when the request's effective scheme is HTTPS. Behind TLS termination, configure the exact proxy addresses in server.trusted_proxies ; an untrusted X-Forwarded-Proto does not enable HSTS or suppress the redirect. hsts_preload also requires hsts_include_subdomains and a max-age of at least one year. Use HSTS only after confirming that HTTPS is available for every covered host: browsers retain the policy after the response. Reverse proxies and request IDs ¶ Forwarded metadata is ignored unless the immediate socket peer matches server.trusted_proxies . Configure only the addresses or CIDRs of proxies that remove client-supplied forwarding headers and write their own values. For example: # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): # The private address used by this deployment's ingress, not every private network. server : settings . ServerSettings = settings . ServerSettings ( trusted_proxies = ( "10.20.0.0/16" ,), request_id_header = "x-correlation-id" , trust_request_id = True , ) From a trusted peer, Hinoki accepts a single X-Forwarded-Proto value of http or https and walks a bounded X-Forwarded-For chain from the peer side to the first untrusted address. Request.scheme and Request.client use those validated values. Invalid, repeated or ambiguous values fall back to the socket scope. X-Forwarded-Host is never used: Host , allowed_hosts and generated URLs continue to use the original Host header. On a listener bound to :: , an IPv4 peer can appear as ::ffff:a.b.c.d , which a plain IPv4 entry does not match (the proxy is then untrusted); see behind a reverse proxy . Request IDs are generated by default. With trust_request_id=True , one inbound configured header is accepted only from a trusted immediate peer and only when it is 1–128 visible ASCII characters without commas or controls. Otherwise Hinoki generates a new ID. The selected value appears in Request.request_id , built-in error JSON and the configured response header. The proxy must sanitize the incoming header before forwarding it; do not trust a broad network range merely because it is private. Set logging.include_request_id=true to add the resolved ID to Hinoki's own log records while a request is being handled. Text logs append request_id=<id> and JSON logs include a request_id field. The ID matches the response's configured request ID header. Startup and other records outside a request omit the field. This setting is off by default, and it does not change application or third-party logger handlers. Errors and edge cases ¶ An invalid allowed_hosts entry, a * mixed with names, or a CORS origin with a path fails when settings load, before any worker starts. redirect_https=True with allowed_hosts left at * is refused at load: the redirect needs a host it can trust. A request for an unlisted host receives 400 disallowed_host ; a preflight from an unlisted origin receives 403 cors_origin_denied . Tests with a restrictive host list pass the header: await client.get("/health", headers={"host": "api.example.com"}) . See also ¶ Settings : how values are loaded, named and inspected. Kiso server : addresses behind a proxy on Kiso. Errors : the JSON bodies of these answers.

ServerSettings ( trusted_proxies = ( "10.20.0.0/16" ,), request_id_header = "x-correlation-id" , trust_request_id = True , ) From a trusted peer, Hinoki accepts a single X-Forwarded-Proto value of http or https and walks a bounded X-Forwarded-For chain from the peer side to the first untrusted address. Request.scheme and Request.client use those validated values. Invalid, repeated or ambiguous values fall back to the socket scope. X-Forwarded-Host is never used: Host , allowed_hosts and generated URLs continue to use the original Host header. On a listener bound to :: , an IPv4 peer can appear as ::ffff:a.b.c.d , which a plain IPv4 entry does not match (the proxy is then untrusted); see behind a reverse proxy . Request IDs are generated by default. With trust_request_id=True , one inbound configured header is accepted only from a trusted immediate peer and only when it is 1–128 visible ASCII characters without commas or controls. Otherwise Hinoki generates a new ID. The selected value appears in Request.request_id , built-in error JSON and the configured response header. The proxy must sanitize the incoming header before forwarding it; do not trust a broad network range merely because it is private. Set logging.include_request_id=true to add the resolved ID to Hinoki's own log records while a request is being handled. Text logs append request_id=<id> and JSON logs include a request_id field. The ID matches the response's configured request ID header. Startup and other records outside a request omit the field. This setting is off by default, and it does not change application or third-party logger handlers.
docs.title: Reverse proxies and request IDs

docs.text: An invalid allowed_hosts entry, a * mixed with names, or a CORS origin with a path fails when settings load, before any worker starts. redirect_https=True with allowed_hosts left at * is refused at load: the redirect needs a host it can trust. A request for an unlisted host receives 400 disallowed_host ; a preflight from an unlisted origin receives 403 cors_origin_denied . Tests with a restrictive host list pass the header: await client.get("/health", headers={"host": "api.example.com"}) .

docs.text: Auth and crypto ¶ JWTAuth delegates signature and registered-claim verification to the Rust core. Its current key and policy values are captured for each token verification, while the application-defined resolve_claims hook remains Python and runs for every verified token. hinoki.auth.Caller dataclass ¶ Caller ( id : str , user : T , permissions : Iterable [ str ] = ()) Who is making the request, as decided by authentication. id is a stable string, user is your own object (the user row, a service account) and permissions is what the caller may do:: Caller(id="u1", user=user, permissions=frozenset({"posts:write"})) hinoki.auth.Permission ¶ Bases: StrEnum Base for an application's typed permission names. Subclass it with the permissions your application uses:: class BlogPermission(Permission): WRITE = "posts:write" Members compare and serialize as their string values. hinoki.auth.Credentials dataclass ¶ Credentials ( headers : dict [ str , str ], query : dict [ str , list [ str ]] ) The parts of a request a provider may inspect. hinoki.auth.BaseAuth ¶ Bases: ABC Base class of providers. authenticate returns a principal, None when the request carries no credentials, and raises Unauthorized when credentials are present but invalid. Providers hold no per-request state. openapi_scheme ¶ openapi_scheme () -> dict [ str , object ] | None OpenAPI security scheme describing this provider, if it has one. authenticate abstractmethod ¶ authenticate ( credentials : Credentials , ) -> Caller [ T ] | Awaitable [ Caller [ T ] | None ] | None async def or plain def (a plain one runs on the sync executor). hinoki.auth.HeaderAuth ¶ Bases: BaseAuth [ T ] Credential carried in a named header; subclasses implement resolve . resolve abstractmethod ¶ resolve ( value : str , ) -> Caller [ T ] | Awaitable [ Caller [ T ] | None ] | None The principal for a header value or None if invalid; async def or plain def . hinoki.auth.BearerAuth ¶ Bases: HeaderAuth [ T ] Authorization: Bearer <token> ; subclasses implement resolve_token . resolve_token abstractmethod ¶ resolve_token ( token : str , ) -> Caller [ T ] | Awaitable [ Caller [ T ] | None ] | None async def or plain def , as resolve . hinoki.auth.APIKeyAuth ¶ Bases: HeaderAuth [ T ] API key in x-api-key (override header to change it). hinoki.crypto.JWTKey dataclass ¶ JWTKey ( kid : str | None , algorithm : str , key : bytes | str , public : bool = False , ) One verification (and optionally signing) key. HMAC secrets must be at least as long as the hash (32/48/64 bytes). For EdDSA the key is the 32-byte private seed, or with public=True the 32-byte public key of a verify-only deployment. kid is required when several keys are configured. The key is excluded from repr . verify_only classmethod ¶ verify_only ( kid : str | None , public_key : bytes ) -> JWTKey An Ed25519 public key (32 bytes) that can verify but never sign. Use this, not the plain constructor, wherever you hold only the public key: a public key passed as a seed would let anyone who knows it forge tokens. hinoki.crypto.JWTAuth ¶ JWTAuth () Bases: BearerAuth [ T ] Bearer-token provider for JWTs. Subclass, set keys (and usually issuer and audience ) and implement resolve_claims :: class Tokens(JWTAuth[User]): keys = [JWTKey("2026-11", "HS256", settings.jwt_secret)] issuer = "https://api.example.com" audience = "blog" async def resolve_claims(self, claims): subject, raw = claims.get("sub"), claims.get("scopes", []) if not isinstance(subject, str) or not isinstance(raw, list): return None # claims are signed, but still untyped JSON try: user = await User.aget_or_none(id=UUID(subject)) except ValueError: # a signed token can still carry any text return None if user is None: return None scopes = frozenset(s for s in raw if isinstance(s, str)) return Caller(subject, user, scopes) now ¶ now () -> int The clock (override in tests). resolve_claims abstractmethod ¶ resolve_claims ( claims : dict [ str , Any ], ) -> Caller [ T ] | Awaitable [ Caller [ T ] | None ] | None The principal for verified claims, or None to refuse; async def or plain def . issue ¶ issue ( claims : dict [ str , Any ], ttl : int = 900 ) -> str A signed token for claims valid for ttl seconds, signed with the first non-public key. iat and exp are always set by the server (a value in claims is replaced); iss and aud are added when configured, unless claims already has them. hinoki.crypto.ClaimsJWTAuth ¶ ClaimsJWTAuth () Bases: JWTAuth [None] A JWT provider whose caller comes from the signed claims alone. Subclass it and set keys (and usually issuer and audience ):: class Tokens(ClaimsJWTAuth): keys = [JWTKey("2026-11", "HS256", settings.jwt_secret)] Caller.id is the non-empty string claim sub , Caller.user is None and Caller.permissions are the strings in the list claim named by scope_claim (none when it is absent). A token without a usable sub , or whose scope claim is not a list, is refused. Nothing is loaded from a database, so a token stays valid until it expires; use JWTAuth when a revoked or deleted account must be refused immediately. Because it runs no application code, the Rust server can authenticate generated CRUD routes that use it without entering Python. Overriding any method keeps the routes on the Python request pipeline. hinoki.crypto.PasswordHasher ¶ PasswordHasher ( * , memory_kib : int = MIN_MEMORY_KIB , time_cost : int = MIN_TIME_COST , lanes : int = 1 , workers : int = 2 , max_pending : int = 64 , allow_weak : bool = False , ) Argon2id hashes in PHC format, computed off the event loop. Parameters below the OWASP floor are refused unless allow_weak=True (tests only). workers bounds concurrent hashing, max_pending the queue; beyond that hash / verify raise HashingBusy (503). A task cancelled while its hash runs frees its slot but the thread finishes, so at most workers extra hashes can be in flight; hash_sync / verify_sync are not bounded. Only argon2id hashes are verified. For unknown users, verify against a fixed dummy hash so timing does not reveal who exists. hash_sync ¶ hash_sync ( password : str ) -> str Blocking hash (for scripts and sync handlers). verify_sync ¶ verify_sync ( password : str , stored : str ) -> bool False for a wrong password; ValueError for a malformed hash. needs_rehash ¶ needs_rehash ( stored : str ) -> bool True when stored was made with other parameters than these. hinoki.crypto.random_token ¶ random_token ( size : int = 32 ) -> str size random bytes (1 to 1024) as URL-safe text, from the OS CSPRNG.

docs.text: Parsers and renderers ¶ hinoki.parsers.Parser ¶ Base class of body parsers. hinoki.parsers.JSONParser ¶ Bases: Parser JSON, decoded by the Rust parser (strict: no NaN, no lone surrogates, depth limit). Customise by overriding prepare(data) to reshape the decoded value (for example rename keys) or media_type ( application/vnd.api+json ). prepare ¶ prepare ( data : object ) -> object Hook: the value the action sees (default: as decoded). hinoki.parsers.FormParser ¶ FormParser ( max_fields : int = DEFAULT_FIELDS ) Bases: Parser application/x-www-form-urlencoded . data holds the last value of each field as text. hinoki.parsers.MultiPartParser ¶ MultiPartParser ( max_parts : int = DEFAULT_PARTS , max_part_bytes : int = DEFAULT_PART_BYTES , ) Bases: Parser multipart/form-data with at most max_parts parts of at most max_part_bytes bytes each (the whole body is capped separately). Selected automatically, with the default limits, for an action that binds an UploadedFile without choosing its parsers; pass it explicitly to change the limits. hinoki.parsers.TextParser ¶ Bases: Parser text/plain bodies as a str (UTF-8, strict). hinoki.parsers.BytesParser ¶ Bases: Parser application/octet-stream bodies as the raw bytes , unchanged. hinoki.parsers.XMLParser ¶ XMLParser ( max_depth : int = DEFAULT_XML_DEPTH , max_elements : int = DEFAULT_XML_ELEMENTS , ) Bases: Parser application/xml . data is the tree under the root element: an element with children is a dict , a repeated child name a list , a text-only element a str and an empty one None . Attributes are not read. DTDs, custom entities, characters XML 1.0 forbids and an encoding other than UTF-8 are refused, and nesting (at most MAX_XML_DEPTH ) and element count are capped. hinoki.parsers.Parsed dataclass ¶ Parsed ( data : object , fields : Mapping [ str , list [ str ]] = dict (), files : Mapping [ str , list [ UploadedFile ]] = dict (), ) What a parser produced: data for request.data plus form fields and files for request.POST / request.FILES . hinoki.errors.InvalidBody ¶ InvalidBody ( code : str , message : str ) Bases: Exception The request body cannot be used at all (wrong media type, bad JSON). hinoki.UploadedFile dataclass ¶ UploadedFile ( name : str , filename : str , content_type : str , content : bytes , ) A multipart file. filename is exactly what the client sent: never use it as a path. hinoki.renderers.Renderer ¶ Base class of response renderers. hinoki.renderers.JSONRenderer ¶ JSONRenderer ( indent : int | None = None , sort_keys : bool = False , default : Callable [[ Any ], Any ] | None = None , ) Bases: Renderer JSON, written by the Rust encoder. Customise without leaving Rust: options: JSONRenderer(indent=2, sort_keys=True, default=fn) where default turns a value that is not JSON (a Decimal , a Path ) into one that is; a subclass overriding prepare(value, request) to reshape the result (envelopes, key renaming) before it is encoded, and/or media_type (for application/vnd.api+json ). prepare ¶ prepare ( value : object , request : Request ) -> object Hook: the value to encode (default: unchanged). hinoki.renderers.HTMLRenderer ¶ Bases: Renderer A handler that returns str answers HTML (UTF-8). The string is sent as is: escape untrusted data before putting it in. hinoki.renderers.TextRenderer ¶ Bases: Renderer A handler that returns str answers plain text (UTF-8). hinoki.renderers.XMLRenderer ¶ XMLRenderer ( root : str = 'response' , item : str = 'item' ) Bases: Renderer The JSON-compatible result as XML (UTF-8, with an XML declaration). A mapping becomes child elements named by its keys, a list becomes repeated item elements, None an empty element, and true / false are written in lower case. Keys are spelled as JSON spells them ( None as null , booleans true / false , integers in decimal) and any other key is refused, as JSON refuses it. A key that is not a valid XML name (it has a space, starts with a digit, begins with xml ) is written as <item key="..."> instead of failing. Characters XML 1.0 cannot carry are replaced by U+FFFD. XMLRenderer(root="orders", item="order") renames the root element and the list item.

docs.text: Database API ¶ For setup, application settings, URL examples and migration workflow, see configure a database . The ORM supports PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB. SQLite is the local-development default; configure an explicit URL to select a server backend. Raw SQL uses the selected driver's placeholders: PostgreSQL uses $1 , while SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB use ? . ORM-generated queries select the dialect automatically. Configure a backend ¶ Database URLs are secrets, so configure them through the environment rather than TOML. For local development, leave the URL unset to use the default SQLite file. The migration commands read the application's database setting too; HINOKI_DATABASE_URL overrides it for them ( which database ). TOML may configure non-secret pool options, for example: [database] max_size = 8 For PostgreSQL, use a driver URL such as postgresql://user:password@host/db . For MySQL, use mysql://user:password@host/db . MySQL connections require TLS by default; the driver verifies the server certificate and hostname. Configure the system trust store to trust your server certificate. require_ssl=false is only suitable for isolated local testing and disables transport encryption. Do not put production credentials in source-controlled settings files. For MariaDB, use mariadb://user:password@host/db ; it is selected and tested as a distinct backend even though it uses the MySQL wire driver and SQL dialect. Backend behavior and limits ¶ Backend Status Notes SQLite Supported Default for local development. SQLite permits one writer at a time. Schema changes that SQLite cannot express directly use a table rebuild. PostgreSQL Supported Uses PostgreSQL-native UUID, timestamp, JSON and byte types. MySQL Supported Uses InnoDB tables, binary UUIDs and MySQL-native JSON. MySQL DDL implicitly commits, so a failed migration can leave earlier DDL applied; inspect migration status and database schema before retrying. RETURNING is not supported by the compiler; ORM create/update operations use follow-up reads. TLS is required by default. MariaDB Supported Tested independently on MariaDB 11.4. Its JSON alias is text, so typed ORM dict / list fields are decoded from the model declaration. Low-level Database.fetch() returns JSON values as bytes because arbitrary text columns cannot be safely inferred as JSON. DDL can implicitly commit; TLS is required by default. SQL Server and Oracle are not currently supported. Do not assume that MySQL compatibility implies MariaDB compatibility. Hinoki does not silently roll back MySQL-family DDL: review generated migrations and keep a recoverable backup before applying schema changes. Datetime values stored in MySQL DATETIME columns use Hinoki's UTC-naive storage convention; values returned by the ORM are interpreted as UTC. MySQL pool capacity and acquisition wait are bounded by the database pool settings. Raw SQL must use the placeholders for the configured backend. Prefer ORM query methods when the same code should work across backends; raw SQL and migration operations may need backend-specific SQL. hinoki.db.Database ¶ Database ( engine : Database ) A connection pool for one configured database backend. engine instance-attribute ¶ engine = engine dialect property ¶ dialect : str The selected dialect: postgres , sqlite , mysql or mariadb . connect async classmethod ¶ connect ( url : str , * , max_size : int = 10 , wait : float = 5.0 ) -> Database Open the pool and check the server; PostgreSQL URLs may configure TLS. active ¶ active () -> ActiveTransaction | None fetch async ¶ fetch ( sql : str , * params : Param ) -> list [ Row ] Rows as dicts, with placeholders selected by the active backend. fetch_models async ¶ fetch_models ( sql : str , params : list [ Any ], plan : _ModelRows ) -> list [ Any ] Rows built into finished model instances (private; QuerySet.fetch ). fetch_one async ¶ fetch_one ( sql : str , * params : Param ) -> Row | None execute async ¶ execute ( sql : str , * params : Param ) -> int Number of affected rows; raw SQL placeholders follow the backend. atomic ¶ atomic () -> AtomicScope async with database.atomic(): — commit on success, roll back on any exception; inside an open scope of the same task, a savepoint. after_commit ¶ after_commit ( callback : Callable [[], object ]) -> None Run callback (sync or async) after the outermost transaction commits, in registration order. A rollback, of the transaction or of the savepoint scope it was registered in, drops it; an exception in a callback is logged and does not undo the commit. migration ¶ migration () -> AtomicScope An exclusive migration transaction with backend locking semantics. close ¶ close () -> None status ¶ status () -> tuple [ int , int ] (connections, idle) in the pool. hinoki.db.atomic ¶ atomic ( func : Callable [ P , Coroutine [ Any , Any , R ]], ) -> Callable [ P , Coroutine [ Any , Any , R ]] atomic ( func : Callable [ P , R ]) -> Callable [ P , R ] atomic () -> Atomic atomic ( func : Callable [ ... , Any ] | None = None ) -> Any async with db.atomic(): , with db.atomic(): , @db.atomic or @db.atomic() : run a block or a function, async def or plain def , atomically on the current database. The sync forms are for sync handlers. hinoki.db.Atomic ¶ db.atomic() : an atomic scope on the current database, as a block or as a decorator. async with db.atomic(): opens current_database().atomic() when the block is entered; with db.atomic(): does the same in a sync handler. Decorating an async def or a plain def opens a fresh scope for every call: returning commits, an exception rolls back, and a call made inside an already atomic scope becomes a savepoint. leave ¶ leave () -> AtomicScope Pop this task's innermost open scope. hinoki.db.DatabaseModule ¶ DatabaseModule ( url : str , * , max_size : int = 10 , wait : float = 5.0 ) Bases: Module Opens a Database for the worker and provides it to other modules. app.install(DatabaseModule(url)) ; actions with atomic=True and other modules obtain it with ctx.get(Database) . The pool is created in the worker's lifespan and closed when it ends. name class-attribute instance-attribute ¶ name = 'database' url instance-attribute ¶ url = url max_size instance-attribute ¶ max_size = max_size wait instance-attribute ¶ wait = wait from_settings classmethod ¶ from_settings ( settings : object ) -> DatabaseModule The module for settings.database (a DatabaseSettings : url and max_size), so Hinoki(settings=..., modules=[DatabaseModule]) works. lifespan async ¶ lifespan ( ctx : ModuleContext ) -> AsyncIterator [ None ] hinoki.db.DatabaseError ¶ Bases: builtins.Exception hinoki.db.UniqueViolation ¶ Bases: hinoki.core.DatabaseError hinoki.db.ForeignKeyViolation ¶ Bases: hinoki.core.DatabaseError hinoki.db.NotNullViolation ¶ Bases: hinoki.core.DatabaseError hinoki.db.CheckViolation ¶ Bases: hinoki.core.DatabaseError

docs.text: For setup, application settings, URL examples and migration workflow, see configure a database . The ORM supports PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB. SQLite is the local-development default; configure an explicit URL to select a server backend. Raw SQL uses the selected driver's placeholders: PostgreSQL uses $1 , while SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB use ? . ORM-generated queries select the dialect automatically.
docs.title: Database API

docs.text: Database URLs are secrets, so configure them through the environment rather than TOML. For local development, leave the URL unset to use the default SQLite file. The migration commands read the application's database setting too; HINOKI_DATABASE_URL overrides it for them ( which database ). TOML may configure non-secret pool options, for example: [database] max_size = 8 For PostgreSQL, use a driver URL such as postgresql://user:password@host/db . For MySQL, use mysql://user:password@host/db . MySQL connections require TLS by default; the driver verifies the server certificate and hostname. Configure the system trust store to trust your server certificate. require_ssl=false is only suitable for isolated local testing and disables transport encryption. Do not put production credentials in source-controlled settings files. For MariaDB, use mariadb://user:password@host/db ; it is selected and tested as a distinct backend even though it uses the MySQL wire driver and SQL dialect.
